d: Two ways to write a graph down. The matrix suits the algebra behind every spectral ranking; compressed lists are how a real web graph fits in memory.
a: Adjacency matrix Adjacency list CSR Compressed sparse row
x: A graph needs a concrete representation before a program can rank it. The adjacency matrix writes it as a table of zeros and ones, which makes linear algebra available: PageRank , Eigenvector centrality , Katz centrality and HITS (hubs and authorities) are all statements about this matrix. The adjacency list stores, for each node, only the nodes it links to, which is the only form that fits a web graph in memory. Every serious implementation thinks in matrices and computes with lists. The adjacency matrix Number the nodes to . The adjacency matrix is the matrix with Row lists ’s out-links and column lists ’s in-links. For the running example, with rows and columns in the order A to G: The last two rows are empty because F and G link nowhere; the fifth column is empty because nothing links to E. What the algebra buys Matrix products answer graph questions directly: Degrees. With the all-ones vector, gives every out-degree and every in-degree (see Degree ). Walks. counts the walks of exactly steps from to . In the example, : E reaches A through D and through C. Katz centrality sums these counts over all with decaying weights. Transition probabilities. Divide each non-empty row by its sum to get the matrix with for each link. Row of is the probability distribution of a random walk that leaves along a random out-link. PageRank is the long-run distribution of a walk on a repaired version of . Spectral rankings. Eigenvector centrality is the dominant eigenvector of , and HITS (hubs and authorities) uses the dominant eigenvectors of and . Why nobody stores the matrix A dense matrix needs entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph, , so even one bit per entry takes bits, about 1.8 petabytes. Yet only 2,450,405,793 entries are ones: 0.000017% of the matrix. Web graphs are extremely sparse , with an average of 20 links per node however large grows. Storage must scale with the number of arcs , not with . Adjacency lists and CSR An adjacency list stores each node’s out-neighbours. The compact way to do this is compressed sparse row (CSR): one array holding every node’s successors back to back, sorted by source, and an offsets array marking where each node’s run begins. For the running example (A = 0, …, G = 6): offsets: 0 2 3 5 7 10 10 10 node u's successors are targets[offsets[u] .. offsets[u+1]) targets: 1 2 | 2 | 0 6 | 0 2 | 2 3 5 Node E (index 4) owns targets[7..10) = 2, 3, 5, that is C, D and F. F and G own empty runs, so their offsets repeat. The costs are easy to state: Structure Size At Common Crawl’s scale Offsets, 32-bit bytes 479 MB Targets, 32-bit bytes 9.8 GB Same again for in-links (the transpose) 10.3 GB The offsets fit in 32 bits only because 2.45 billion arcs is below ; a page-level graph with tens of billions of arcs needs 64-bit offsets. CSR makes the inner loop of PageRank a straight scan. A “pull” iteration walks each node’s in-links in the transposed graph and sums contributions, reading the targets array once from start to end. Sequential reads of the arc array cost little; the random reads of score vectors cost the most (see PageRank at scale ). Compressed lists Sorted successor lists have structure that CSR ignores. Neighbouring nodes in a well-chosen order link to similar targets, and consecutive targets differ by small gaps. The WebGraph framework exploits both and stores Common Crawl’s domain graph in 15.1 bits per arc, 4.6 GB instead of 9.8 GB for the targets alone, while still decoding a node’s successors quickly. How well this works depends on the order of the nodes; see Node orderings . The transpose Many measures look at in-links: Harmonic centrality needs distances to a node, and pull-style PageRank sums over in-links. Both use the transposed graph , which reverses every arc. Common Crawl ships its graph in both directions for this reason: domain.graph holds out-links and domain-t.graph holds in-links, 4.6 GB each. References Saad, Y. (2003). Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems (2nd ed.). SIAM, section 3.4 on sparse storage formats. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004). The WebGraph Framework I: Compression techniques. WWW 2004 , 595–602.

d: The clickable words of a link. Search engines have used them since 1998 to learn what the target is about, which made them a prime target for manipulation and makes them the quickest way to read a domain's past.
a: Anchor Link text Exact-match anchor Google bomb
x: The anchor text of a link is its visible, clickable text: in <a href="https://example.com/">best hiking boots</a> , the words “best hiking boots”. It is written by the person linking, not by the owner of the target, so it is a description of the target page from the outside. Search engines learned early that such descriptions are often more accurate than a page’s own text. A link graph, which keeps only who links to whom, throws anchor text away, but most link-based ranking systems use it alongside the graph. Anchors as descriptions Brin and Page’s 1998 Google paper treated anchor text specially, associating the words of each link with the page it points to as well as the page it appears on. They gave two reasons. Anchors often describe a page better than the page itself, and they make it possible to return pages that were never crawled, as well as images, programs and other content with no indexable text. Oliver McBryan’s World Wide Web Worm had indexed anchor text as early as 1994. A query for a company name can thus return the company’s home page even if the name appears only in an image on it, because thousands of other sites link to it with that name. Kinds of anchors Link analysts classify anchors roughly as: Type Example for hikingboots.example Branded “Hiking Boots Example” Naked URL “hikingboots.example” Exact match “hiking boots” Partial match “these lightweight hiking boots” Generic “click here”, “this site”, “read more” Image the alt text of a linked image A site that earns links naturally tends to get mostly branded, naked-URL and generic anchors: people link to things by their names. Exact-match anchors in large numbers usually mean someone chose the words, which in practice means the links were placed by the site’s owner or bought. Manipulation and response Because anchors influenced rankings, they were manipulated: Google bombs. Coordinated groups linked to a target with the same phrase until the target ranked for it, regardless of its content. The best-known case made a politician’s biography the top result for “miserable failure” in the mid-2000s. Google changed its algorithm in January 2007 to defuse most such bombs. Exact-match link building. SEO campaigns bought or placed links with commercial keyword anchors. Google’s Penguin update in 2012 targeted exactly this pattern of over-optimised anchors, and its spam policies still list links with optimised anchor text in articles or press releases as link schemes (see Link penalties and the disavow tool ). What the graph loses Common Crawl’s domain graph, like any link graph, records only that one domain links to another. The anchor text survives in Common Crawl’s WAT metadata files, from which the graph is built, but not in the graph itself. Commercial link indexes keep anchors and report a domain’s anchor text distribution : the share of its referring links using each phrase. Reading a domain’s anchors For a domain buyer, anchor text is the fastest way to learn what a domain used to be: Topic and language. Anchors reveal what the old site was about and in which language. A domain whose anchors are in Japanese and about car parts was not a hiking blog, whatever the name suggests. Spam history. Anchors for casino, pharmacy, replica goods or loan keywords on an unrelated domain usually mean it was used for link spam, or that its old site was hacked. Such links may already be discounted, and they can attract penalties if redirected to a new site (see Expired domains ). Manufactured profiles. A high share of exact-match commercial anchors suggests bought links. Branded and generic anchors from varied sites suggest natural ones. Repurposing risk. Google’s spam policy on expired domain abuse targets domains bought for their old reputation and filled with unrelated low-value content. Anchors that describe a very different topic from the planned use are a warning sign. References Brin, S., & Page, L. (1998). The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine. Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30(1–7), 107–117. McBryan, O. A. (1994). GENVL and WWWW: Tools for taming the Web. Proceedings of the First International World Wide Web Conference . Eiron, N., & McCurley, K. S. (2003). Analysis of anchor text for web search. SIGIR 2003 . Google Search Central. Spam policies for Google web search (link spam). developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies.

d: Semrush's compound 100-point score combining link power, estimated organic traffic and spam signals. Designed to resist manipulation, and in the 2026-09-23 auction data almost constant.
a: AS Semrush AS Semrush Authority Score
x: Authority Score (AS) is Semrush’s measure of a domain’s overall quality, on a 100-point scale. Unlike scores built on links alone, it is a compound metric: Semrush describes three ingredients, link power, organic traffic and spam signals, and says the current version, introduced in early 2023, was redesigned to be harder to manipulate. For domain buyers it is one of the columns that GoDaddy’s auction inventory includes, which lets this encyclopedia check how it behaves on real listings. What goes into it Semrush’s knowledge base describes Authority Score as “a compound metric that grades the overall quality of a website or a webpage,” built from: Link Power: the quality and quantity of backlinks, the heaviest-weighted part. Organic Traffic: Semrush’s estimate of the domain’s monthly search traffic, the next heaviest. Spam Factors (also called Natural Profile ): signs of manipulation, such as an unnaturally high share of dofollow links, an imbalance between links and traffic, many referring domains sharing IP addresses, or domains with near-identical backlink profiles. Semrush says the score is recalculated regularly, and it does not publish the weights or the formula. The design reflects lessons from Link spam : a domain whose links are plentiful but whose traffic is negligible, or whose referring domains look like a network, should not score as highly as its link count alone suggests. In this encyclopedia’s terms, it combines a PageRank -like link signal with a usage signal and a Spam mass -like penalty. What the auction data shows GoDaddy’s inventory for 2026-09-23 lists an Authority Score for each of its 1,068,241 domains. Its distribution is extraordinarily narrow: Authority Score Domains Share 2 936,908 87.7% 0 99,799 9.3% any other value 31,534 3.0% Splitting the domains by how many referring domains they have in Common Crawl’s graph barely moves the median: it is 2 for domains Common Crawl never saw linked and still 2 for the 676 domains with more than 100 Common Crawl referring domains. Only the upper tail responds: the 90th percentile rises from 2 to 6 and the 99th from 6 to 27 between those groups. Across the 119,453 listed domains present in Common Crawl’s graph, the Spearman correlation between Authority Score and Common Crawl in-degree is 0.16. For filtering an auction list, the column is close to constant: nine domains in ten share the same value. That is plausible for a metric that discounts links unaccompanied by traffic, since most expiring domains have little of either, but it means the score carries almost no information for ranking such a list. The same feed’s “Indexed Pages” column matches its Semrush backlink count to within 2% on 95.9% of rows (Spearman correlation 0.999), so it duplicates the backlink count rather than adding a separate signal (see Auditing vendor metrics ). These numbers describe Semrush’s values as delivered in GoDaddy’s feed on one day; Semrush’s own tools may show different or more current values. Reading AS for a domain Treat it as a filter for the top, not a ranking for the bulk. Differences among low scores mean little; a high score on an expiring domain is rare and worth investigating. Remember the traffic component. A parked or expired domain has lost its traffic, so its AS reflects that, whatever links remain. A low AS on an expired domain does not mean its links are worthless. Look at the referring domains. Semrush’s referring-domain counts for auction domains include a floor of roughly a hundred domains that link to nearly every listed domain; check whether the domain has links beyond that floor. Cross-check with Domain Rating (Ahrefs) , Domain Authority (Moz) , Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) and Common Crawl’s open centralities (see Reading a domain’s link metrics ). References Semrush Knowledge Base. Authority Score. semrush.com/kb/747-authority-score. Semrush Blog (2023). How Semrush’s new Authority Score works, early 2023.

d: A backlink is a link from someone else's page to yours; referring domains count the distinct sites those links come from. Both are in-degree at different granularities, and both depend entirely on whose crawl counted them.
a: Backlink Inbound link Inlink Referring domain Ref domains Linking root domains
x: In SEO vocabulary, a backlink is a hyperlink on another site’s page that points to your site. A referring domain is a distinct domain that hosts at least one such link. In the language of this encyclopedia, backlinks are arcs of the page graph that end on your pages, and referring domains are your in-degree in the domain graph (see Degree and Page, host and domain graphs ). They are the raw material of every link metric, from PageRank to the vendors’ 0–100 scores, and the first numbers anyone checks when evaluating a domain. Backlinks versus referring domains The two counts differ because one site can link to another many times: A sitewide link, in a footer, sidebar or blogroll, appears on every page of the linking site. A 50,000-page site with a footer link contributes 50,000 backlinks and one referring domain. Many links from one domain come from a single decision by one owner. Counting them separately mostly measures the size of the linking site. Referring domains are therefore the better first measure of breadth, and most vendors’ authority scores are built on referring domains rather than raw backlinks. In GoDaddy’s 2026-09-23 auction inventory, Semrush reports a median of 127 backlinks for domains that Common Crawl never saw linked, and 6,186 for domains with more than 100 referring domains in Common Crawl’s graph, against medians of 96 and 775 referring domains. What a link index records Every count comes from a particular crawl, and crawls differ: Coverage. No index crawls the whole web. Each vendor discovers a different subset of pages, so the same domain gets different counts from different tools, often by a factor of several. Freshness. Links disappear when pages change or vanish. Majestic, for example, separates a Fresh index of links seen in roughly the last 120 days from a Historic index going back to 2006. A count without a time window mixes live links with dead ones. What counts as a link. Indexes differ on whether they count image links, redirects, canonical tags, links in scripts or iframes, and links marked nofollow (see Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) ). Common Crawl’s graph counts every URL a page references, including scripts, fonts and <link> elements, which is why infrastructure domains top its rankings (see The Common Crawl web graph ). Spam handling. Some indexes filter link farms and auto-generated pages; others keep everything. In the 2026-09-23 auction data, the same handful of domains appear among the top three referring domains of most listed domains, inflating every count by a similar amount (see Auditing vendor metrics ). Not all links are equal Two domains with the same number of referring domains can have entirely different link profiles. The things that distinguish a valuable backlink: Who links. A link from a domain that is itself well linked passes more weight. That is the core idea of PageRank , and Harmonic centrality and the vendor scores encode versions of it. How many other links the page carries. PageRank divides a page’s weight among its out-links, so a link on a page with three outbound links is worth more than one on a page with three hundred (see The random surfer ). Placement. Links in the body of an article are more likely to be clicked and, by most accounts, weighted more than footer or sidebar links. Relevance and anchor text. A link from a site about the same topic, with descriptive Anchor text , says more than an unrelated one. Attributes. nofollow , sponsored and ugc mark links that their publisher does not vouch for, and search engines treat them as hints rather than endorsements. Naturalness. A sudden burst of links from unrelated new domains with identical anchors looks manufactured, because it usually is (see Link spam ). Reading the counts for a domain Start with referring domains , not backlinks, and look at the list , not just the count. Recognisable, topically related sites matter more than the total. Check against a second source. Counts from two vendors, or a vendor and Common Crawl, should broadly agree for a genuinely well-linked domain. Large disagreements usually mean one index is counting spam or stale links. Subtract the floor. If a vendor reports a hundred-odd referring domains for nearly every domain in a list, those links carry no information about any particular domain. Look at the history. For an expired domain , links earned by the previous site may point to pages that no longer exist; they can still count, but a redirect strategy decides whether they help (see Redirects and canonicalisation ). References Majestic. Glossary (Fresh and Historic Index, Referring Domains). majestic.com/help/glossary. Ahrefs. What is Domain Rating (DR)? ahrefs.com/blog/domain-rating. Common Crawl. cc-pyspark: wat_extract_links.py (link types extracted for the host graph).

d: A node is central if many shortest paths between other nodes pass through it. Betweenness finds bridges and brokers, not popular destinations.
a: Betweenness Freeman betweenness Brokerage
x: Betweenness centrality scores a node by how often it lies on the shortest paths between other nodes. Linton Freeman defined it in 1977 to capture brokerage: the person through whom information between two groups must pass holds power even if few people know them directly. On a link graph, a high-betweenness node is a bridge that connects regions which would otherwise be far apart. It answers a different question from PageRank or Harmonic centrality , which score destinations. Definition Let be the number of shortest paths from to , and the number of those that pass through . The betweenness of is summed over ordered pairs with reachable from . When several shortest paths tie, each gets an equal share of the credit. On a directed graph, dividing by scales the result to . Worked example On the running example only three nodes lie inside any shortest path: Node C A D B, E, F, G Betweenness 6 3 1 0 C earns 6. It is the only route for A → G, B → A, B → G, D → G and E → G, which gives 5, and it lies on one of the two shortest paths for E → A (E → C → A and E → D → A) and for E → B (E → C → A → B and E → D → A → B), which gives two halves. A earns 3: C → B, D → B and E → B all pass through it. D earns 1 from the other halves of E → A and E → B. E, the hub with three out-links, scores 0: shortest paths start at E but never pass through it, because nothing links to E. What betweenness captures Bridges and bottlenecks. A node joining two otherwise separate communities collects every path between them. Removing it lengthens or breaks those paths. Betweenness is the standard tool for finding single points of failure in networks. Brokers, not stars. A node can have small in-degree and huge betweenness, and a popular node deep inside one community can have little. In the running example, G has in-degree 1 and harmonic centrality 3 but zero betweenness, because no shortest path continues past it. Community structure. The Girvan–Newman algorithm removes the arcs with the highest betweenness, the arcs between communities, one at a time until the graph falls apart into groups (see Community detection ). Axioms In Boldi and Vigna’s tests betweenness satisfies only the half of the size axiom: in a graph made of a clique and a separate long cycle, cycle nodes carry many paths while clique nodes carry none, because every pair of clique nodes is directly linked. It fails density and score monotonicity: a new link to can create shortcuts that bypass and lower its score (see Axioms for centrality ). These are not defects so much as a reminder that betweenness measures brokerage, not prominence. Computing it The naive method counts shortest paths for every pair, or worse. Brandes’ algorithm (2001) computes exact betweenness for all nodes in time on unweighted graphs: one breadth-first search per source, followed by a backward sweep that accumulates each node’s share. That is the algorithm behind every serious implementation, and behind the numbers above. is still out of reach on a web graph. For Common Crawl’s domain graph it means about arc visits. Large-scale betweenness is therefore estimated by sampling: Source sampling (Brandes and Pich, 2007) runs the BFS from a random sample of sources and scales up. A few thousand sources rank the top nodes well. Path sampling (Riondato and Kornaropoulos, 2014) samples random shortest paths and uses VC-dimension bounds to fix the sample size needed for a given additive error, independent of the graph’s size. Neither Common Crawl nor the commercial link indexes publish betweenness for domains. Betweenness on the web On a domain graph, nodes with high betweenness are the connectors between linguistic, national and topical regions: large portals, reference sites, platforms hosting content from many communities, and infrastructure domains that appear in pages everywhere. Betweenness explains network resilience better than it explains importance. A domain can be a crucial bridge and still attract little traffic or trust. For a domain buyer, betweenness rarely matters directly. It becomes useful when mapping a suspected Link spam network: computed on the network’s own subgraph, it shows which few domains hold the network together. Variants Edge betweenness counts shortest paths through each arc instead of each node. It drives Girvan–Newman community detection. Load and flow betweenness spread credit along all paths or along network flows rather than only along shortest paths. Random-walk betweenness (Newman, 2005) counts how often a random walk from to passes through , which suits networks where things do not travel along shortest paths. References Freeman, L. C. (1977). A set of measures of centrality based on betweenness. Sociometry 40(1), 35–41. Brandes, U. (2001). A faster algorithm for betweenness centrality. Journal of Mathematical Sociology 25(2), 163–177. Brandes, U., & Pich, C. (2007). Centrality estimation in large networks. International Journal of Bifurcation and Chaos 17(7), 2303–2318. Riondato, M., & Kornaropoulos, E. M. (2014). Fast approximation of betweenness centrality through sampling. WSDM 2014 , 413–422.

d: Seen from its largest strongly connected component, the web looks like a bow tie. Pages that reach the core sit on one side, pages the core reaches sit on the other, and stragglers hang off both.
a: Bow tie Bowtie model IN component OUT component Tendrils
x: In 1999 a team from AltaVista, IBM and Compaq mapped a crawl of 203 million pages and found that its connectivity had a shape. A giant core of pages all reach each other. An IN set of pages reach the core but cannot be reached from it, and an OUT set can be reached from the core but cannot get back. Drawn with IN on the left and OUT on the right, the picture looks like a bow tie. The model gives names to the parts of any directed graph relative to its largest strongly connected component , and those parts behave very differently under every ranking method. CORE largest SCC IN reaches the core OUT reached from it tube: IN to OUT, bypassing the core tendril tendril disconnected The bow-tie decomposition. Every node belongs to exactly one part, defined by whether it can reach the core, can be reached from it, both, or neither. The parts Let be the largest strongly connected component. Every other node falls into one part: CORE: the nodes of . Every core node reaches every other. IN: nodes that reach but cannot be reached from it. New sites that link to popular sites before anyone links back live here. OUT: nodes reachable from that cannot reach it. Corporate sites that link only internally, and pages the crawler found but did not fetch, live here. TENDRILS: nodes reachable from IN that cannot reach the core, and nodes that reach OUT without being reachable from the core. TUBES: paths from IN to OUT that bypass the core. DISCONNECTED: nodes with no path to or from the core in either direction. In the running example (see The web graph ) the core is {A, B, C}. D and E form IN, since both reach the core and nothing in the core reaches them. G is OUT. F is a tendril: E, in IN, reaches it, but F cannot reach the core. Computing the decomposition The decomposition costs a few linear passes: Find the strongly connected components and pick the largest, (Tarjan’s algorithm, one depth-first search). Run a breadth-first search forward from all of at once. Every node it reaches outside belongs to OUT or to the parts hanging off it. Run a breadth-first search backward, on the transposed graph, from . Every node it reaches outside belongs to IN. Search forward from IN and backward from OUT, skipping the core, to separate tendrils and tubes from the disconnected remainder. Each search costs , so the whole decomposition is linear in the size of the graph (see Paths, distance and reachability ). How big are the parts? The proportions depend heavily on the crawl: Part Broder et al., 1999 crawl Meusel et al., Common Crawl 2012 Pages 203 million 3.5 billion CORE 27.7% 51.3% IN 21.3% 32.0% OUT 21.2% 6.1% Everything else (tendrils, tubes, disconnected) 29.7% 10.7% Broder’s crawl gave four parts of nearly equal size, a striking symmetry that became textbook material. Thirteen years later, Meusel, Vigna, Lehmberg and Bizer found a core twice as large and a tiny OUT set in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. They argued that the proportions depend largely on how a crawl is gathered, so they describe the crawler as much as the web. The shape recurs; the sizes do not. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph has a core of 30,219,288 domains, 25.2% of the total. Its 76 million domains with no recorded out-links cannot be in the core or in IN, so they must sit in OUT, the tendrils or the disconnected remainder. Most of them are domains the crawl saw only as link targets. Why the parts matter for ranking Random surfers drain into OUT. A random walk can leave the core for OUT but never return. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would end up in OUT and in other sinks. The The damping factor and the treatment of Dangling nodes exist largely because of this part of the bow tie. IN pages have no in-link credit from the core. Under Eigenvector centrality , IN nodes score exactly zero, since no walk from the core reaches them. Harmonic centrality gives them small but nonzero scores, from whatever IN nodes link to them. Core membership is a quality signal. A site that the core links to and that links back into it is embedded in the web’s mainstream. Spam networks often sit outside the core: they link to popular sites, or to each other and their targets, but the core rarely links back. TrustRank exploits the same asymmetry by spreading trust outward from hand-checked sites, which seldom link to spam. The fractal view Each part of the bow tie, examined alone, often looks like a smaller bow tie. Dill and colleagues found the pattern in thematically and geographically defined subsets of the web as early as 2002. The bow tie is less a fixed architecture than the generic shape of a directed graph built by many independent actors who link mostly to things that already exist. References Broder, A., Kumar, R., Maghoul, F., Raghavan, P., Rajagopalan, S., Stata, R., Tomkins, A., & Wiener, J. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320. Meusel, R., Vigna, S., Lehmberg, O., & Bizer, C. (2014). Graph structure in the web — revisited: a trick of the heavy tail. WWW 2014 Companion , 427–432. Dill, S., Kumar, R., McCurley, K. S., Rajagopalan, S., Sivakumar, D., & Tomkins, A. (2002). Self-similarity in the web. ACM Transactions on Internet Technology 2(3), 205–223.

d: Exact betweenness centrality for every node in O(nm) time. One breadth-first search per source counts shortest paths, and one backward sweep hands each node its share.
a: Brandes Dependency accumulation Betweenness algorithm
x: Betweenness centrality asks, for every node, what fraction of the shortest paths between other pairs pass through it. Summing over all pairs naively costs or more. In 2001 Ulrik Brandes showed how to compute every node’s betweenness in time on unweighted graphs, by processing one source at a time and accumulating each node’s share in a single backward sweep. Every major graph library implements his algorithm, and every approximate method for large graphs builds on it. Counting shortest paths From a source , a breadth-first search finds each node’s distance and the number of shortest paths from to . Paths are counted along the way: , and for every node , where holds the nodes with an arc and . The search also records the order in which nodes are reached. Accumulating dependencies The dependency of on is the share of shortest paths from , to all targets, that pass through : Brandes’ key observation is a recurrence that computes all dependencies from the far end back: Each successor on a shortest path passes back to the fraction of its paths that come through , for the paths ending at itself (the 1) and for those continuing beyond it (). Visiting nodes in reverse BFS order guarantees that is final before needs it. The betweenness is the sum over sources: Worked example Take $s = $ E in the running example. Breadth-first search reaches C, D and F at distance 1, A and G at distance 2, and B at distance 3. A has two shortest paths, through C and through D, so ; B inherits them, ; every other node has one. Sweeping back from the farthest node: B and G end no one else’s path: . A passes on B’s paths: . D carries half of A’s paths: . C carries the other half of A’s paths and all of G’s: . Source E thus gives C 2, A 1 and D 1. Repeating from every source and summing gives the final betweenness of the running example: C 6, A 3, D 1, and 0 for the rest. The lab on the Betweenness centrality page runs exactly this code. Cost Each source costs one BFS, , and one backward sweep over the same arcs, so all sources cost , written for connected graphs. Memory is : one source’s distances, path counts, predecessor lists and dependencies at a time, plus the betweenness totals. On weighted graphs, Dijkstra’s algorithm replaces BFS and the cost becomes . Sources are independent, so the algorithm parallelises perfectly across sources: each thread processes its own sources and keeps its own totals, summed at the end. Too slow for the web, so sample is quadratic in practice. For Common Crawl’s domain graph it means about arc visits. The standard remedy samples: Random sources. Run the algorithm from random sources and multiply the totals by (Brandes and Pich, 2007). The estimate is unbiased, and a few thousand sources rank the top nodes well. Adaptive sampling for one node. Bader and colleagues sample sources until the target node’s accumulated dependency passes a threshold, which estimates high-betweenness nodes with few samples. Random shortest paths. Riondato and Kornaropoulos sample one random shortest path at a time and bound the sample size with VC-dimension arguments, giving an additive error guarantee for all nodes at once. KADABRA (Borassi and Natale, 2016) samples paths with a balanced bidirectional search and adaptive stopping, which made betweenness estimates on graphs with billions of arcs practical. d: Boldi and Vigna's three tests (size, density and score monotonicity) check whether a centrality measure agrees with intuition on graphs simple enough that the right answer is obvious. Only harmonic centrality passes all three.
a: Size axiom Density axiom Score monotonicity Boldi–Vigna axioms
x: With dozens of centrality measures in use, how do you pick one? In 2014 Paolo Boldi and Sebastiano Vigna proposed to test measures against small graphs where everyone agrees on the right answer, the way physical theories are tested against simple experiments. They defined three axioms , checked eleven classical measures against them, and found that only one, Harmonic centrality , satisfies all three. Common Crawl, which had Vigna’s help building its graph tooling, has ranked hosts by harmonic centrality since 2017. The size axiom Consider the graph : a -clique (every pair of the nodes linked both ways) next to a directed cycle of nodes, with no arcs between the two. Which nodes should be more central? Intuition says size should win. If the cycle is long enough, its nodes should beat the clique’s, because they belong to a larger community; if the clique is large enough, its nodes should win instead. Formally, a measure satisfies the size axiom if: for every there is a such that for all , cycle nodes score strictly higher than clique nodes; and for every there is a such that for all , clique nodes score strictly higher than cycle nodes. A measure that satisfies only the second half is marked “only ” below, and one that satisfies only the first, “only ”. Harmonic centrality passes. A clique node is at distance 1 from the other clique nodes, so it scores . A cycle node is at distances from the others along the cycle, so it scores , the harmonic number, which grows like without bound. Each side wins once it is large enough. Closeness fails: a clique node’s closeness is and a cycle node’s is , so growing the clique lowers its score. PageRank fails both halves: every node of gets exactly , whatever the sizes. The density axiom Now join a -clique and a -cycle by a single bidirectional arc between a clique node and a cycle node . Call the graph . When both sides have the same number of nodes, but the clique has far more arcs. A measure satisfies the density axiom if, for , scores strictly higher than : being embedded in a denser neighbourhood should help. Most spectral measures pass this test, since the dominant eigenvector concentrates where arcs are dense. Closeness, Lin’s index and betweenness fail it. Betweenness fails because also carries the cycle’s own traffic: in a directed cycle, every path between two other nodes that wraps past runs through it, while the clique’s nodes are all adjacent and carry none of each other’s paths. Score monotonicity The third axiom is about change. A measure satisfies score monotonicity if, for every graph and every pair of nodes and with no arc from to , adding the arc strictly increases ’s score. Receiving a new link should always help. It sounds trivial, yet several famous measures fail it. Adding an arc never lengthens a distance, yet it can lower ’s closeness: nodes that could not reach before now can, and each adds a term to ’s sum of distances. Eigenvector centrality and HITS can shift their dominant eigenvector away from ’s part of the graph. The results Boldi and Vigna’s table: Measure Size Density Score monotonicity Degree only yes yes Harmonic yes yes yes Closeness no no no Lin’s index only no no Betweenness only no no Dominant eigenvector only yes no Seeley’s index no yes no Katz only yes yes PageRank no yes yes HITS only yes no SALSA no yes no Degree satisfies only the half of the size axiom because cycle nodes always have in-degree 1, however long the cycle. Betweenness satisfies only the half because clique nodes lie on no shortest paths between other nodes, so they score zero, while a long cycle routes many paths through each of its nodes. What the axioms do and do not say The axioms are tests, not a definition. A measure that fails one is not useless; it formalises a different notion of importance. Betweenness is the right tool for finding bridges and bottlenecks precisely because it ignores density. The tests do expose behaviour that matters on the web: Closeness fails everything because of how it treats unreachable nodes. On a web graph, where most pairs cannot reach each other, that is fatal (see Closeness centrality ). PageRank fails size because it normalises scores to a probability distribution and spreads teleportation evenly. A large community and a small one of the same shape get the same per-node scores. Harmonic centrality passes all three , at the cost of being expensive to compute exactly: it needs the distances from every node. The HyperBall algorithm makes approximate harmonic centrality affordable on graphs with billions of arcs. Later work by Boldi, Luongo and Vigna added rank monotonicity , which asks that a new link to never let a node that was below overtake it. That axiom, too, separates measures that look alike on paper. References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Boldi, P., Luongo, A., & Vigna, S. (2017). Rank monotonicity in centrality measures. Network Science 5(4), 529–550. Sabidussi, G. (1966). The centrality index of a graph. Psychometrika 31(4), 581–603.

d: A centrality measure assigns every node a score of importance computed from the graph's structure alone. Different measures formalise different ideas of importance, and they disagree.
a: Centrality measure Node importance Link analysis
x: A centrality is a function that assigns every node of a graph a number, computed from the arcs alone, meant to say how important the node is. “Important” has no single meaning, so there is no single centrality. A node can matter because many nodes link to it, because it is close to everything, because shortest paths pass through it, or because important nodes link to it. Each idea leads to a family of measures, and on the same graph they produce different rankings. Three families Boldi and Vigna sort the classical measures into three families: Geometric measures score a node by its distances from the other nodes. In-degree counts the nodes at distance 1; Closeness centrality , Harmonic centrality and Lin’s index aggregate all distances. Path-based measures count paths through or into a node. Betweenness centrality counts the shortest paths passing through a node; Katz centrality counts all walks ending at it, weighting long walks less. Spectral measures take the dominant eigenvector of a matrix derived from the graph. Eigenvector centrality , PageRank , HITS (hubs and authorities) and SALSA belong here, and so does Katz, viewed differently. Spectral measures embody the recursive idea, important nodes are those that important nodes link to, which is why they dominate web search. Geometric measures are easier to explain and, as the Axioms for centrality entry shows, often behave better. One graph, many rankings Here is every measure on the running example (see The web graph ), with nodes ordered from highest to lowest score. Ties share a position. Measure Ranking (highest first) Top score In-degree C · A · B = D = F = G · E 4 Harmonic C · A = G · B · D = F · E 4 Closeness D = F · C · A · B · G · E 1 Betweenness C · A · D · B = E = F = G 6 Eigenvector C · A = G · B · D = E = F 0.325 Katz () C · A · G · B · D = F · E 1.868 PageRank () C · A · G · B · D = F · E 0.298 HITS authority C · A · D = F · B · G · E 0.438 HITS hub E · D · A · B · C · F = G 0.289 Most measures agree that C is the most important node; it receives four of the ten links and sits in the middle of the core. Below C they diverge: Closeness puts D and F first. Each is reached only from E, at distance 1, so the average distance to them is 1, the best possible. The measure rewards having few, close in-neighbours, an artefact the Closeness centrality entry explains. Eigenvector centrality gives D, E and F exactly zero. The core cannot reach them, and the dominant eigenvector lives on the core and what it feeds (see Strongly connected components ). G outranks B under harmonic, Katz, eigenvector and PageRank, though both have one in-link. G’s in-link comes from C, the most central node, and B’s from A. HITS hubs reverse the picture. E links to three nodes that are good authorities, so it is the best hub, though nothing links to it. You can change the graph and compare the measures yourself: Incoming or outgoing? On a directed graph every measure comes in two versions: one built from in-links and one from out-links. For importance on the web the incoming version is the meaningful one, because what links to a site is controlled by others, while what a site links to is controlled by its owner (see The web graph ). All the measures in this encyclopedia use incoming links unless they say otherwise. The outgoing versions have uses too: HITS hubs score good link lists, and CheiRank and 2DRank is PageRank on the reversed graph. Choosing a measure Four questions narrow the choice: What does importance mean here? Attention (PageRank), reachability (harmonic), brokerage (betweenness) and endorsement by the right sources ( TrustRank , Personalized PageRank ) are different questions. Does the measure behave sensibly? The Axioms for centrality entry tests measures against simple graphs where the right answer is obvious. Harmonic centrality passes all three tests; closeness fails all three. Can you afford it? Degree costs one pass over the arcs and PageRank a few dozen. Exact betweenness and closeness need a search from every node, which is impossible on a billion-arc graph without approximation (see HyperBall and Brandes’ algorithm ). Can it be gamed? Any measure that rewards incoming links can be inflated by manufacturing them. Measures differ in how much a spammer gains per fake link (see Link spam and Spam mass ). Centrality on the real web Common Crawl publishes two centralities for every host and domain: Harmonic centrality and PageRank . On its 2026 domain graph they agree at the top: the same infrastructure domains ( googleapis.com , google.com , facebook.com ) lead both. Their Spearman correlation over the 119,453 auction domains present in the graph on 2026-09-23 is 0.69 (see Spearman’s rho ). Large disagreements further down reveal what each measure rewards, as the PageRank entry shows with domains that rank in PageRank’s top 30 but outside harmonic centrality’s top 900. References Freeman, L. C. (1978). Centrality in social networks: conceptual clarification. Social Networks 1(3), 215–239. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Newman, M. E. J. (2018). Networks (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press, chapter 7.

d: PageRank computed on the graph with every link reversed. It scores nodes by how well they link out to the rest of the graph, and paired with ordinary PageRank it places every node on a two-dimensional map.
a: CheiRank 2DRank Inverse PageRank Reverse PageRank
x: Ordinary PageRank rewards nodes that the rest of the graph links to . Reverse every arc and compute PageRank again, and you reward nodes that link out well: nodes whose out-links lead, directly or in a few steps, to much of the graph. Gyöngyi and colleagues used this inverse PageRank in 2004 to pick seeds for TrustRank . Alexei Chepelianskii, studying the call graph of the Linux kernel in 2010, named it CheiRank , and Zhirov, Zhirov and Shepelyansky combined the two rankings into 2DRank to map Wikipedia. Where PageRank measures how popular a node is, CheiRank measures how communicative it is. Definition Let be the transposed Adjacency matrices and lists matrix, the graph with every link reversed. CheiRank is PageRank on that graph: A node gains CheiRank by linking to nodes that have high CheiRank themselves and few in-links. Nodes with no out-links get only the floor value, exactly as nodes with no in-links do under ordinary PageRank. Worked example On the running example: Node E C A D B F G CheiRank 0.282 0.176 0.172 0.166 0.093 0.056 0.056 PageRank 0.051 0.298 0.205 0.065 0.138 0.065 0.177 E, which nothing links to and which has the lowest PageRank, has by far the highest CheiRank: its three links reach every other node within three steps. F and G, which link nowhere, share the floor. C is near the top of both rankings: it is popular and it links back into the core. D links to A and C and scores well on CheiRank while scoring low on PageRank. 2DRank Each node now has two positions: in the PageRank order and in the CheiRank order. Plotting gives a map with four regions: Low , low : popular and communicative. Major portals and core reference sites. Low , high : popular destinations that link out little. Brand sites, infrastructure, sinks of attention. High , low : sites that link out widely but receive little. Directories, aggregators, and link sellers. High , high : the periphery. Zhirov and colleagues defined 2DRank by sweeping out squares from the origin of this plane: nodes enter the ranking as the square grows to include them. 2DRank therefore favours nodes that do reasonably well on both axes. On Wikipedia, PageRank’s top articles were countries and broad concepts, CheiRank tended to favour list-like, navigational articles, and 2DRank picked articles that do well on both. Why it matters for links On the web, a high CheiRank with a low PageRank is the profile of a site that links far more than it is linked. Some such sites are useful directories. Many are link sellers, comment-spam targets or generated pages. mp3fresh.net , which links to 6,113,126 domains in Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, more than any other domain, would rank near the top of the CheiRank order and nowhere near the top of PageRank. For a domain buyer the reverse direction matters too. A domain whose old site linked out to thousands of unrelated sites may carry a footprint of link selling, and search engines’ link-spam systems look for sites “used for the purpose of passing outgoing links” (see Link penalties and the disavow tool ). The domain’s own out-links, as well as its in-links, are worth checking. Computing it CheiRank costs exactly what PageRank costs: one pass over the arcs per iteration, on the graph with arcs reversed. A system that stores a graph and its transpose, as WebGraph-based pipelines do, computes both from the same data. Because the reversed web graph has its own dangling nodes, the 14.9 million domains with no in-links in Common Crawl’s graph, the same care about Dangling nodes applies. References Chepelianskii, A. European Physical Journal B 77(4), 523–531. Ermann, L., Frahm, K. M., & Shepelyansky, D. L. (2015). Google matrix analysis of directed networks. Reviews of Modern Physics 87(4), 1261–1310. d: A node is central if it is close, on average, to all other nodes. A classic idea from social network analysis that breaks down on graphs where most pairs cannot reach each other, like the web.
a: Closeness Bavelas closeness Lin's index Lin centrality
x: Closeness centrality scores a node by how near the rest of the graph is. Alex Bavelas proposed it in 1950 for small communication networks, where the person who can reach everyone in the fewest steps is best placed to coordinate. The idea is appealing and the formula is simple: one over the sum of distances. On graphs that are not strongly connected, which includes every web graph, the formula needs patching, and the patches produce rankings that defy common sense. Harmonic centrality fixes the problem, which is why it has largely replaced closeness in link analysis. Definition On a strongly connected graph, the closeness of is the reciprocal of the sum of distances to it: Some authors multiply by , turning the sum into an average distance. On a directed graph you choose a direction: distances to measure how easily the graph reaches , distances from how easily reaches the graph. For importance on the web, distances to are the meaningful choice (see Centrality ). The unreachable-node problem If even one node cannot reach , the sum contains and closeness collapses to zero. On the web almost every pair is unreachable in one direction (see Paths, distance and reachability ), so the textbook formula assigns nearly every node zero. The usual repair sums only over nodes that can reach , and gives closeness 0 to nodes nothing reaches: That repair creates a new problem: a node reached by one neighbour at distance 1 gets closeness , the maximum possible, beating a node that the whole graph reaches in two or three steps. Worked example On the running example the repaired closeness gives: Node D F C A B G E Closeness 1 1 0.250 0.167 0.125 0.111 0 Nodes that reach it 1 1 4 4 4 5 0 D and F come first. Each is reached only by E, at distance 1. C, which every node with an out-link reaches, gets a quarter as much, because its sum of distances is over four nodes. G, reachable from more nodes than any other, ranks second to last. The measure rewards being hard to reach, as long as the few nodes that do reach you are close. The lab below lets you check: Lin’s index Nan Lin proposed in 1976 to weight closeness by how many nodes reach . With the number of nodes that can reach (counting itself), with the convention that a node nothing reaches scores 1. On a strongly connected graph for every node, so Lin’s index ranks exactly as closeness does. On the running example it gives C 6.25, A 4.17, then D, F and G tied at 4, B at 3.13 and E at 1. That is much more sensible, though the three-way tie still puts F level with G. Lin’s index satisfies the half of the size axiom but fails density and score monotonicity (see Axioms for centrality ). Axioms Closeness fails all three of Boldi and Vigna’s axioms: Size. In a graph made of a -clique and a separate -cycle, clique nodes score , which falls as the clique grows. Density. When a clique and a cycle of equal size are joined by one bidirectional arc, the cycle-side endpoint does not lose to the clique-side endpoint as it should. Score monotonicity. A new link to can lower its closeness. The link makes reachable from nodes that could not reach it before, and each adds a distance to the sum. Cost Exact closeness needs the distances from every node to every node: a breadth-first search from each node, in total. That is fine for a social network of a few thousand people and impossible for a web graph of a hundred million domains. Approximate methods sample sources, or count balls of growing radius with HyperLogLog counters as HyperBall does. Why harmonic centrality replaced it Replace the reciprocal of a sum of distances by a sum of reciprocals, and unreachable nodes contribute with no special case. That is Harmonic centrality , proposed for networks by Marchiori and Latora in 2000 and advocated by Boldi and Vigna as the measure that passes all three axioms. On a strongly connected graph harmonic and closeness centrality usually rank nodes similarly. On the web they do not, and harmonic is the one whose ranking makes sense. References Bavelas, A. (1950). Communication patterns in task-oriented groups. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 22(6), 725–730. Sabidussi, G. (1966). The centrality index of a graph. Psychometrika 31(4), 581–603. Lin, N. (1976). Foundations of Social Research . McGraw-Hill. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262.

d: How often two neighbours of a node are also neighbours of each other. Real networks form far more triangles than chance predicts, and unnaturally dense triangles are a classic fingerprint of link farms.
a: Clustering Transitivity Triangles Local clustering coefficient
x: If site A links to sites B and C, how likely is it that B and C are also linked? In a random graph with the web’s density, almost never. In real link graphs, often: sites on the same topic, in the same language or run by the same people link to each other in clusters. The clustering coefficient measures this tendency to form triangles. It is one of the two statistics, with short typical distances, that define a Small worlds network, and it is a useful signal when hunting for Link spam . Definitions Clustering is usually defined on the undirected version of a graph, where a link in either direction counts as a connection. The local clustering coefficient of a node with neighbours is the fraction of pairs of neighbours that are themselves connected: where counts the triangles through . It is undefined, or set to 0, for nodes with fewer than two neighbours. The global clustering coefficient , or transitivity , looks at the whole graph: where a connected triple is a path of length two, . Each triangle contains three such paths. The average local coefficient and the transitivity are different numbers and can differ widely: the average gives every node equal weight, while transitivity is dominated by high-degree nodes, which sit at the centre of most triples. Directed versions distinguish cycles () from transitive triples (, , ); Fagiolo catalogues the variants. Worked example Ignoring directions, the running example has three triangles: A–B–C, A–C–D and C–D–E. Node A B C D E F G Neighbours 3 2 5 3 3 1 1 Linked neighbour pairs 2 of 3 1 of 1 3 of 10 2 of 3 1 of 3 – – Local coefficient 0.67 1.00 0.30 0.67 0.33 – – C, the best-connected node, has the lowest coefficient: its five neighbours span the whole graph, and few of them know each other. B, with two neighbours who are linked, has the highest possible value. This inverse relation between degree and clustering is typical of real networks. The average over nodes with at least two neighbours is 0.59; the transitivity is , lower because C’s ten neighbour pairs weigh heavily. Clustering in real networks A random graph with nodes and average degree has clustering about : for Common Crawl’s domain graph, around . Real social, biological and information networks have clustering coefficients many orders of magnitude higher, often 0.1 to 0.5 for the average local coefficient. Watts and Strogatz’s 1998 observation that networks combine high clustering with short distances launched the modern study of Small worlds networks. On the web, clustering comes from topical communities, regional webs, blogrolls and sites under common ownership. Community detection methods exploit exactly this density of links within groups. Triangles and link spam Legitimate sites cluster moderately. Link farms cluster extremely: a set of domains created to boost each other often links every member to every other, forming a near-clique in which nearly every pair of neighbours is linked. Becchetti, Boldi, Castillo and Gionis showed in 2008 that triangle counts per node, computed approximately in a few passes, separate spam hosts from normal ones well enough to be a useful feature in spam classifiers. A domain whose referring domains are all densely linked to each other, and to little else, deserves suspicion. Computing it Counting triangles exactly takes, for each arc, an intersection of two neighbour lists. Processing nodes in order of degree and only counting each triangle from its lowest-degree vertex bounds the work at , which is feasible for billions of arcs on a large machine but slow. For estimates: Wedge sampling samples random paths of length two and checks whether they close, estimating transitivity with error independent of graph size. Semi-streaming local counts (Becchetti and colleagues) estimate each node’s triangle count from a few sequential passes using min-wise hashing of neighbour sets. Degree-bucketed sampling handles the hubs, whose neighbour pairs number in the trillions, separately. What it means for a domain Clustering is not a quality score. A local business linked by a dozen local sites that also link to each other has high clustering, and so does a private blog network. What distinguishes them is everything else: whether the cluster also receives links from the wider web, whether its members have independent histories and audiences, and whether the links make sense to a reader. Use clustering as a prompt to look closer, together with Spam mass and the Auditing vendor metrics checks. References Watts, D. J., & Strogatz, S. H. (1998). Collective dynamics of “small-world” networks. Nature 393, 440–442. Fagiolo, G. (2007). Clustering in complex directed networks. Physical Review E 76(2), 026107. Becchetti, L., Boldi, P., Castillo, C., & Gionis, A. (2008). Efficient semi-streaming algorithms for local triangle counting in massive graphs. KDD 2008 , 16–24. Seshadhri, C., Pinar, A., & Kolda, T. G. (2013). Triadic measures on graphs: The power of wedge sampling. SDM 2013 , 10–18.

d: Common Crawl publishes free host- and domain-level link graphs every few months, with harmonic centrality and PageRank for every node. What the files contain, how they are built, and how to read them.
a: Common Crawl CC web graph Common Crawl ranks hyperlinkgraph cc-main
x: Common Crawl is a non-profit that crawls the web and publishes the data for free. Alongside its page archives, it releases web graphs : one at the host level and one at the domain level, each built from three consecutive monthly crawls, with Harmonic centrality and PageRank computed for every node. These graphs are the only large, open, reproducible source of link-based rankings for the whole web, which makes them the natural reference against which commercial metrics can be checked. This encyclopedia’s real-world numbers come from the release cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug . The 2026 June–August release The release combines the crawls CC-MAIN-2026-25, CC-MAIN-2026-30 and CC-MAIN-2026-34: Host graph Domain graph Nodes 235,013,701 119,722,885 Arcs 3,104,683,414 2,450,405,793 Dangling nodes (no out-links) 173.0 million (73.6%) 76.4 million (63.8%) Largest strongly connected component 35.9 million (15.3%) 30.2 million (25.2%) BVGraph size, bits per link 15.6 15.1 The domain graph folds hosts into registered domains: on average 1.96 hosts per domain (see Page, host and domain graphs ). The files For the domain graph: File Content …-domain-vertices.txt.gz (852 MiB) id , reversed domain name, number of hosts, one line per node, sorted by reversed name …-domain-edges.txt.gz (8.8 GiB) from_id , to_id , one line per arc …-domain.graph , …-domain-t.graph (4.3 GiB each) the graph and its transpose in WebGraph’s BVGraph format ….properties , ….stats compression parameters and graph statistics …-domain-ranks.txt.gz (2.2 GiB) harmonic centrality and PageRank for every domain Node ids are positions in reversed-name order, so com.google and com.googleapis are numerically close (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ). The ranks file has one line per domain, sorted by harmonic centrality: #harmonicc_pos #harmonicc_val #pr_pos #pr_val #host_rev #n_hosts 1 2.881964E7 1 0.015169512448465185 com.googleapis 2860 2 2.8571234E7 3 0.009397995804377878 com.facebook 3126 3 2.8490256E7 2 0.015103803560313364 com.google 24993 Positions are 1-based. Ties in value keep vertex order, that is reversed-name order, because the files are produced by a stable sort (see Ranks and scores ). How the graph is built Extract links. From the WAT metadata of every crawled page, Common Crawl’s extractor collects every URL the page references: anchors, <link> elements, scripts, many <meta> URLs such as og:image , HTTP redirects, Link and Content-Location headers, and sitemap lines from robots.txt . It does not filter nofollow . Only links between different hosts are kept. Normalise hosts. Host names are lower-cased, IDNA-encoded and reversed; IP addresses and single-label hosts are dropped. Build the host graph from the distinct host-to-host pairs, then fold it into domains . The folding treats blogspot.com (4,113,910 hosts) and github.io (310,784 hosts) each as one domain, although the Public Suffix List’s private section lists both as public suffixes. Compress with WebGraph and compute ranks with the LAW library: HyperBall for harmonic centrality, with counters on disk, and PageRankParallelGaussSeidel for PageRank, both on the transposed graph. Reading the ranks The top is infrastructure. Because scripts, fonts and <link> elements count as links, the domains embedded in millions of pages lead both rankings: googleapis.com , google.com , facebook.com , googletagmanager.com , gstatic.com . gmpg.org , whose only role is a profile link in WordPress page headers, is tenth by both measures. A high position means “referenced from many places”, not “popular with readers”. Harmonic values are approximate and flat. They come from probabilistic counters (see HyperBall ), only 5.9 million distinct values occur, and position 10 million still scores 43% of the top value. PageRank sits on a floor. 14.9 million domains with no in-links share the floor value , which implies that dangling domains hold about 41% of all PageRank (see Dangling nodes ). Absent is not the same as last. A domain missing from the graph was never linked from a crawled page, or never seen. Of GoDaddy’s 2026-09-23 auction inventory, 88.8% is absent. The two rankings disagree in instructive ways. parastorage.com is 16th by PageRank and 81,305th by harmonic centrality; the PageRank entry explains why. Limits A crawl is a sample. Common Crawl fetches billions of pages per month but not the whole web, and its graph reflects its crawl priorities, which themselves use harmonic centrality. Three months of links. Links seen in any of the three crawls count; older links do not. This makes the graph fresh but blind to history. No weights or anchors. Every arc is equal, whatever the number of links behind it, their placement or their text (see Anchor text ). No spam filtering. Link farms appear as they are, which is useful for studying them and means the raw in-degree can be inflated (see Link spam ). References Common Crawl. d: Finding groups of nodes that link to each other much more than to the rest of the graph. Modularity, Louvain, Leiden, label propagation and Infomap are the standard tools; on the web they find topics, regions and link farms.
a: Communities Clustering Modularity Louvain Leiden Label propagation Infomap Graph partitioning
x: Link graphs are not uniformly tangled. Sites about the same topic, in the same language or run by the same owner link to each other far more than to outsiders. Community detection finds such groups automatically from the links alone. The problem has no single correct answer, since “community” has no single definition, but a few methods dominate practice because they are fast and usually sensible. On web graphs they find topical clusters and national webs, they produce the node orders that make graphs compress well, and they expose link farms, which are communities by construction. Modularity The most widely used quality measure, Newman and Girvan’s modularity , compares the links inside groups with what a random graph of the same degrees would put there: where is the undirected adjacency matrix, the degree of node , the number of edges and the group of node . Each pair inside a group earns 1 if linked and loses its expected number of links, . is 0 for a single group containing everything and rises as groups become denser than chance. Leicht and Newman gave a directed version. Worked example Treating the running example as undirected gives 9 edges (A ⇄ C counts once). Checking all 877 ways to partition the seven nodes, the best modularity is 0.142, for the split {A, B, C, G} and {D, E, F}: Partition Modularity {A, B, C, G}, {D, E, F} 0.142 {A, B, C, D, G}, {E, F} 0.124 {A, B, C}, {D, E, F}, {G} 0.093 everything together 0 The core and its satellite G form one community; the feeders D, E and F form the other. Exhaustive search is possible only for tiny graphs: the number of partitions grows faster than exponentially, and maximising modularity is NP-hard. Real methods are heuristics. The main methods Louvain (Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte and Lefebvre, 2008). Start with every node alone. Move each node to the neighbouring group that most increases modularity, until no move helps; then collapse each group into a single node and repeat on the smaller graph. It runs in roughly linear time and handles graphs with billions of edges. Leiden (Traag, Waltman and van Eck, 2019). Louvain can produce groups that are internally disconnected. Leiden adds a refinement step that guarantees connected communities and converges to better partitions; it has largely replaced Louvain. Label propagation (Raghavan, Albert and Kumara, 2007). Give every node its own label, then repeatedly let each node adopt the label most common among its neighbours. Labels flood dense regions and stop at sparse boundaries. It is very fast and needs no objective function, but results vary between runs. Layered label propagation uses it to order nodes for compression (see Node orderings ). Infomap (Rosvall and Bergstrom, 2008). Treats communities as regions where a random walker tends to stay, and finds the partition that gives the shortest description of the walk, the map equation . It suits directed link graphs well because it follows the flow of links rather than counting edges. Girvan–Newman (2002). Repeatedly remove the edge with the highest edge betweenness, the edge most likely to bridge communities (see Betweenness centrality ). Historically important, too slow for large graphs. Local methods. Personalized PageRank from a seed, followed by a sweep for the lowest-conductance cut, finds the community around one node without touching the rest of the graph (see Push algorithms ). Pitfalls Resolution limit. Fortunato and Barthélemy showed that modularity optimisation cannot detect communities smaller than a scale that depends on the size of the whole graph: small, genuine groups get merged into larger ones. Resolution parameters help but add a free choice. Many near-optimal answers. Modularity landscapes are flat at the top; very different partitions can score almost the same. Treat any single partition as one plausible view. Directions matter. Most methods symmetrise the graph, which loses the difference between a group that links to the core and a group the core links to. Communities and link spam A link farm is a community designed to be one: many domains that link to each other and to a few targets, with few links from the rest of the web. In modularity terms it is a dense group with almost no external edges, which methods find easily. The suspicious pattern is the combination of high internal density, low external in-degree and a few external targets that receive the group’s links. The bump of about 39,000 domains with 19,000 to 29,000 in-links in Common Crawl’s 2026 degree distribution (see Degree distributions and power laws ) has the degree signature of such a group. Detection systems combine community structure with Spam mass , TrustRank and content signals, since legitimate communities, such as a university’s departmental sites, can look structurally similar. d: The probability α that PageRank's random surfer follows a link rather than jumping. It trades link structure against uniformity, sets the speed of convergence, and is conventionally 0.85 for no deep reason.
a: Alpha α Teleportation probability 0.85
x: The damping factor is the one parameter of PageRank . At each step the random surfer follows a link with probability and teleports with probability . Brin and Page used , and almost everyone since has copied them, including Common Crawl’s PageRank and the default of most graph libraries. The choice matters more than its conventional status suggests: it decides how far link influence travels, how fast the computation converges, and how stable the ranking is. What α controls The PageRank equation weights two terms: At , links are ignored and every node scores . As grows, the link term takes over. Expanding the solution as a series makes the trade-off explicit: PageRank sums the influence of paths of every length, with a path of length weighted by . With , a path of 5 links keeps 44% of its weight and a path of 20 links keeps 4%. With , the same paths keep 3% and one in a million. Small makes PageRank local, close to a weighted in-degree; large makes it global. Worked example The running example’s PageRank at several damping factors: α C A G B D, F E Iterations 0.10 0.165 0.148 0.141 0.140 0.137 0.133 10 0.50 0.242 0.176 0.150 0.134 0.105 0.090 24 0.85 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 0.065 0.051 43 0.99 0.319 0.216 0.193 0.143 0.047 0.035 57 At the scores barely differ from the uniform . As grows, probability flows into the core (A, B, C) and towards G, which hangs off it, and drains from D, E and F, which only feed the core. On this small graph the order never changes; on large graphs it does, as the next sections show. Iterations are counted until the total change falls below . Move the α slider in the lab and watch the same flow: Convergence Power iteration reduces the error by a factor of about per iteration, the second-largest eigenvalue modulus of the PageRank matrix. Haveliwala and Kamvar proved , with equality whenever the graph has at least two closed strongly connected components, which every web graph has. So to reach an error of takes about iterations: 113 for at , but 1,833 at . The running example converges faster than the bound because its two dangling nodes teleport every visitor, which shortens every walk. Higher is more faithful to the link structure and much more expensive. Sensitivity as α approaches 1 As the teleport vanishes, and PageRank approaches the stationary distribution of the raw walk, which puts all its mass in closed components such as the OUT side of the The bow-tie structure and dense spam clusters that link only to themselves. Boldi, Santini and Vigna studied PageRank as a function of and showed that the limit as exists but concentrates on those closed components, the nodes “where the surfer gets stuck.” Rankings near are therefore dominated by rank sinks and change sharply with . Small has the opposite risk: the ranking barely uses the link structure at all. Why 0.85? The value is a compromise that Brin and Page reported without derivation. It keeps substantial link influence (mean run of 5.7 clicks between jumps), converges in about a hundred iterations, and keeps rank sinks in check. Several researchers have argued for other values. Avrachenkov, Litvak and Pham, analysing how mass splits between the giant component and the rest, suggested . None of these displaced the convention: 0.85 remains the standard because everyone else uses it, which makes results comparable. Practical advice Report α with every PageRank. A score computed with is not comparable with one computed at 0.5. The same holds for the dangling-node treatment and the teleport distribution (see Dangling nodes and Personalized PageRank ). Check stability. If a ranking you care about changes a lot between and , it rests on fragile structure, often a rank sink or a single strong link. Do not chase precision you cannot use. The Ranks and scores entry explains why the tenth digit of a PageRank value carries no information about a domain. Stopping at a relative change of or usually fixes every position that matters. d: Nodes with no out-links, where a random surfer has nowhere to go. On a crawled web graph they are the majority, and how a PageRank implementation treats them changes the scores of everyone.
a: Dangling node Dangling page Sink Dangling mass
x: A dangling node has no out-links. For a random walk it is a dead end: the surfer arrives and cannot leave by following a link, so the row of the transition matrix for that node is empty and the probability that reaches it disappears. On a real web graph dangling nodes are not a corner case. Most of them are pages or sites the crawler knows about only because something links to them, and they can be the majority of all nodes. Every PageRank implementation must decide what the surfer does next, and the decision shifts every score in the graph. Where dangling nodes come from The crawl frontier. A crawler discovers far more URLs than it fetches. Every discovered but unfetched page enters the graph with in-links and no recorded out-links. Eiron, McCurley and Tomlin called this the web frontier and showed that it dominates the dangling set. Files without links. PDFs, images, scripts and fonts appear as link targets; most link nowhere. Pages that link only internally. In a host or domain graph, links within the same host or domain are dropped, so a site whose links all point inside itself has no out-links at that level. Blocked or failed fetches. robots.txt exclusions, errors and timeouts. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, 76,352,306 of 119,722,885 domains, 63.8%, have no outgoing arcs. The standard fix: jump uniformly The usual treatment, and the one in the definition used throughout this encyclopedia, sends the surfer from a dangling node to a uniformly random node, as if the dangling node linked to everything. Equivalently, the total PageRank sitting on dangling nodes, the dangling mass , is spread evenly over the graph at every step: In the running example, F and G are dangling, with . Each step gives every node from that mass, nearly as much as the teleport term . Reading the dangling mass off Common Crawl’s ranks A domain with no in-links receives only the teleport share and its share of the dangling mass, so every such domain sits at the same floor value, Common Crawl’s 2026 domain ranks put that floor at : the 14.9 million domains with no in-links all sit at that value, to six significant digits. Assuming the LAW library’s defaults, with uniform redistribution, the floor implies , so . The 63.8% of domains that link nowhere hold about 41% of all PageRank. That much mass flowing back uniformly is why the floor sits at 3.3 times the bare teleport share . Other treatments Remove, rank, restore. Page and colleagues’ 1999 report removed dangling nodes (repeatedly, since removing some creates others), computed PageRank on the rest, and then gave each dangling node a score from its in-links. This is cheaper but leaves dangling nodes out of the redistribution. Jump to the preference vector. In Personalized PageRank , the surfer can leave a dangling node according to the personalisation vector (“strongly preferential”) or uniformly (“weakly preferential”). Boldi, Posenato, Santini and Vigna showed that the two give noticeably different rankings, and that mixing them up is a common bug. Self-loops. Adding a link from each dangling node to itself keeps the matrix stochastic but turns every dangling node into a trap that soaks up probability. It inflates exactly the nodes that should not be inflated and is generally a mistake. Let it leak. Ignore the problem: probability reaching a dangling node vanishes, and the result sums to less than 1. Normalised afterwards, this pseudo-PageRank ranks nodes exactly like the uniform-jump version, a result shown by Del Corso, Gullì and Romani, and it is linear in the teleport vector, which Spam mass relies on. Why the choice matters Dangling nodes absorb probability and hand it back according to whatever rule applies. With uniform redistribution, a large dangling mass raises every node’s baseline and compresses the range of scores. A ranking computed with a different rule, or on a crawl that fetched more of its frontier, can reorder mid-ranked nodes substantially. For a domain, the practical lessons are: “No out-links” usually means “not crawled”. A domain with zero out-degree in a crawl-based graph is not necessarily a site that links nowhere. The floor is not zero. Every domain gets at least , so a PageRank barely above the floor means “no meaningful in-links,” however small the number looks next to the top value of 0.015. Compare like with like. Two PageRank datasets with different dangling treatments, damping factors or crawl coverage are not comparable value for value (see The damping factor and Ranks and scores ).
