d: Score each node by how many nodes link to it. The oldest, cheapest and most transparent centrality, and the one that "referring domains" reports.
a: In-degree centrality Prestige Popularity Citation count
x: Degree centrality ranks nodes by their Degree . On a directed link graph the meaningful version counts incoming arcs: a site is important if many sites link to it. It is what a citation count measures for a paper and what “referring domains” measures for a website. Every more elaborate measure in this encyclopedia can be read as a fix for one of its weaknesses. Definition The in-degree centrality of is sometimes divided by so that it lies between 0 and 1. Social network analysts call it prestige or popularity . The outgoing version, , measures activity : how many others a node points to. On the web, activity is free, so only in-degree carries information about how others see a site. Worked example In the running example, C receives four links, A two, and B, D, F and G one each; E receives none. Degree centrality ranks C first, A second, a four-way tie in third place and E last. The tie is the measure’s first visible weakness: G’s single link comes from C, the best-connected node, and F’s from E, which nothing links to, yet degree treats them identically. PageRank and Harmonic centrality both separate them (G scores 3 and F scores 1 under harmonic centrality). Strengths Cheap. One pass over the arcs, no iteration, no convergence threshold (see Degree ). Transparent. Anyone can verify an in-degree by listing the linking nodes. A centrality you can explain in one sentence is easier to trust and to audit. Monotone. Adding a link to always raises its score, and the measure satisfies the density axiom (see Axioms for centrality ). Strongly correlated with the rest. Across the 119,453 domains from the 2026-09-23 auction inventory that appear in Common Crawl’s graph, in-degree and harmonic centrality have a Spearman correlation of 0.69. For many purposes in-degree is a fair first approximation. Weaknesses Every link counts the same. A link from a national newspaper and a link from a site created yesterday add one each. This is the gap PageRank was designed to close. It is local. Degree sees only immediate neighbours. A site linked by three sites that are themselves linked by millions is, by degree, less important than one linked by four abandoned blogs. It is cheap to inflate. Manufacturing in-links needs only domains, and domains are cheap. A link farm of a thousand domains linking to a target adds a thousand to its in-degree. Recursive measures limit the damage, because the farm’s domains have little importance of their own to pass on. It fails half of the size axiom. Nodes on a long cycle always have in-degree 1, however large their community (see Axioms for centrality ). In-degree on the real web The top of Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph by in-degree: Domain Referring domains googleapis.com 17,119,122 facebook.com 16,967,941 google.com 16,347,517 gmpg.org 8,137,388 cloudflare.com 3,776,898 These numbers count every kind of reference Common Crawl extracts, including scripts, fonts and <link> elements, not only clickable anchors (see The Common Crawl web graph ). gmpg.org illustrates the effect: WordPress themes have long included a <link rel="profile" href="https://gmpg.org/xfn/11"> element in every page header, so the site of a small 2003 microformat project receives links from more than 8 million domains. At the other end, the median domain has exactly one referring domain, and 12.4% have none. Among the auction domains that appear in the graph at all, the median in-degree is 1, the 90th percentile 5 and the 99th percentile 57. Degree in SEO tools Every link index reports in-degree in two forms (see Backlinks and referring domains ): Backlinks count individual links, so a sitewide footer link on a 10,000-page site counts 10,000 times. Referring domains count distinct linking domains: the in-degree of the domain graph. Referring domains is the more robust of the two, but it inherits all of degree centrality’s weaknesses, and vendors’ counts include domains that link to almost everything. The Auditing vendor metrics entry shows that one vendor reports a median of 96 referring domains even for auction domains that no page in Common Crawl links to, mostly the same handful of spam domains, so a raw count near that floor says nothing at all. When degree is the right choice Use in-degree when you need a quick, explainable signal on a graph you trust, or as a sanity check on fancier scores. A domain whose PageRank is high but whose in-degree is tiny deserves a closer look, because a single strong link carries it, and the PageRank entry shows how fragile such scores are. When links may be manufactured, combine degree with a measure that weighs who links, such as Harmonic centrality , TrustRank or Spam mass . References Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications . Cambridge University Press, chapter 5. Freeman, L. C. (1978). Centrality in social networks: conceptual clarification. Social Networks 1(3), 215–239. Garfield, E. (1972). Citation analysis as a tool in journal evaluation. Science 178(4060), 471–479.

d: In-degree counts the links a node receives and out-degree the links it makes; their distributions shape everything built on a link graph.
a: In-degree Out-degree Indegree Outdegree
x: Degree is the simplest thing you can measure about a node: how many arcs touch it. In a directed graph every node has two degrees. Its in-degree counts the arcs that point at it, and its out-degree counts the arcs it sends. On a domain graph, in-degree is the number of distinct domains that link to a domain, the quantity SEO tools call referring domains (see Backlinks and referring domains ). Definition For a node in a directed graph : Each arc leaves one node and enters another, so the in-degrees and the out-degrees each sum to the number of arcs : and both average to . The averages agree, but the distributions do not. Popular sites collect in-links by the million, while out-degree tops out at whatever a site’s owner chooses to publish. Worked example In the running example (see the The web graph entry), the ten arcs give these degrees: Node A B C D E F G In-degree 2 1 4 1 0 1 1 Out-degree 2 1 2 2 3 0 0 Both rows sum to 10. C receives the most links, E sends the most and receives none, and F and G send none. A node with is a source ; a node with is a sink , which ranking algorithms call a dangling node . Degrees in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph has 2,450,405,793 arcs among 119,722,885 domains, so both degrees average 20.47. The averages mislead badly: Statistic In-degree Out-degree Domains with degree 0 14,903,407 (12.4%) 76,352,306 (63.8%) Domains with degree 1 52,450,210 (43.8%) 7,021,336 (5.9%) Median 1 0 99th percentile 138 149 99.9th percentile 1,856 2,374 Largest 17,119,122 6,113,126 Share of all arcs held by the top 1% of domains 79.4% 78.6% The typical domain receives one link and sends none, while the top 1% of domains receive four in five of all links. That skew is the subject of the Degree distributions and power laws entry. The out-degree column says as much about the crawl as about the web. A domain the crawler never fetched has out-degree 0 whatever it links to in reality. The extremes are instructive. The largest in-degree belongs to googleapis.com , which serves fonts and scripts that millions of sites embed. The largest out-degree, 6,113,126, belongs to mp3fresh.net , a single domain that links to roughly one in twenty domains in the graph. No editorial process produces that many links; generated pages do. Extreme out-degree is a classic signal of Link spam . Computing degrees Degrees cost one pass over the arcs. Keep one counter per node, read each arc , and increment out[u] and in[v] . For the Common Crawl graph that means two arrays of 119.7 million 32-bit counters, 479 MB each, and a stream of 2.45 billion arcs. Reading the 9.4 GB gzipped edge list dominates: decompression takes a few minutes on one core, and the counting itself is noise. A compressed graph in the WebGraph format stores each node’s out-degree directly, so out-degrees come free; in-degrees need the transposed graph or one pass over the arcs. Degree as a measure of importance In-degree is the oldest ranking signal. Citation counts in science and “number of referring domains” in SEO are both in-degree. The Degree centrality entry examines it as a centrality measure: it is cheap, easy to explain and hard to fool at small scale, but it treats a link from a major newspaper and a link from a link farm as equal. PageRank and Harmonic centrality fix that by weighing who links, not only how many. Degree also feeds other measures. PageRank divides each node’s score among its out-links, so, per unit of the linker’s own score, a link from a node with out-degree 1 passes 6.1 million times more than a link from mp3fresh.net . assortativity asks whether high-degree nodes link to each other, and k-core decomposition decomposition peels a graph by degree. Weighted degree Collapsing parallel links throws away counts. A page graph knows that one domain links to another 5,000 times across its pages; a domain graph keeps one arc. Tools that report “backlinks” count the raw links, while “referring domains” counts the distinct linking domains, which is the domain graph’s in-degree. The two differ by orders of magnitude for sites with sitewide footer links, which is why referring domains is the better-behaved number (see Backlinks and referring domains ). References Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications . Cambridge University Press, chapter 4. Broder, A., et al. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320.

d: Moz's 1–100 score that predicts how likely a domain is to rank in search results, computed by a machine-learning model over Moz's own link index. A comparative, logarithmic-feeling number, not a Google metric.
a: DA Moz DA Page Authority PA Domain Authority 2.0
x: Domain Authority (DA) is a score from 1 to 100 published by the SEO software company Moz. Moz describes it as a prediction of how likely a website is to rank in search engine results pages, with higher scores meaning a greater likelihood. It is computed from Moz’s own web index, which its Link Explorer tool exposes, by a model trained on how domains actually rank. DA is probably the most widely quoted third-party domain metric, and like all of them it is a vendor’s estimate, not a number Google uses. What goes into it Moz does not publish the formula. It describes the inputs and method in general terms: Link data from Moz’s index , chiefly the number of distinct linking root domains (referring domains, see Backlinks and referring domains ) and the total number of links, along with signals of the quality of those linking domains. A machine-learning model. Since Domain Authority 2.0 , released in March 2019, the score comes from a model trained to predict whether one domain outranks another in Google’s results, rather than from a hand-tuned combination of link counts. Moz said the 2019 version also incorporated its Spam Score and patterns of link manipulation to resist inflated profiles. Scaling to 1–100. The model’s output is mapped onto a 1–100 scale on which, by Moz’s account, it is much easier to move from 20 to 30 than from 70 to 80, the behaviour of a logarithmic scale (see Ranks and scores ). Page Authority (PA) is the page-level counterpart, predicting how well a single page will rank. How to read it It is comparative. Moz positions DA as a way to compare sites, particularly competitors in the same niche, not as an absolute measure. A DA of 40 is strong for a local bakery and weak for a national newspaper. It moves when the index moves. Because the score is calibrated against the whole index, a domain’s DA can change when Moz’s crawl grows or its model is retrained, even if the domain’s own links did not change. Compare scores taken at the same time. Small differences are noise. One or two points rarely mean anything, especially at the low end where most domains sit. It is not Google’s. Google does not use Domain Authority. A higher DA correlates with better rankings because both depend on links, not because one causes the other. Relation to the graph measures DA is, roughly, a learned function of in-degree and of the strength of the linking domains, which is the information PageRank and Harmonic centrality use as well. Where it differs: The graph. Moz’s index is its own crawl, with its own coverage and freshness, and its own choices about which links count (see The web graph ). The target. DA is fitted to predict rankings, so it can absorb any link feature that predicts them, while PageRank and harmonic centrality are fixed definitions. Spam handling. DA explicitly tries to discount manipulative patterns; Common Crawl’s open centralities do not filter anything (see Link spam ). Using it for domain evaluation DA is a reasonable first filter, and a poor final judge: Look at the linking domains Moz lists , not only the score. A DA built on a few strong, relevant domains is worth more than the same DA built on many weak ones. Cross-check with other sources. Compare DA with Domain Rating (Ahrefs) , Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) and Common Crawl’s positions (see Reading a domain’s link metrics ). When they disagree strongly, find out why before trusting any of them. Watch for inflated profiles. A high DA on a domain with no traffic, a short history and links mostly from unrelated sites is a classic sign of a manufactured link profile, which Google may already ignore. GoDaddy’s auction inventory, which this encyclopedia’s Auditing vendor metrics examines, does not include Moz metrics, so the audit cannot test DA directly. The same questions apply to it as to the metrics it does include: how much of the score comes from links that carry information about this particular domain? References Moz. What is Domain Authority? moz.com/learn/seo/domain-authority. Moz Blog (2019). Domain Authority 2.0 announcement, March 2019. Moz. Link Explorer. moz.com/link-explorer.

d: Ahrefs' 0–100 score for the strength of a domain's backlink profile. By Ahrefs' own description it is a PageRank-like computation on a domain graph of followed links, mapped to a logarithmic scale.
a: DR Ahrefs DR URL Rating UR
x: Domain Rating (DR) is Ahrefs’ measure of “the relative strength of a website’s backlink profile”, on a logarithmic scale from 0 to 100. Of the commercial domain metrics, it is the one whose vendor describes its mechanics most concretely, and the description is recognisably PageRank applied to a domain-level graph. That makes it a useful bridge between the open centralities in this encyclopedia and the proprietary scores domain buyers see every day. How Ahrefs describes the calculation Ahrefs lists the steps: Count the unique domains that have at least one dofollow link to the target. Take into account the DR of each of those linking domains. Take into account how many unique domains each linking domain links to: a domain’s “DR juice” is divided among the domains it links to. Compute raw scores from these inputs. Map the raw scores onto the 0–100 scale. Ahrefs adds two rules. Only the first link from a given domain counts: further links from the same domain add nothing. And links marked nofollow do not count at all (see Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) ). In graph terms: build a domain graph from followed links only, collapse parallel links (which a domain graph does anyway, see Page, host and domain graphs ), and let each domain pass its score in equal shares to the domains it links to. That is the PageRank recursion on a domain graph. Ahrefs does not say how it handles teleportation, Dangling nodes or convergence, nor exactly how raw scores map to 0–100. The logarithmic scale Raw PageRank-like scores are extremely skewed: on Common Crawl’s domain graph the top domain’s PageRank is 3.7 million times the floor (see Ranks and scores ). Mapping them linearly to 0–100 would put almost every domain at 0. A logarithmic mapping spreads them out, and Ahrefs notes the consequence: going from DR 70 to 71 is far harder than from 20 to 21. Because the scale is relative to Ahrefs’ whole index, a domain’s DR can also drift as other domains gain links, even if its own links do not change. URL Rating (UR) is the page-level counterpart, computed on pages rather than domains. Relation to Common Crawl’s PageRank DR and Common Crawl’s domain PageRank share their core idea but differ in inputs: Ahrefs DR Common Crawl domain PageRank Graph Ahrefs’ crawl, followed links only Common Crawl’s three-month crawl, every reference including nofollow , scripts and <link> elements Link counting first link per linking domain one arc per domain pair Output 0–100, logarithmic raw probability, sums to 1 Spam handling not described in detail none Availability commercial free, reproducible The differences in link definitions matter most at the top: Common Crawl’s ranking is led by script and font hosts that a followed-anchor graph would rank much lower. For ordinary domains the two should broadly agree in order, if not in scale. Where they disagree strongly, the cause is usually crawl coverage, spam links counted by one and not the other, or nofollow links. Reading DR for a domain Look at the referring domains and their DR. The score is driven by a few strong linking domains more than by many weak ones, so check which domains contribute. Remember what DR ignores. Traffic, content, topical relevance and spam signals are not in Ahrefs’ description. A domain can have high DR from links that search engines discount (see Link spam ). Compare at the same time. DR values from different dates are not strictly comparable, because the scale moves with the index. Cross-check. Compare with Domain Authority (Moz) , Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) and Common Crawl’s positions (see Reading a domain’s link metrics ). GoDaddy’s auction inventory does not include Ahrefs metrics, so this encyclopedia’s Auditing vendor metrics cannot test DR directly. References Ahrefs. What is Domain Rating (DR)? ahrefs.com/blog/domain-rating. Ahrefs Help Center. How is Domain Rating (DR) calculated? Page, L., Brin, S., Motwani, R., & Winograd, T. (1999). The PageRank citation ranking: Bringing order to the Web. Stanford InfoLab Technical Report 1999-66.

d: A node's score is proportional to the sum of the scores of the nodes linking to it. The cleanest form of "important nodes are those linked by important nodes", and the parent of PageRank.
a: Eigenvector Bonacich centrality Dominant eigenvector
x: Eigenvector centrality takes the recursive idea of importance literally: each node’s score is proportional to the total score of the nodes that link to it. Phillip Bonacich formalised it for social networks in 1972. The scores form an eigenvector of the Adjacency matrices and lists matrix, hence the name. The idea is elegant, and on strongly connected graphs it works. On web graphs it breaks in instructive ways, and Katz centrality and PageRank are best understood as repairs. Definition Ask for a vector with is an eigenvector of with eigenvalue . Eigenvector centrality takes the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, the spectral radius , scaled to sum to 1 (or to have unit length; only ratios matter). The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem says that this eigenvector can be chosen with no negative entries, and that it is unique and strictly positive when the graph is strongly connected. Compared with in-degree, the change is one word: a link counts with the score of its source instead of counting as 1. Compared with PageRank, two things are missing: the source’s score is not divided among its out-links, and there is no teleportation. Worked example On the running example the dominant eigenvalue is , and the scores are: Node C A G B D E F Eigenvector centrality 0.325 0.245 0.245 0.185 0 0 0 The eigenvalue has a neat origin. Inside the core, , and . Substituting gives , whose real root is the so-called plastic number, 1.3247. The core’s two cycles, of lengths 2 and 3, set the growth rate. The zeros are the important part. D, E and F score exactly 0, though D and E link into the core and D even has an in-link. Nothing in the core can reach them, and the equation propagates scores only forward from the core. E has no in-links, so ; D’s only in-link comes from E, so too; and F likewise. G, downstream of C, scores exactly as much as A, since each receives a link from one core node with the same equation. Where it breaks Zero outside the dominant component. On a graph that is not strongly connected, every node that the dominant strongly connected component cannot reach scores zero. On the web, that means most of the IN set of the The bow-tie structure and everything hanging off it. No dilution by out-degree. A node with a million out-links passes its full score along each one. Hubs inflate the scores of everything they touch, and a link farm whose members link densely to each other can build a large eigenvalue of its own and capture the whole vector. Localisation. On large graphs with heavy-tailed degrees, the dominant eigenvector tends to concentrate on the highest-degree node and its immediate neighbours, giving vanishing scores to everyone else. Martin, Zhang and Newman showed this in 2014 and proposed a non-backtracking variant to avoid it. Periodicity. Computing the vector by Power iteration fails to converge on graphs whose cycles all share a common length divisor; the iterates oscillate. The running example is safe because its core has cycles of lengths 2 and 3. In Boldi and Vigna’s Axioms for centrality eigenvector centrality satisfies density, only the half of size, and fails score monotonicity. The repairs Each fix addresses one failure: Katz centrality adds a constant to every node: . Every node gets a baseline, so nodes outside the core no longer vanish. PageRank divides each node’s score among its out-links, which tames hubs, and adds teleportation, which makes the graph strongly connected and aperiodic in effect. Its scores come from the stationary distribution of a random walk instead of the adjacency matrix itself. HITS (hubs and authorities) splits the role of a node in two, hub and authority, and takes eigenvectors of and . PageRank’s success on the web is largely the success of these repairs. Computing it Power iteration multiplies a vector by and renormalises until it stops changing. Each iteration costs one pass over the arcs; the number of iterations depends on the ratio between the two largest eigenvalue moduli, , which on real graphs can be close to 1. Unlike PageRank, nothing bounds this ratio, so convergence can be slow. Where it is used Eigenvector centrality is common in social network analysis on small, connected networks such as friendship or trade networks, where its assumptions hold. On web-scale link graphs, practitioners use its repaired descendants. Knowing the raw form remains useful: when a spectral metric gives exact zeros or wildly concentrated scores, the failure modes above are usually the reason. References Bonacich, P. (1972). d: Domains whose owners let the registration lapse, sold at auction or re-registered by someone else. Their links often outlive their sites, which is why buyers value them and why search engines watch how they are reused.
a: Expired domain Dropped domain Domain auction Aged domain Link equity
x: A domain name is rented, not owned: registrations last one to ten years and must be renewed. When an owner stops renewing, the domain eventually returns to the pool, usually after being offered at auction by the registrar. The links that other sites made to the old site do not disappear with it. Pages around the web still point at the domain, link indexes still count those links, and Common Crawl’s graph still contains the arcs if its crawlers saw them. That leftover link profile, sometimes called link equity , is what makes expired domains a market. It is also what Google’s spam policies watch most closely. The life cycle of an expiring domain For generic top-level domains such as .com , the sequence after the expiry date runs roughly: Auto-renew grace period , up to 45 days. The registrar may keep the domain active; the owner can still renew at the normal price. Many registrars auction expiring domains during this window, with the original owner able to renew until the auction closes. Redemption grace period , 30 days. The domain is deleted from the registrar’s account; the owner can recover it for a fee. Pending delete , 5 days. Nobody can recover it. Drop. The registry releases the name, and anyone can register it, usually through services that try to catch popular names the instant they drop. Country-code domains follow their own rules. GoDaddy’s daily auction inventory, the data behind this encyclopedia’s examples, mixes expiring domains, closeouts and domains listed by their owners: 1,068,241 domains on 2026-09-23. What carries over and what does not Carries over Does not Links on other sites that still point at the domain The old site’s content (unless restored) Type-in traffic and bookmarks The old owner’s reputation with customers The name itself, its length, words and TLD Any guarantee that search engines treat the domain as before Entries in link indexes and archives Manual actions are not public, so you cannot check them before buying Links decay over time: pages are edited, sites close, and links to a dead domain are removed by careful webmasters. A link index’s historic data can overstate what still exists, which is why fresh-versus-historic distinctions matter (see Backlinks and referring domains ). How much link equity is there, really? Most auctioned domains have almost none. Of the 1,068,241 domains in GoDaddy’s 2026-09-23 inventory: 948,788 (88.8%) do not appear in Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph at all: no page in its crawl linked to them. Of the 119,453 that do appear, the median has one referring domain in Common Crawl, the 90th percentile 5 and the 99th percentile 57. Only 676 domains, 0.06% of the inventory, have more than 100 referring domains in Common Crawl’s graph. Vendor metrics paint a rosier picture because they include links that carry no information: one vendor reports a median of 96 referring domains even for domains Common Crawl never saw linked, mostly from the same few spam domains (see Auditing vendor metrics ). Uses of an expired domain Rebuilding the old site or a close successor, which keeps the links relevant. A new site on a good name , using the domain for its brandability and any residual type-in traffic. Redirecting it to a related site, as after an acquisition (see Redirects and canonicalisation ). Link schemes : building a private blog network on domains with existing links, or redirecting unrelated domains into a commercial site. These are the uses search engines target (see Link spam ). Google’s position Google’s March 2024 spam policies define expired domain abuse : buying an expired domain and repurposing it primarily to manipulate rankings with content that provides little to no value to users. Google’s example is a former medical site’s domain reused for low-quality casino content. Google staff have also said for years that its systems try to recognise when a domain has changed hands and purpose, in which case the old links may not count for the new site. Neither the policy nor those statements forbid buying expired domains; they make old links worth little unless the new use makes sense for them. Checklist for evaluating one Who links, and are the links still live? Look at the referring domains themselves, not counts. Prefer recent crawl data. Is the domain in Common Crawl’s graph? If so, what are its in-degree, harmonic position and PageRank position? See Reading a domain’s link metrics and The Common Crawl web graph . What was it? Archived snapshots and anchor texts reveal the old topic, language and any spam history (see Anchor text ). Do the links fit your plan? Links from a former bakery’s suppliers help a bakery, not a crypto exchange. Does it redirect, or did it? A domain redirecting elsewhere shares its link profile with its target in many indexes. Trademarks. A name that matches someone else’s mark can be lost in a dispute, whatever its links. References ICANN. What web creators should know about our March 2024 core update and new spam policies. 5 March 2024. Google Search Central. Spam policies for Google web search (expired domain abuse).

d: The same links give three different graphs depending on whether a node is a URL, a host name or a registered domain. Each level answers different questions and hides different problems.
a: Host graph Domain graph Page graph Granularity
x: A link joins two URLs, but a link graph can treat its nodes at three levels of detail. In a page graph every URL is a node. In a host graph every host name ( blog.example.com , www.example.com ) is a node, and every link between pages on two different hosts becomes an arc between those hosts. In a domain graph every registered domain ( example.com , example.co.uk ) is a node, and all its hosts merge into it. Moving up a level shrinks the graph by orders of magnitude and changes what the rankings mean. Folding one level into the next Going from pages to hosts, or from hosts to domains, is a quotient : replace each node by the group it belongs to, keep one arc between two groups if any arc joined their members, and drop arcs inside a group. Map every URL to its host name, lower-cased. Map every host to its registered domain using the Public Suffix List, so that a.example.co.uk maps to example.co.uk , not to co.uk (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ). Collapse parallel arcs and drop self-loops. Step 3 discards most links. All internal navigation (a site’s menus, pagination, related-article blocks) links pages of the same host and disappears at the host level. Links between a domain’s own hosts, such as shop.example.com → www.example.com , disappear at the domain level. Common Crawl’s host-level extraction keeps only links between different hosts to begin with. The three levels compared Page graph Host graph Domain graph Node URL host name registered domain Typical size of a large crawl billions of nodes, tens to hundreds of billions of arcs hundreds of millions of nodes, billions of arcs about 120 million nodes, a few billion arcs Keeps internal linking yes no no Separates subdomains yes yes no Natural question which page answers a query? which site is important? which registrable name is important? Common Crawl publishes host-level and domain-level graphs. Its 2026 domain graph has 119,722,885 domains folded from the host graph; the n_hosts column of its ranks file says how many hosts went into each domain. The hosts average 1.96 per domain, about 235 million in total, and 90,515,169 domains (75.6%) consist of a single host. What merging hides Folding hosts into domains is right for most sites, where www.example.com and example.com are one organisation. It is wrong for platforms that give each customer a host of their own: blogspot.com folds 4,113,910 hosts, each a separate blog, into one node. wordpress.com folds 1,958,600 hosts. googleapis.com includes storage.googleapis.com , where Google Cloud Storage serves whatever files its customers upload. At the domain level, every link to any blog on blogspot.com counts toward one node, and every link from any customer page counts as a link from the platform. The PageRank entry shows a consequence: chaussurespuma.net sits at PageRank position 10,000 because of a single link credited to googleapis.com , whatever page actually carries it. Hosting pages on a reputable shared domain to borrow its standing is a recognised spam tactic, and the domain graph rewards it. What splitting hides The host level has the opposite problem. A site that moves from www.example.com to example.com , or spreads content across shop. , blog. and help. hosts, splits its in-links across several nodes. A host graph then underrates it, while the domain graph sums the pieces. Many sites also link heavily between their own hosts, which a host graph counts as external links and a domain graph rightly drops. Choosing a level Search ranking needs pages, because queries are answered by pages. Google’s original PageRank ran on the page graph. Crawl prioritisation works well at the host level, which is the unit of politeness for crawlers. Common Crawl ranks hosts by Harmonic centrality to decide what to fetch next. Domain valuation needs the domain level, because a registered domain is the asset that changes hands. When you buy example.com you get every host under it, including links pointing at a long-dead forum.example.com (see Expired domains ). Commercial link indexes report both levels. Ahrefs’ URL Rating and Moz’s Page Authority score pages; Domain Rating (Ahrefs) and Domain Authority (Moz) score domains. The same backlink appears in both, so a strong page on a weak domain and a weak page on a strong domain look different depending on which number you read. Granularity changes rankings The same crawl ranked at different levels gives different answers, and none of them is the “true” one. A popular blog on blogspot.com is a top host in the host graph but invisible in the domain graph, where blogspot.com itself takes the credit. When you compare a domain’s rank across sources, check that they measured the same kind of node: a host-level rank for www.example.com and a domain-level rank for example.com are not the same quantity. d: Add up one over the distance from every other node. Nodes that the whole graph reaches in few steps score high, unreachable nodes simply count zero, and link farms gain almost nothing.
a: Harmonic Harmonic closeness hc harmonicc
x: Harmonic centrality scores a node by summing the reciprocals of the distances to it from every other node. A node at distance 1 adds 1, a node at distance 2 adds ½, a node at distance 3 adds ⅓, and a node that cannot reach it adds nothing. It fixes the flaw that makes Closeness centrality useless on the web, it is the only classical measure that passes all three of Boldi and Vigna’s Axioms for centrality , and it is one of the two rankings Common Crawl publishes for every host and domain. Definition For a node in a directed graph, Grouping nodes by distance gives an equivalent form. If is the number of nodes at distance exactly from which can be reached, so the first term is the in-degree. Harmonic centrality is in-degree plus a discounted count of everyone further away. Dividing by scales it to , with 1 meaning every other node links directly to . Marchiori and Latora introduced the harmonic mean of distances for networks in 2000, Rochat proposed it as a centrality for disconnected graphs in 2009, and Boldi and Vigna’s 2014 analysis made the case for it as the geometric centrality. Worked example On the running example: Node C A G B D F E Harmonic centrality 4 3 3 2.33 1 1 0 In-degree 4 2 1 1 1 1 0 C scores 4: A, B, D and E each link to it directly. G scores 3 from a single in-link, because almost the whole graph reaches it in two steps: from C plus each from A, B, D and E. D and F score 1 each, from E alone. Compare Closeness centrality , which ranks D and F first on the same graph. Why it behaves well Unreachable nodes need no special case. They contribute zero, so the formula works unchanged on graphs that are not strongly connected, which is every real web graph. It satisfies all three axioms. Size: a clique node scores while a cycle node scores the harmonic number , so either side wins once large enough. Density: the clique side of a bridge beats the cycle side. Score monotonicity: a new arc shortens or creates distances to and can never lengthen one, so rises (see Axioms for centrality ). It rewards reach, not concentration. Unlike PageRank , it does not care how a linking node splits its attention. A link from a site with a million out-links helps exactly as much as a link from a site with one. Why link farms gain almost nothing Suppose a spammer registers 1,000 fresh domains, each linking only to a target that had no in-links. Nothing links to the farm domains, so each contributes exactly 1 to the target’s harmonic centrality, for a total of 1,000. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph a harmonic value of 1,000 sits below position 100,000,000 of 119.7 million; the domain at position 100 million already scores 7.4 million. Under PageRank the same farm is worth far more. Each farm domain holds the graph’s floor score of and passes 85% of it to the target, so 1,000 of them deliver about . That is the PageRank of the domain at position 10,000. The same thousand cheap domains that move a target from nowhere to the top ten thousand under PageRank leave it in the bottom fifth under harmonic centrality. To score well, a domain must be close to a large share of the whole web, and only links from well-reached domains provide that. Common Crawl ranks hosts by harmonic centrality to prioritise its crawl largely for this reason (see Link spam ). Computing it at scale Exact harmonic centrality needs a breadth-first search from every node on the transposed graph, in total, about steps for Common Crawl’s domain graph. Nobody computes it exactly at that scale. The HyperBall algorithm computes it approximately. It keeps one HyperLogLog counter per node estimating the size of the ball of nodes within distance , and grows every ball by one step per pass over the graph. The harmonic centrality is then The passes stop when no counter changes, which takes as many passes as the longest shortest path in the graph. Common Crawl runs WebGraph’s HyperBall on the transposed graph, with counters kept on disk ( --offline ), to produce the #harmonicc_val column of its ranks files. The approximation shows in the data. Of the 119.7 million domains, only 5,940,987 distinct harmonic values occur, and 14,903,700 domains have value 0. That is 293 more than the 14,903,407 domains with no in-links: for a few domains with a single in-link, the counters missed it. Treat harmonic values as estimates with a few percent of relative error, and differences in the last digits as noise. Position 100,000 still scores 57% of the top value, and position 10 million 43%. Small differences in value therefore become enormous differences in position: wixstatic.com and parastorage.com each receive links from about three million domains and differ in harmonic value by 18%, yet they sit at positions 26 and 81,305. When you compare two domains, compare values or log-ratios, not positions (see Ranks and scores ). googleapis.com ’s value has a direct reading: its 17.1 million referring domains contribute 17.1 million, and the remaining 11.7 million comes from domains two or more steps away. d: Every node gets two scores. A good authority is linked by good hubs, and a good hub links to good authorities. Kleinberg's algorithm computes both from the links around a query's results.
a: HITS Hubs and authorities Hub score Authority score Kleinberg
x: In 1998 Jon Kleinberg noticed that pages play two different roles on the web. Some pages are authorities , the sources worth citing on a topic. Others are hubs , curated lists that point to many authorities. The roles reinforce each other: a good authority is one that good hubs link to, and a good hub is one that links to good authorities. His algorithm, Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search (HITS), turns this circular definition into two eigenvector problems. It was developed at the same time as PageRank , at IBM’s Almaden lab rather than Stanford, and it differs in two ways: it gives each node two scores, and it was designed to run on a small graph built around each query, not on the whole web. Definition Give every node an authority score and a hub score . Starting from , repeat: normalising both vectors after each round. In matrix form, and , so after each full round and . The iteration converges to the dominant eigenvectors of (authorities) and (hubs). Kleinberg normalised to unit length; this encyclopedia scales both to sum to 1 so they read like shares. Worked example On the running example: Node C A D F B G E Authority 0.438 0.148 0.137 0.137 0.104 0.035 0 Hub 0.074 0.220 0.238 0 0.178 0 0.289 E, which nothing links to, is the best hub: it links to C, the strongest authority, and to D and F. That lifts D and F to authority 0.137, ahead of B and far ahead of G. G’s only in-link comes from C, which has the lowest hub score of any node with out-links, so G collects little authority. Under PageRank the order is reversed: G inherits C’s large PageRank and ranks third. HITS rewards being pointed at by good lists ; PageRank rewards being pointed at by important nodes . The query-time algorithm Kleinberg did not run HITS on the whole web. For each query: Take the top results from a text search engine, around 200 pages: the root set . Add pages that the root set links to, and up to about 50 pages linking to each root page: the base set , typically a few thousand pages. Drop links between pages of the same host, which mostly reflect navigation, not endorsement. Run the iteration on the base set and return the top authorities and hubs. Running at query time makes the scores topic-specific, which PageRank’s single global vector is not. It also makes every query cost a graph construction and an eigenvector computation, which is why HITS in its original form never ran at the scale of a major search engine. The search engine Teoma, later the core of Ask.com, built its ranking on a related idea of hub and authority communities within each topic. Weaknesses Topic drift. If the base set contains a dense, tightly knit group of pages on a different subject, its mutual links dominate the dominant eigenvector, and the results drift to that group. Lempel and Moran called this the tightly knit community effect; SALSA was designed to resist it. Easy to game. Anyone can make a strong hub: publish a page linking to well-known authorities. Then add links from that hub to your own pages. The hub score is earned by out-links, which cost nothing. Non-uniqueness. If the largest eigenvalue of is repeated, which happens when the base set splits into disconnected parts, the limit depends on the starting vector, and small changes to the graph can swing the results. Axioms. HITS authority satisfies density and only the half of size, and fails score monotonicity: a new in-link can shift the dominant eigenvector to another part of the graph and lower a node’s authority (see Axioms for centrality ). Improvements Bharat and Henzinger (1998) weighted links so that many links from one host to another count as one vote in total, and pruned base-set pages whose text did not match the query. Both changes reduced drift. SALSA replaced the eigenvectors of with the stationary distribution of a random walk that alternates forward and backward steps, which makes authority scores proportional to in-degree within each connected piece and immune to the tightly knit community effect. HITS beyond search The hub–authority split fits any bipartite-looking relationship. It has been used to rank users and items in recommendation, reviewers and products, and citing and cited papers. On the web, hubs survive as an idea: link directories, “resources” pages and curated lists are hubs, and a link from a page that links mostly to strong authorities in a field is still a better signal than one from a page that links to anything. d: Grow a probabilistic counter around every node by one link per pass over the graph. After a few dozen passes you know, for every node, roughly how many nodes lie within each distance, and with it harmonic centrality, closeness and the distance distribution.
a: HyperANF ANF Approximate neighbourhood function
x: Geometric centralities and distance statistics need, for each node , the number of nodes within distance of it, for every . Computing that exactly takes a breadth-first search from every node, impossible on a graph with a hundred million nodes (see Paths, distance and reachability ). HyperBall , by Paolo Boldi and Sebastiano Vigna, computes it approximately for all nodes at once: it keeps one HyperLogLog counter per node and grows all the counters together, one step per pass over the graph. Common Crawl computes the Harmonic centrality of every host and domain with it. The idea: balls grow by union Let be the ball of radius around : the nodes within distance . Balls satisfy a simple recurrence: Everything within steps of is ’s own ball plus everything within steps of one of its successors. Storing the balls as sets would be hopeless, but HyperLogLog counters merge by a register-wise maximum, so the union of counters is cheap. One pass over all arcs, taking maxima, turns every node’s radius- counter into its radius- counter. The size estimate is read off each counter after each pass. For centralities based on incoming distances, such as harmonic centrality on the web, the same recurrence runs on the transposed graph, so that balls collect the nodes that can reach . Common Crawl runs HyperBall on domain-t.graph . From balls to centralities The number of nodes at distance exactly is , so every geometric measure follows: Harmonic centrality: . Closeness and Lin’s index: from the sum of distances, , and the final ball size. The neighbourhood function: summing over all counts the pairs within distance , from which come the distance distribution, the average distance and the effective diameter (see The neighbourhood function ). The passes continue until no counter changes, which takes as many passes as the longest shortest path in the graph. Real graphs have long, thin tendrils, so the last passes change few counters; HyperBall tracks which counters changed and, in later passes, only processes nodes with a changed successor. History ANF (Palmer, Gibbons and Faloutsos, 2002) introduced the approach with Flajolet–Martin counters. HyperANF (Boldi, Rosa and Vigna, 2011) switched to HyperLogLog counters, packed registers into machine words and computed register-wise maxima with broadword tricks, many registers per instruction. It made the neighbourhood function of billion-node graphs routine on a single machine. HyperBall (Boldi and Vigna, 2013) generalised HyperANF to compute geometric centralities for every node, added the changed-counter optimisation, and could keep counters on disk ( --offline ) to fit very large graphs. HyperANF produced the most-cited distance result of its era. In 2011, Backstrom, Boldi, Rosa, Ugander and Vigna ran it on Facebook’s entire friendship graph, 721 million active users and 69 billion friendship links, and found an average distance of 4.74: “four degrees of separation”, not six. Cost Each pass reads the graph once, sequentially, which is fast for a graph in compressed WebGraph form, and touches every counter. Memory is dominated by the counters: nodes times registers of 5 or 6 bits, times two if the previous and current counters are kept separately. For 119.7 million domains with registers of 5 bits, one set of counters takes 4.8 GB. Halving the error means quadrupling , and the memory with it, which is why HyperBall’s offline mode streams counters from disk. Accuracy Each counter’s estimate has a relative standard error of about , and errors in successive ball sizes are correlated, so derived quantities inherit an error of the same order. HyperANF’s authors reported relative errors for the neighbourhood function in line with the counter error. Individual centralities can be noticeably off, especially for small values: in Common Crawl’s 2026 ranks, 293 domains with in-links have an estimated harmonic centrality of exactly 0, and only 5.9 million distinct values occur among 119.7 million domains. Positions near the top, where values differ by large margins, are reliable; positions among millions of near-equal values are not (see Ranks and scores ). When to use something else Exact values for a few nodes. A breadth-first search from each node of interest, on the transposed graph, gives its exact harmonic centrality in per node. Betweenness. HyperBall counts reachable nodes, not shortest paths through a node; Betweenness centrality needs Brandes’ algorithm or sampling. Small graphs. Below a few million arcs, exact all-pairs BFS is fast enough and avoids the approximation entirely. References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2013). d: A counter that estimates how many distinct items it has seen, within a few percent, using a few bytes. Its counters merge by taking maxima, which is what lets HyperBall count reachable nodes for a hundred million nodes at once.
a: HLL Distinct counting Cardinality estimation Approximate counting
x: How many distinct domains link to a site? How many nodes lie within three links of a node? Counting distinct items exactly requires remembering every item seen, which for a hundred million nodes, each needing its own count, is far too much memory. HyperLogLog (HLL), published by Philippe Flajolet, Éric Fusy, Olivier Gandouet and Frédéric Meunier in 2007, estimates the number of distinct items with a relative error around using tiny registers, and two counters can be merged into a counter for the union of their sets with a register-by-register maximum. That merge is what makes approximate Harmonic centrality computable on web-scale graphs (see HyperBall ). The idea Hash each item to a long string of random-looking bits. In a uniformly random bit string, the first 1 appears at position 1 with probability ½, at position 2 with probability ¼, and at position with probability . If you have seen distinct items, the largest such position among their hashes is likely to be around . Remember only that maximum, a number below 64 that fits in 6 bits, and you have a rough estimate of : . Duplicates do not matter, because the same item always hashes to the same string. One maximum is a very noisy estimate. HyperLogLog splits the stream: the first bits of each hash choose one of registers , and each register keeps the maximum first-1 position of the items routed to it. The estimate combines all registers with a harmonic mean, which tames the outliers: where is register ’s maximum and a bias-correcting constant (about 0.7213 for large ). The standard error is about . Accuracy against memory Registers Memory at 6 bits each Typical relative error 16 12 bytes 26% 128 96 bytes 9.2% 1,024 768 bytes 3.3% 16,384 12 KB 0.8% The memory does not depend on how many items are counted: 12 KB estimates a billion distinct items as well as a million. The error does not shrink with more data, only with more registers. Merging counters Two HLL counters built with the same hash function and the same merge by taking, for each register, the larger of the two values. The result is exactly the counter that would have been built from the union of the two streams. No other common sketch makes union this cheap, and it is the property that graph algorithms exploit: the set of nodes within distance of is the union of ’s own ball and the balls of its neighbours, so one round of register-wise maxima over all arcs grows every node’s ball by one step. Intersections are not so easy. Estimating the overlap of two sets from their HLL counters, by inclusion–exclusion, has large errors when the overlap is small relative to the sets. Practical refinements Small cardinalities. When many registers are still empty, the raw estimate is biased; the original paper switches to linear counting , with empty registers. HyperLogLog++. Heule, Nunkesser and Hall at Google used 64-bit hashes to avoid collisions at large cardinalities, an empirical bias correction for the mid range, and a sparse representation for small counts. Most production systems implement this variant. Hash quality. The analysis assumes the hash behaves like a random function. A weak hash on structured inputs, such as sequential integer node ids, can bias every counter the same way. Uses in link analysis Neighbourhood functions and centralities. HyperBall keeps one HLL counter per node and computes, for every node, how many nodes lie within each distance. From those counts come Harmonic centrality , closeness, the The neighbourhood function and the effective diameter of graphs with billions of arcs. Distinct referring domains. Counting the distinct domains that link to each site over a stream of crawled links is a cardinality problem per target; HLL counters answer it in a fixed small memory per site. Deduplication statistics. Estimating how many distinct URLs, hosts or pages a crawl has seen. The approximation leaves traces. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain ranks, computed with HyperBall, 293 domains with at least one in-link have harmonic value 0: for those domains the counters failed to register a single arrival, which happens when the newcomer’s hash lands in a register that already holds an equal or larger value. Treat HLL-based values as estimates with a known relative error, not as exact counts. References Flajolet, P., Fusy, É., Gandouet, O., & Meunier, F. (2007). HyperLogLog: The analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm. AofA 2007 , DMTCS Proceedings, 137–156. Heule, S., Nunkesser, M., & Hall, A. (2013). HyperLogLog in practice: Algorithmic engineering of a state of the art cardinality estimation algorithm. EDBT 2013 , 683–692. Flajolet, P., & Martin, G. N. (1985). Probabilistic counting algorithms for data base applications. Journal of Computer and System Sciences 31(2), 182–209.

d: Repeatedly peel off every node with fewer than k links until none is left. The layer at which a node falls off, its core number, measures how deeply it is embedded in a dense part of the graph, in linear time.
a: k-core Core number Coreness k-shell Degeneracy Peeling
x: The k-core of a graph is the largest subgraph in which every node has at least neighbours within the subgraph . Stephen Seidman introduced it in 1983 as a way to find cohesive groups in social networks. Computing every node’s core number , the largest for which it belongs to the -core, takes a simple peeling procedure that runs in time linear in the number of links. The result separates a graph into nested shells, from the loosely attached periphery to the densest core, and it is one of the cheapest structural signals for spotting artificially dense groups such as link farms. Definition and peeling On an undirected graph: Set . Repeatedly remove every node with fewer than remaining neighbours. Removing a node lowers its neighbours’ degrees, which may trigger more removals. When no node can be removed, the survivors form the -core. Nodes removed at this stage have core number . Increase and continue. The cores are nested: the 3-core lies inside the 2-core, which lies inside the 1-core. The largest with a non-empty core is the graph’s degeneracy . The set of nodes with core number exactly is the -shell . Batagelj and Zaversnik showed how to compute all core numbers in time by keeping nodes in buckets by current degree and always peeling from the lowest bucket. Worked example Ignore directions in the running example. Degrees are A 3, B 2, C 5, D 3, E 3, F 1, G 1. 2-core. F and G have one neighbour each and fall off first. E’s degree drops to 2 and C’s to 4. Everyone left has at least 2 neighbours, so the 2-core is {A, B, C, D, E}. 3-core. Within the 2-core, B (neighbours A and C) and E (neighbours C and D) have only 2. Removing them leaves A, C and D with two neighbours each, so they fall too. The 3-core is empty. Core numbers: A, B, C, D and E have 2; F and G have 1. The degeneracy is 2. C has the highest degree, 5, yet its core number is no higher than B’s: degree measures how many neighbours a node has, core number how well connected those neighbours are to each other. Directed graphs Link graphs are directed, and two variants keep the direction. An in-core requires every node to have at least in-links from within the subgraph; an out-core requires out-links. Giatsidis, Thilikos and Vazirgiannis combined the two in D-cores : subgraphs where every node has at least in-links and out-links inside. A group of domains that all link to each other forms a D-core with large and ; a popular site linked from everywhere but linking to few of its linkers does not. What core numbers are good for Finding the dense centre. The innermost cores of social and information networks contain the tightly interlinked elite: in a web graph, major portals, platforms and infrastructure domains that link to each other. Predicting influence. Kitsak and colleagues found that a node’s k-shell predicted how far an epidemic starting there would spread better than its degree or betweenness: what matters is being embedded among other well-connected nodes. Spotting link farms. A clique of domains, each linking to all others, is a -core by itself. Large organic communities rarely interlink that completely, so an unusually deep core with few in-links from outside is a structural signature of a farm. A domain whose in-links come mostly from members of such a core deserves scrutiny. Speeding up other algorithms. Processing nodes in degeneracy order bounds the work of triangle counting and clique enumeration (see Clustering coefficient ). Limits Core numbers are coarse: in a large graph many nodes share each value, so they rank poorly on their own. They are also sensitive to a handful of links near the threshold, since one removed link can drop a node, and through it its neighbours, by a whole shell. Use them as a structural feature next to Degree , PageRank and Community detection , not as a centrality in their own right. References Seidman, S. B. (1983). Network structure and minimum degree. (2011). D-cores: Measuring collaboration of directed graphs based on degeneracy. ICDM 2011 , 201–210. Kitsak, M., Gallos, L. K., Havlin, S., Liljeros, F., Muchnik, L., Stanley, H. E., & Makse, H. A. (2010). Identification of influential spreaders in complex networks. Nature Physics 6, 888–893.

d: Count every walk that ends at a node, weighting a walk of length k by β to the power k. Short walks count most, everyone gets a baseline, and one parameter slides the measure from in-degree to eigenvector centrality.
a: Katz Katz index Attenuation factor Alpha centrality
x: Leo Katz proposed in 1953 to measure a person’s status by counting not only who chooses them directly but also who chooses those people, and so on, with each extra step counting less. On a link graph, Katz centrality counts every walk that ends at a node, weighting walks of length by for some attenuation factor . It sits between Degree centrality , which counts walks of length 1, and Eigenvector centrality , which it approaches as grows. It also fixes eigenvector centrality’s habit of giving most of the web a score of zero. Definition Since counts the walks of length from to (see Adjacency matrices and lists ), the number of length- walks ending at each node is the vector . Katz centrality sums them with geometric weights: The series converges if and only if , where is the largest eigenvalue of . Rearranging gives a recursive form that shows the connection to eigenvector centrality: Each in-link contributes its source’s score plus one . The “+1” is the whole difference from eigenvector centrality: every node passes on at least a baseline, so nodes outside the dominant strongly connected component no longer vanish. The two limits As , walks of length 1 dominate, and the ranking converges to in-degree. As , long walks dominate, the series grows without bound, and the ranking converges to eigenvector centrality. Between the limits, is a dial between local popularity and global, recursive prestige. Bonacich’s alpha centrality and PageRank both belong to the same family, differing in what they add to each node and whether they divide by out-degree. Worked example The running example’s largest eigenvalue is 1.3247, so must stay below . With : Node C A G B D F E Katz () 1.868 1.250 0.860 0.675 0.300 0.300 0 Eigenvector 0.325 0.245 0.245 0.185 0 0 0 D and F each receive one walk of length 1, from E, and nothing longer, since nothing reaches E: their score is exactly . Unlike eigenvector centrality, Katz separates A from G: A gets walks from inside the core, G only through C. Drag β towards 0.75 in the lab and watch the scores explode as the series approaches divergence: Axioms Katz satisfies density and score monotonicity, and the half of the size axiom (see Axioms for centrality ). Adding a link adds new walks into and removes none, so ’s score always rises. In that respect Katz behaves better than eigenvector centrality and as well as PageRank . Computing it The recursive form gives an iteration: start from and repeat . Each step costs one pass over the arcs and the error shrinks by a factor of about per step. Alternatively, solve the sparse linear system with Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel iterations, as for PageRank (see PageRank as a linear system ). The trouble with β on the web The admissible range of depends on , and on a web graph that number is set by its densest corner. The spectral radius of a graph is at least the smallest in-degree inside any of its subgraphs, counting only arcs within the subgraph. One cluster of a few thousand domains that all link to each other therefore pushes into the thousands and forces below for the whole graph. With that small, Katz centrality is in-degree plus a rounding error everywhere outside the cluster. On a graph full of link farms , the farms decide the parameter. PageRank avoids this by dividing each node’s score among its out-links, which caps the spectral radius of its matrix at 1. Where it is used Katz centrality and its relative, the Katz index between pairs of nodes, are popular in social network analysis and in link prediction, where the weighted count of walks between two nodes predicts future links between them. In web ranking it is mostly of historical and conceptual importance: it showed in 1953 how to count indirect endorsements with decay, an idea PageRank refined forty-five years later. References Katz, L. (1953). A new status index derived from sociometric analysis. Psychometrika 18(1), 39–43. Bonacich, P., & Lloyd, P. (2001). Eigenvector-like measures of centrality for asymmetric relations. Social Networks 23(3), 191–201. Vigna, S. (2016). Spectral ranking. Network Science 4(4), 433–445.

d: Compare two rankings by counting pairs of items they order the same way and pairs they order oppositely. The standard measure of agreement between centralities, computable in O(n log n) time.
a: Kendall tau Kendall rank correlation τ Concordant pairs Discordant pairs
x: Two centralities rarely produce the same ranking. Kendall’s τ (tau), introduced by Maurice Kendall in 1938, measures how much two rankings agree by looking at every pair of items. A pair is concordant if both rankings put the same item first, and discordant if they disagree. τ is the excess of concordant over discordant pairs, scaled to lie between −1 (one ranking is the reverse of the other) and +1 (identical). It is the most common way to report how similar two link-based rankings are. Definition For items scored by and by , look at all pairs . With concordant pairs (the signs of and agree) and discordant pairs (they differ), and no ties, Equivalently, . A τ of 0.5 means three quarters of pairs agree and one quarter disagree. Ties Rankings from centralities are full of ties: equal in-degrees, PageRank floors, harmonic values shared by millions. τ_b corrects for them: where counts pairs tied in only and pairs tied in only; pairs tied in both are left out. τ_b reaches ±1 exactly when the two rankings agree, or exactly disagree, including on their ties. Most software computes τ_b by default. Worked example Compare PageRank on the running example with other measures: Compared with PageRank Concordant Discordant Tied in one only τ_b Harmonic centrality 19 0 1 0.975 In-degree 15 0 5 0.866 HITS authority 15 5 0 0.500 Closeness 11 9 0 0.100 Harmonic centrality agrees with PageRank on every pair except one it calls a tie (A and G both score 3). In-degree never contradicts PageRank but ties five pairs that PageRank separates. Closeness, which ranks D and F first, agrees on barely more pairs than it contradicts. On real data For a random sample of 4,000 domains from the 2026-09-23 auction inventory that appear in Common Crawl’s graph: Pair of rankings Kendall τ_b Spearman ρ (all 119,453 such domains) Harmonic position, PageRank position 0.51 0.69 Harmonic centrality, in-degree 0.53 0.69 PageRank, in-degree 0.58 Kendall’s τ is typically smaller in magnitude than Spearman’s ρ on the same data, so the two are not interchangeable; always say which one you report (see Spearman’s rho ). A τ of 0.51 means that for a random pair of these domains, the two Common Crawl centralities order them the same way about three times in four. Computing it fast Counting all pairs costs : about pairs for Common Crawl’s 119.7 million domains. William Knight’s 1966 algorithm reduces it to : sort the items by , then count, while merge-sorting by , how many inversions the merge has to perform. Each inversion is a discordant pair. Ties need extra bookkeeping, and the algorithm handles them in the same time bound. With it, τ between two full web-scale rankings takes seconds. What τ does not say Every pair counts the same. Swapping positions 1 and 2 costs as much as swapping positions 50,000,001 and 50,000,002. For rankings, where the top matters far more than the tail, that is usually wrong. Weighted tau weights pairs by their importance, and Rank-biased overlap compares only the tops. Ties in the tail dominate. On web-scale data, most pairs involve two tail nodes. Millions of near-floor PageRank values, ordered by noise, can swamp the agreement at the top. Small differences look big. Two rankings computed from the same graph with slightly different parameters can disagree on billions of tail pairs while agreeing on everything that matters. Always look at the top separately. That observation, that classical τ between two web-scale rankings is driven by the unimportant majority of nodes, is what led Vigna to design Weighted tau . References Kendall, M. G. (1938).
