A computer method for calculating Kendall’s tau with ungrouped data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 61(314), 436–439. Vigna, S. (2015). A weighted correlation index for rankings with ties. WWW 2015 , 1166–1176.

d: The rel values that let a publisher say a link is not an endorsement. Introduced in 2005 against comment spam, extended in 2019, and since then treated by Google as hints rather than commands.
a: nofollow rel=nofollow sponsored ugc dofollow rel attribute
x: An HTML link can carry a rel attribute describing its relationship to the target. Three values matter for link analysis. nofollow says “I do not vouch for this link.” sponsored says it was paid for. ugc says a user, not the site owner, put it there. Search engines use these values to decide how much, if anything, a link should contribute to rankings like PageRank . The attributes exist because links became valuable enough to manufacture, and every site that accepts user content became a target. Nofollow, 2005 In January 2005, Google, Yahoo! and MSN jointly introduced rel="nofollow" to fight comment spam : automated posting of links in blog comments, guestbooks and wikis to raise the target’s ranking. Blog software added the attribute to every comment link, so that spam links would pass nothing and the incentive would disappear. Nofollow soon spread beyond comments. Sites used it on links they did not want to endorse, and Google asked that paid links carry it, so that bought links would not pass PageRank. Some site owners also used it on their own internal links, trying to steer PageRank towards important pages, a practice called PageRank sculpting . In 2009 Google explained that a nofollowed link still takes its share of the page’s PageRank, which then simply evaporates instead of being redistributed, which ended the practice. Sponsored and ugc, 2019 On 10 September 2019 Google added two values: Value Meaning Typical use rel="sponsored" the link is an advertisement, sponsorship or other paid placement affiliate links, paid reviews, advertorials rel="ugc" the link appears in user-generated content comments, forum posts, profiles rel="nofollow" any link the site does not want to vouch for catch-all, still valid Values can be combined, as in rel="ugc nofollow" . In the same announcement Google changed what all three mean: they became hints about which links to consider or exclude within Search, rather than directives to ignore the link. From 1 March 2020 they also became hints for crawling and indexing. Google may now use a nofollowed link as a signal, for example to discover a URL or understand a page, when it judges that useful. How link graphs treat them The attribute lives in the HTML, so whether a link graph honours it depends on the pipeline: Common Crawl’s graph ignores it. Its extractor records every link a page references, with no filtering on rel . A nofollowed link and a followed link become identical arcs (see The Common Crawl web graph ). Vendors usually distinguish. Link indexes label each backlink “dofollow” or “nofollow”. Ahrefs states that its Domain Rating (Ahrefs) counts only dofollow links, so a domain linked only through nofollow links gains no Domain Rating from them. Other vendors fold the distinction into their models in undisclosed ways. Search engines weigh them case by case , as hints, since 2019. “Dofollow” is not an HTML value; it simply means a link without nofollow , sponsored or ugc . Other rel values Several common rel values have nothing to do with ranking. noopener and noreferrer control security and the Referer header when a link opens a new window. canonical , on a <link> element rather than an anchor, names a page’s preferred URL and affects how search engines consolidate duplicates (see Redirects and canonicalisation ). A page-wide <meta name="robots" content="nofollow"> asks crawlers not to follow any link on the page. What it means for a domain A natural link profile includes nofollow links. Social profiles, forum mentions and news comments are nofollowed by default. A profile made entirely of followed links from small sites is more suspicious than one with a realistic mix. Nofollowed links still bring visitors and help search engines discover pages, even when they pass little ranking weight. Paid links without sponsored or nofollow violate Google’s spam policies. Buying a domain whose links were mostly bought, unlabelled, carries a risk that those links are, or will be, discounted (see Link penalties and the disavow tool ). Compare like with like. A referring-domain count that includes nofollow links and one that excludes them are different quantities. References Google Official Blog (2005). Preventing comment spam. 18 January 2005. Google Search Central Blog (2019). Evolving “nofollow”: new ways to identify the nature of links. 10 September 2019. Google Search Central. Qualify your outbound links to Google. developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/qualify-outbound-links.

t: Link penalties and the disavow tool
d: How Google acts on manipulative links, from the 2012 Penguin update and manual actions to today's practice of silently ignoring spam links, and what the disavow tool does.
a: Penguin Manual action Unnatural links Disavow Link spam update SpamBrain
x: Search engines cannot stop people from manufacturing links, so they decide what such links are worth. Google’s approach has moved in stages: from crude penalties for sites with manipulative link profiles, to a mix of algorithmic demotions and human review, to the current emphasis on detecting spam links and simply giving them no weight. Knowing the history matters to anyone buying a domain, because past link practices can leave lasting marks, some visible only to the domain’s owner. Timeline Date Change January 2005 rel="nofollow" introduced to neutralise comment spam (see Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) ) 24 April 2012 Penguin update: demotes sites violating guidelines with manipulative links 16 October 2012 Disavow links tool launched in Webmaster Tools September 2016 Penguin 4.0 : runs in real time as part of the core algorithm and devalues spam links rather than demoting whole sites September 2019 sponsored and ugc added; all three attributes become hints July 2021 Link spam update targeting links from sponsored, guest and affiliate content without proper attributes 14 December 2022 Link spam update using SpamBrain to neutralise unnatural links, both bought links and sites built to pass outgoing links March 2024 Spam policies add expired domain abuse and site reputation abuse Algorithmic devaluation Penguin’s first versions ran periodically and demoted whole sites, sometimes for many months until the next refresh. Penguin 4.0 changed both properties: it updates as pages are recrawled, and it acts on the spam signals themselves, adjusting rankings by ignoring manipulative links rather than punishing the site. Google describes its current link spam systems the same way: SpamBrain identifies links that look built for manipulation and neutralises them, and any ranking those links provided disappears. In graph terms, devaluation deletes arcs before the ranking is computed. A site that relied on spam links falls back to the standing its remaining links support. Nobody outside the search engine can see which arcs were deleted, which is why a domain’s third-party metrics can stay high after its links stopped counting. Manual actions Google’s human reviewers can apply a manual action for unnatural links to your site (links pointing in look manipulative) or unnatural links from your site (the site sells or exchanges links). A manual action is reported in the site owner’s Search Console account, can affect part of a site or all of it, and stays until the owner fixes the problem and files a reconsideration request . Only a verified owner can see manual actions, so a domain’s buyer usually learns about one only after taking ownership. The disavow tool The disavow tool lets a site owner upload a list of URLs or whole domains whose links to the site Google should ignore. It was launched in October 2012, primarily for sites with a manual action that could not get spam links removed. Google’s guidance has since narrowed its use: most sites never need it, because Google already ignores most spam links on its own; it is meant for cases where you have a significant number of spammy, artificial or low-quality links pointing to the site that resulted, or will likely result, in a manual action. Disavowing good links can harm a site, since they then stop counting. Disavow files are private to Google and to the site’s owner. Third-party link metrics cannot see them and keep counting disavowed links. Expired domain abuse The 2024 policy on expired domain abuse defines it as buying an expired domain and repurposing it primarily to manipulate rankings by hosting content of little or no value to users, relying on the domain’s past reputation. Google’s example is a domain that used to belong to a medical site being used for low-quality casino content. The policy targets the use, not the purchase: buying an expired domain to build a genuine site, or to continue the previous one, is not abuse (see Expired domains ). What it means for a domain Check the history before buying. Archived snapshots, anchor texts and the topics of referring sites show whether the domain was used for link schemes (see Anchor text ). Assume spam links count for nothing. Value comes from links a search engine would keep: links from real sites, in context, that make sense for the domain. Check Search Console after buying. Verify ownership and look for manual actions and existing disavow files left by a previous owner. Do not treat vendor scores as proof. A high score built on links Google ignores is a number about the vendor’s crawl, not about rankings (see Auditing vendor metrics ). References Google Search Central Blog (2012). A new tool to disavow links. 16 October 2012. Google Search Central. Disavow links to your site. support.google.com/webmasters/answer/2648487. Google Search Central. Manual actions report. support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9044175. Google Search Central Blog (2022). December 2022 link spam update. 14 December 2022. Google Search Central Blog (2024). What web creators should know about our March 2024 core update and new spam policies. 5 March 2024.

d: Links created to manipulate rankings rather than to help readers. Link farms, bought links, private blog networks and parasite pages, what each does to PageRank and harmonic centrality, and the traces they leave in a link graph.
a: Link farm PBN Private blog network Link scheme Paid links Parasite hosting Comment spam
x: Once links influence rankings, links have a price, and some people manufacture them. Link spam is any link placed primarily to manipulate a ranking rather than to serve a reader. Google’s spam policies call such practices link schemes and name examples: buying or selling links that pass ranking credit, excessive link exchanges, large-scale guest posting with keyword-rich anchors, automated link creation, and links hidden in widgets and footers. Every link metric in this encyclopedia is a target, and each responds to spam differently. The main techniques Link farms. Many sites created to link to each other and to a few target sites. Gyöngyi and Garcia-Molina analysed the optimal structure: a set of “booster” pages that each link only to the target, with the target linking back, traps the random surfer and multiplies the target’s PageRank. Private blog networks (PBNs). A more careful farm: sites built on Expired domains that already have links of their own, each made to look independent, with different hosts, designs and owners on record, linking out to the operator’s commercial sites. Bought links. Paid placements in articles or sidebars on real sites, without the sponsored or nofollow attribute (see Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) ). Comment, forum and profile spam. Automated posting of links wherever a site accepts user input. This is what nofollow was invented for in 2005. Parasite pages. Pages hosted on a reputable domain, through user uploads, hacked sites or rented sections, to borrow its standing. In a domain graph they are credited to the host domain: in Common Crawl’s 2026 graph, a single link credited to googleapis.com , which serves Google Cloud Storage files, lifts chaussurespuma.net to PageRank position 10,000 on seven referring domains (see PageRank ). Google’s 2024 site reputation abuse policy targets the rented-section version of this practice. Mass out-linking. Generated pages that link to millions of sites, to sell links or to catch traffic. mp3fresh.net links to 6,113,126 domains in Common Crawl’s 2026 graph, one domain in twenty, the largest out-degree of any domain. Subdomain farms. Wildcard DNS lets one domain answer for unlimited hosts. In the 2026 graph hub.biz folds 1,222,261 hosts and adgo.kr 423,413 (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ). What spam buys under each metric Metric Effect of 1,000 new domains that link only to a target In-degree, referring domains +1,000, full effect PageRank about , from the floor to position ~10,000 in Common Crawl’s graph Harmonic centrality +1,000 to a value where the median domain has millions: still below position 100,000,000 TrustRank nothing, unless a trusted site links into the farm The difference comes from what each metric counts. In-degree counts links; PageRank counts probability flowing in, and even worthless farm domains pass their teleport share; harmonic centrality counts closeness to the whole web, which farm domains, linked by nobody, cannot provide. The Harmonic centrality entry works through the arithmetic. Traces in the graph Spam leaves structural fingerprints: Degree anomalies. Common Crawl’s 2026 in-degree distribution has a bump of about 39,400 domains with in-degree between 19,000 and 29,000, where the smooth tail predicts fewer than 2,000, with a matching bump in out-degree (see Degree distributions and power laws ). Organic link growth produces smooth distributions; coordinated networks produce bumps. Dense, isolated clusters. Farms link internally far more than to the outside, so they show up as tight communities with high clustering , deep cores and few in-links from the rest of the web (see Community detection ). Mass from outside the trusted web. A high-ranking node whose PageRank comes mostly from nodes unreachable from reputable seeds has high Spam mass . Uniform patterns. Identical anchor texts, links appearing in bursts on newly registered domains, shared hosting, templates and analytics IDs. These are not graph features, but link indexes and search engines combine them with graph features. How search engines respond Google’s responses have shifted from punishing to ignoring. The 2012 Penguin update demoted sites with manipulative link profiles; since Penguin 4.0 in 2016, Google says it mostly devalues spam links rather than demoting whole sites. Its December 2022 link spam update used SpamBrain, an AI-based system, to detect both sites buying links and sites used to pass outgoing links, and to neutralise their links. Manual actions for unnatural links remain for flagrant cases (see Link penalties and the disavow tool ). What it means for a domain Link spam is the main reason a domain’s metrics can look strong and be worth little: Metrics can be bought. Referring-domain counts, and scores built mainly on them, rise with farm links. Check who links, not how many. Discounted links are invisible in the numbers. A domain whose links search engines already ignore keeps its vendor scores, because vendors cannot see the discount. A spam past can follow a domain. An expired domain used in a PBN or for parasite pages may carry manual actions, or links that attract new ones if reused (see Expired domains ). Prefer metrics that resist farms. Harmonic centrality and trust-based scores are harder to inflate than counts; compare several sources (see Reading a domain’s link metrics ). References Gyöngyi, Z., & Garcia-Molina, H. (2005). Web spam taxonomy. AIRWeb 2005 . Gyöngyi, Z., & Garcia-Molina, H. (2005). Link spam alliances. VLDB 2005 , 517–528. Google Search Central. Spam policies for Google web search (link spam; site reputation abuse; expired domain abuse). Google Search Central Blog (2022). December 2022 link spam update. 14 December 2022.

d: Checking Semrush and Majestic numbers from one day of GoDaddy's auction inventory against Common Crawl's open graph. A referring-domain floor made of the same few domains, a Majestic feed that is mostly empty, and a nearly constant Authority Score.
a: Metric audit Vendor metric quality Spam floor Semrush referring domains
x: Link metrics are only useful if they vary with the thing they claim to measure. This entry tests the third-party metrics in GoDaddy’s public auction inventory against an independent reference, Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph. The results are specific to one day and one population, auction listings, and to the vendor values as delivered in GoDaddy’s feed, but the method applies to any metric and any list of domains. Data and method Listings. GoDaddy’s inventory export of 2026-09-23: 1,068,241 domains with, among other fields, Semrush Authority Score, referring domains, backlinks, “Indexed Pages” and the top three referring domains, and Majestic Trust Flow, Citation Flow, backlinks and referring domains. Reference. For each listed domain, its presence, in-degree, harmonic position and PageRank position in Common Crawl’s cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug domain graph, joined by domain name (see The Common Crawl web graph ). 119,453 listed domains (11.2%) are in the graph; 948,788 are not. Statistics. Medians and percentiles within groups defined by Common Crawl in-degree; shares of zero values; Spearman rank correlations (see Spearman’s rho ); and the probability that a metric ranks a random in-graph domain above a random absent one (the AUC). Common Crawl is not ground truth: it is one crawl, it counts more link types than most vendors, and it ignores nofollow . It is, however, independent, open and the same for every domain, which is what a reference needs. d: Estimate PageRank by actually running random surfers and counting their visits. A few walks per node rank the important nodes well, the walks parallelise trivially, and they can be updated as links change.
a: Random walk sampling Complete path method End-point method Fingerprints
x: The The random surfer story can be run literally. Launch surfers, let each follow random links until it decides to teleport, and count how often each node is visited. The visit frequencies estimate PageRank . Avrachenkov, Litvak, Nemirovsky and Osipova analysed such estimators in 2007 and found, as their title put it, that “one iteration is sufficient”: a single short walk from every node already ranks the important nodes well. Monte Carlo methods trade precision on unimportant nodes for simplicity, trivial parallelism and cheap updates, and they are the standard way to compute Personalized PageRank for many seeds at once. The estimators Each walk starts at a node, and at every step it stops with probability ; otherwise it follows a random out-link, or jumps to a random node if it stands on a dangling node. The number of steps is geometric, with mean for . End-point method. Start walks at uniformly random nodes and record only where each walk stops. The stopping position of a walk is distributed exactly as PageRank, so the fraction of walks ending at estimates . Complete-path method. Start walks from every node and count every visit along every walk, not only the last. The share of all visits that land on estimates . Using every step reduces the variance for the same number of walks. Both estimators are unbiased. The complete-path method with walks from every node is the one Avrachenkov and colleagues recommended. Worked example On the running example, with walks from each of the 7 nodes: Walks per node Total steps C A G B Largest error 1 48 0.292 0.188 0.208 0.104 0.034 10 453 0.294 0.181 0.203 0.135 0.026 100 4,456 0.302 0.211 0.168 0.144 0.010 1,000 46,939 0.297 0.202 0.179 0.138 0.003 10,000 466,370 0.297 0.205 0.177 0.139 0.001 exact 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 One walk per node, 48 steps in all, already identifies C as the top node. The error shrinks like : a hundred times more walks buy ten times more precision. Exact power iteration needs about 43 passes over 10 arcs to reach , so on this tiny graph sampling is no bargain. On a graph of billions of arcs, where one pass is expensive and only the top of the ranking matters, it can be. Why the top is easy and the tail is hard For a node with PageRank , the number of visits among total steps is roughly Poisson with mean , so the relative error is about . A node with ten times the average PageRank gets ten times the visits and times better relative precision. With one walk per node on a graph of nodes, each walk makes visits counting its start, so and a node at the average score gets about 7 visits, a relative error near 40%. A node at a thousand times the average gets 6,700 visits and an error near 1.2%. This matches what rankings need: precise positions at the top, rough positions in the tail. Advantages Embarrassingly parallel. Walks are independent. Each machine runs walks from its own nodes and sums visit counts at the end; no synchronisation between iterations is needed. Incremental updates. Bahmani, Chowdhury and Goel stored walk segments per node and showed that when a link is added or removed, only the few segments passing through the affected node need to be rerun. A graph receiving a stream of new links can keep its PageRank current at a small fraction of the cost of recomputing it. Personalised vectors. A walk that always restarts at seed estimates the personalized PageRank from . Fogaras, Rácz, Csalogány and Sarlós precomputed a few such walks per node, fingerprints , so that any node’s personalised scores could be estimated at query time. Low memory. A walker needs only the graph and a counter per node, not the two full score vectors of power iteration. Disadvantages Random access. Each step jumps to an arbitrary node’s adjacency list, which is slow when the graph lives on disk or in compressed form, where sequential scans are cheap and random access is not (see PageRank at scale ). Noisy tails. Nodes near the floor get a handful of visits or none, so their positions are essentially random. For the 63.8% of Common Crawl domains with no out-links and most of the 87.6% with fewer than 10 in-links, sampled positions would mean little. Ties broken by chance. Two nodes with identical true PageRank, such as D and F in the running example, get different estimates and different positions in every run. Where it is used Monte Carlo methods power personalised recommendation and “who to follow” systems on social graphs, where millions of seeds each need their own personalised ranking and the graph changes every second. For a static global ranking of a crawl, like Common Crawl’s, deterministic solvers remain the norm because every node gets a precise and reproducible score. References Avrachenkov, K., Litvak, N., Nemirovsky, D., & Osipova, N. (2007). Monte Carlo methods in PageRank computation: When one iteration is sufficient. Internet Mathematics 2(3), 333–358. Bahmani, B., Chowdhury, A., & Goel, A. (2010). Fast incremental and personalized PageRank. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 4(3), 173–184.

d: For each distance t, how many pairs of nodes are within t links of each other. From it come the distance distribution, the average distance and the effective diameter, the robust ways to say how "small" a graph is.
a: Distance distribution Effective diameter Average distance Hop plot spid
x: The neighbourhood function of a graph counts the ordered pairs of nodes with : the pairs within links of each other. It summarises the whole distance structure of a graph in one increasing curve, and its derivatives give the statistics that network scientists actually use to compare graphs: the distribution of distances, the average distance and the effective diameter. Palmer, Gibbons and Faloutsos called its plot the hop plot and showed how to approximate it for large graphs; HyperANF made the approximation fast enough for billion-node graphs. Definitions where is the ball of radius around . , since every node reaches itself, and stops growing once passes the longest finite distance. From it: Distance distribution. The share of reachable pairs at distance exactly : . Average distance over the reachable pairs. Effective diameter. The distance within which 90% of reachable pairs lie, interpolated between integers. Unlike the diameter, the largest finite distance, it does not depend on a few freak chains. Spid , the shortest-path index of dispersion : the variance of the distance distribution divided by its mean. Boldi, Rosa and Vigna observed that social networks tend to have spid below 1 and web graphs above 1, a cheap way to tell the two kinds of graph apart. Worked example The running example (see the distance table in Paths, distance and reachability ) has 19 ordered pairs of distinct nodes with a directed path: Distance Pairs at distance Share of reachable pairs within 0 7 (each node to itself) 7 1 10 (the arcs) 17 52.6% 2 8 25 94.7% 3 1 (E to B) 26 100% The average distance is , and the effective diameter, interpolating where 90% is reached, is about 1.9. The diameter is 3. Of the 42 ordered pairs of distinct nodes, 23 have no path at all, which is why every statistic above is computed over reachable pairs only. Computing it at scale Exact computation needs all distances, a breadth-first search from every node. ANF and its successors estimate every ball size with a probabilistic counter per node and grow all balls one step per pass over the graph (see HyperBall ). Summing the estimates gives with a relative error close to that of the individual counters, in as many passes as the graph’s longest shortest path. HyperANF computed the neighbourhood function of Facebook’s 2011 friendship graph, 721 million nodes, giving the famous average distance of 4.74. What it reveals How small the world is. Average distance and effective diameter quantify the Small worlds property and allow graphs of different sizes to be compared. Change over time. Leskovec, Kleinberg and Faloutsos tracked real networks as they grew and found that effective diameters shrink while the graphs densify , the number of arcs growing faster than the number of nodes. Both contradict the assumptions of earlier random-graph models. Crawl health. A crawl that breaks URL normalisation or stops following some link type produces a neighbourhood function with a long tail or an abrupt plateau. Comparing successive crawls’ curves is a quick diagnostic. Robustness. Removing nodes in order of some centrality and recomputing shows which nodes hold the graph together. Boldi, Rosa and Vigna used this to compare removal strategies and found that social networks and web graphs react very differently to losing their most central nodes. Why it matters for rankings Harmonic centrality is the per-node version of the same information: for balls built from in-links. A graph whose distance distribution is concentrated at 3 or 4 steps gives almost every well-connected node a similar harmonic value, because most of the graph sits at the same few distances from each of them. The flatness of Common Crawl’s harmonic values near the top (see Ranks and scores ) is the distance distribution showing through. References Palmer, C. R., Gibbons, P. B., & Faloutsos, C. (2002). d: Renumbering a graph's nodes changes nothing about its structure and everything about its cost. Good orders shrink compressed graphs, speed up PageRank through cache locality and balance parallel work.
a: Graph reordering Layered label propagation LLP BFS order Locality
x: A graph’s nodes need integer ids, and any permutation of the ids describes the same graph. Rankings do not care which permutation you pick, apart from how ties are broken. Computers care a great deal. Compression depends on the gaps between consecutive successor ids, and a PageRank pass depends on whether the scores it reads sit near each other in memory. Choosing the order is often the cheapest large speed-up available. Why order matters Compression. WebGraph stores each successor list as gaps. If a node’s successors have ids close to its own and to each other, the gaps are small and cost few bits. A random order makes every gap about and every link cost nearly bits. Cache locality. A pull-style PageRank pass reads the score of every in-neighbour of every node (see Power iteration ). If in-neighbours have nearby ids, those reads hit the processor cache; if they are scattered across a 958 MB vector of doubles, nearly every read goes to main memory. Partitioning. Splitting a graph across threads or machines by id ranges works well when most links stay within a range. Name order The first good order for web graphs was free: sort pages by URL, with host names reversed so that pages of the same host, and hosts of the same domain, sit together (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ). Most links on the web are internal to a site, so most links connect nodes with nearby ids. Common Crawl numbers its domain graph’s vertices in reversed-name order. At the domain level the trick loses most of its force. The links that name order makes local, links within a site, are gone; what remains are links between unrelated domains. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph records an average distance of about 19.8 million ids between a node and its successors, and an average log₂ gap between consecutive successors of 10.8, which is why it costs 15 bits per link where page graphs cost 2 or 3. Orders built from structure When names carry no locality, as in social networks, or too little, as in domain graphs, the order must come from the links themselves: Breadth-first order. Number nodes in the order a breadth-first search visits them. Neighbours get nearby ids almost by construction. Apostolico and Drovandi built a compression scheme around it. Shingle order. Chierichetti and colleagues sorted nodes by a min-hash shingle of their successor lists, so that nodes with similar lists become neighbours, which helps reference compression. Layered label propagation (LLP). Boldi, Rosa, Santini and Vigna ran label propagation, a fast community-detection method (see Community detection ), at many resolutions, from coarse clusters to fine ones, and combined the resulting labelings into one order: nodes in the same fine cluster are adjacent, fine clusters in the same coarse cluster are adjacent, and so on. LLP produced the best compression known at the time on both web and social graphs, and an implementation ships with the LAW tools. Locality-driven orders for computation. Reverse Cuthill–McKee from numerical linear algebra, Rabbit Order and similar community-based methods target cache behaviour rather than bits, and speed up PageRank-style passes on shared-memory machines. Degree sorting. Putting the highest-degree nodes first packs the most frequently read scores into the fewest cache lines. It is crude but effective when a few hubs receive most of the reads, which on the web they do (see Degree distributions and power laws ). Costs and trade-offs Computing a good order costs a few passes over the graph, sometimes many more for LLP, but it is done once and amortised over every later use. Reordering is a permutation: the graph must be rewritten with new ids, and every id-indexed side file (names, ranks, labels) must be permuted to match. Different goals favour different orders. The best order for compression is not always the best for parallel PageRank, and an order tuned for one graph’s structure ages as the graph changes. Orders and ties Rankings are invariant under renumbering except for ties. Common Crawl sorts its ranks file by score with a stable sort, so domains with equal scores appear in vertex-id order, which is reversed-name order. Harmonic centrality has only 5.9 million distinct values across 119.7 million domains, so ties are common, and their order is alphabetical by reversed name. Renumber the graph and the tied positions change while the scores do not (see Ranks and scores ). A rule of thumb If a graph algorithm is slow, check the order before optimising the code. A random or crawl-order numbering can make the same PageRank computation several times slower than a locality-preserving one, and make the compressed graph twice as large or more. The fix needs no change to the algorithm at all. References Boldi, P., Rosa, M., Santini, M., & Vigna, S. (2011). IPDPS 2016 , 22–31.

d: The arithmetic of ranking a hundred million nodes and billions of links. What must fit in memory, what each pass costs, why random reads dominate, and why one well-programmed machine often beats a cluster.
a: Large-scale PageRank Semi-external PageRank Distributed PageRank COST
x: The PageRank formula fits on a line; computing it for Common Crawl’s 119,722,885 domains and 2,450,405,793 links is an exercise in memory budgets. This entry works through the numbers for that graph. The same arithmetic applies, with larger constants, to page-level graphs with tens of billions of links. What must be stored Item Size per element Total for the CC domain graph Score vector, 64-bit doubles 8 bytes per node 958 MB Second score vector (for Jacobi-style passes) 8 bytes per node 958 MB Out-degrees (or their reciprocals) 4 bytes per node 479 MB Transposed graph as CSR, 32-bit ids 4 bytes per arc + offsets 10.3 GB Transposed graph in WebGraph format about 15 bits per arc 4.6 GB A pull-style computation (each node sums over its in-links) needs the transposed graph, the out-degrees and one or two score vectors: about 6.5 GB with the compressed graph, or 12 GB with plain CSR. Gauss–Seidel updates scores in place and needs only one vector (see PageRank as a linear system ). Single-precision floats would halve the vectors, but the smallest scores sit near and are sums of many tiny contributions; most serious implementations, including LAW’s, use doubles. What one pass costs A pass reads every arc once. The arcs themselves stream sequentially: 9.8 GB of CSR targets takes well under a second at the 20–30 GB/s a modern server’s memory delivers. The expensive part is the score lookup that each arc triggers. In a pull pass, the arc reads , and can be anywhere in a 958 MB vector. If every such read misses the cache, each costs a full 64-byte cache line from main memory: roughly 5 to 8 seconds of pure memory traffic per pass, far more than the sequential reads. Locality decides the real cost. A locality-preserving order makes many neighbouring arcs read neighbouring scores, so one cache line serves several arcs. Heavy-tailed in-degrees help too: the scores of the few hub nodes that appear in millions of in-lists stay in cache. With 50 to 100 passes for a tight tolerance, or about half that with Gauss–Seidel, a well-ordered in-memory computation on one multicore machine takes minutes. When the graph does not fit Compressed in memory. At 4.6 GB, the WebGraph form fits where CSR may not. Decoding costs CPU but saves memory bandwidth, usually a good trade. This is what Common Crawl’s pipeline does, with the LAW library’s parallel Gauss–Seidel solver reading a memory-mapped graph. Semi-external. Keep the score vectors (2 GB) in memory and stream the arcs from disk on every pass. A raw edge list of 32-bit pairs is 19.6 GB; at 3 GB/s from an NVMe drive, a pass takes about 7 seconds, comparable to the in-memory random-read cost above. Fully external. When even the vectors do not fit, sort-based methods process arcs and scores in matching order, at the price of sorting every pass. This was necessary in the early 2000s and is rarely needed now for domain or host graphs. Clusters and their COST Distributed graph systems split the nodes across machines and exchange score messages along cut arcs each pass. They scale to graphs that no single machine can hold, but communication dominates: every arc between machines becomes network traffic on every pass. McSherry, Isard and Murray’s “Scalability! But at what COST?” (2015) measured the configuration that outperforms a single thread, and found that several published distributed systems needed dozens to hundreds of cores just to match one well-written single-threaded PageRank on a laptop for graphs with billions of links. For graphs the size of Common Crawl’s domain graph, a single large machine is the practical choice. Load balance and hubs Pull-style parallel passes split nodes among threads. A node with 17 million in-links, such as googleapis.com , makes one thread do 17 million additions while the others idle, unless the work is split by arcs rather than nodes. Edge-balanced partitioning, or splitting the in-lists of the largest hubs, keeps all cores busy. Push-style passes avoid the hub problem but need atomic additions on targets. Stopping and verifying Pick the tolerance from the use. If you publish positions, stop when the positions you care about have stopped changing; the tail of a 120-million-node ranking is decided by floating-point noise long before values converge (see Ranks and scores ). Check the invariants. Scores must be positive and sum to 1 within rounding, every node with no in-links must sit at the same floor, and two runs with different thread counts should agree to the tolerance. Cross-check on a sample. Monte Carlo PageRank gives an independent estimate for the top nodes in minutes. References McSherry, F., Isard, M., & Murray, D. G. (2015). Scalability! But at what COST? d: From a Stanford research project to Google's founding idea, a 0–10 number on millions of toolbars, a market in links, and finally a retired public metric that Google says it still uses internally.
a: Toolbar PageRank TBPR PageRank patent BackRub PageRank sculpting
x: PageRank began as an academic idea, became the technical story of the world’s largest search engine, and spent sixteen years as a public number that website owners obsessed over. Its history explains why so many link metrics exist today, and why the industry still talks about “link juice” and 0–10 scores long after Google stopped showing them. Origins at Stanford, 1996–1998 Larry Page and Sergey Brin started the project in 1996 as Stanford graduate students, crawling the web with a system first called BackRub. The idea drew on citation analysis, where a paper cited by influential papers is itself influential, and on earlier work such as Katz’s 1953 status index (see Katz centrality ). In April 1998 they presented “The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine” at the WWW7 conference, describing Google and its use of PageRank. A companion technical report with Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd, “The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web”, gave the mathematics, including the The random surfer interpretation and personalisation. Jon Kleinberg’s HITS (hubs and authorities) appeared the same year, independently, at IBM. The patent Page filed US patent 6,285,999, “Method for node ranking in a linked database”, on 9 January 1998; it was granted on 4 September 2001. The patent belonged to Stanford, not Google, which held an exclusive licence. Stanford received 1.8 million Google shares for the licence and sold them in 2005 for about $336 million, one of the most lucrative university licensing deals ever. The patent ran for twenty years from filing and has expired; the method has been free to use for years, and graph libraries ship it as a standard function. Toolbar PageRank, 2000–2016 On 11 December 2000 Google released the Google Toolbar, a browser add-on that, among other features, displayed a green bar scoring the current page from 0 to 10. This Toolbar PageRank (TBPR) was a coarse, roughly logarithmic bucketing of the page’s internal PageRank, updated only every few months. Google never published the bucket boundaries. The number became a currency. Site owners checked it obsessively, link sellers priced links by the TBPR of the selling page, and expired domains were valued by the TBPR they had accumulated (see Expired domains ). Google’s response was a series of steps away from the public number: 2005: Google introduced rel="nofollow" with other search engines, to let sites mark links they did not vouch for (see Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) ). 2007: Google lowered the displayed TBPR of sites it judged to be selling links that passed PageRank, a visible penalty for an invisible offence. 2009: Google removed PageRank from its Webmaster Tools in October, saying it was telling site owners not to focus on the number while showing it to them. In the same year it clarified that links marked nofollow still use up a page’s PageRank share, ending the practice of “PageRank sculpting” with nofollow . December 2013: the last Toolbar PageRank update. 2014: Google’s John Mueller said the public scores would probably not be updated again. April 2016: Google confirmed that Toolbar PageRank had been removed entirely. Still in use, says Google Retiring the public number did not retire the algorithm. In 2017, Google’s Gary Illyes wrote that Google still used PageRank, among hundreds of other signals, in ranking. How it is computed today, on what graph, with which spam filtering and link weighting, is not public. Google has published patents describing variants, such as weighting links by how likely a reader is to click them (the “reasonable surfer”) and computing scores by distance from trusted seed pages, but patents describe possibilities, not confirmed practice. After the toolbar: third-party metrics The demand that Toolbar PageRank created did not go away when it did. SEO software companies built their own link indexes and their own 0–100 or 0–10 scores to fill the gap: Moz’s Domain Authority (Moz) , Ahrefs’ Domain Rating (Ahrefs) , Majestic’s Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) and Citation Flow, and Semrush’s Authority Score (Semrush) . Each is computed from its vendor’s own crawl, with its own definitions and, usually, without disclosed formulas. Several free services also publish 0–10 “PageRank-style” scores derived from open data such as Common Crawl’s graph (see The Common Crawl web graph ). None of these numbers is Google’s PageRank, and none should be read as a prediction of how Google ranks a site. The Auditing vendor metrics entry compares several of them against Common Crawl’s open centralities on one day’s auction inventory and finds large disagreements. What the history teaches A public ranking number invites manipulation. Once TBPR had market value, sites manufactured links to raise it, which corrupted the signal it summarised. Every successor metric faces the same pressure (see Link spam ). Coarse buckets hide a lot. A TBPR of 4 covered pages whose underlying scores differed several-fold. Logarithmic 0–10 or 0–100 scales still compress enormous differences into a few points (see Ranks and scores ). The method is open; the inputs are not. Anyone can compute PageRank. What distinguished Google’s version was its crawl, its spam filtering and its link weighting, none of which the formula captures. References Brin, S., & Page, L. (1998). The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine. Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30(1–7), 107–117. Page, L., Brin, S., Motwani, R., & Winograd, T. (1999). The PageRank citation ranking: Bringing order to the Web. Stanford InfoLab Technical Report 1999-66. Page, L. (2001). Method for node ranking in a linked database. US Patent 6,285,999. d: PageRank is also the solution of a sparse system of linear equations. That view brings faster solvers such as Gauss–Seidel, explains why the problem is well conditioned, and makes PageRank linear in the teleport vector.
a: Gauss–Seidel Jacobi method Linear system formulation Pseudo-PageRank
x: Power iteration treats PageRank as an eigenvector problem: find the vector that one surfer step leaves unchanged. The same vector is the solution of a sparse linear system. Del Corso, Gullì and Romani, and Langville and Meyer, worked out the connection in the mid-2000s. The linear view matters for three reasons: it opens the door to faster iterative solvers, it shows that the problem is numerically easy, and it makes PageRank linear in the teleport vector, the property behind Personalized PageRank mixtures and Spam mass . From eigenvector to linear system Let be the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix with empty rows for dangling nodes, and the teleport distribution (uniform: ). Consider the system Its solution is the pseudo-PageRank : probability that reaches a dangling node leaks away instead of jumping, so sums to less than 1. Normalising it, gives exactly the PageRank vector in which dangling nodes jump according to . In the running example, the pseudo-PageRank sums to 0.42, and dividing by 0.42 recovers the PageRank of C, A, G, B, D, F and E to every digit shown elsewhere in this encyclopedia. Nothing about dangling nodes needs special handling in the solver: they simply contribute nothing to anyone. A well-behaved system The matrix is about as friendly as a sparse matrix can be: It is diagonally dominant : each diagonal entry is 1 and each row’s off-diagonal entries sum to at most in absolute value. It is an M-matrix , so its inverse has only nonnegative entries and the solution is nonnegative. Its condition number in the 1-norm is at most , which is 12.3 for , as Kamvar and Haveliwala showed. Rounding errors cannot be amplified by more than that. All classical stationary methods converge on such a system, and the convergence rate is again governed by . Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel and friends Writing the system node by node gives . The solvers differ in which values of they use on the right-hand side: Jacobi uses only values from the previous sweep. This is power iteration in different clothes. Gauss–Seidel uses each new value as soon as it is computed, within the same sweep. Information propagates further per sweep, typically halving the number of sweeps. The price is that the result of a sweep depends on the order in which nodes are visited, and a strictly sequential sweep is hard to parallelise. Krylov methods such as GMRES and BiCGSTAB converge in fewer iterations still on some graphs, at the cost of extra vectors in memory. Gleich, Zhukov and Berkhin found them competitive on large parallel machines. A good order follows the direction of the links. Parallel Gauss–Seidel at web scale Common Crawl computes PageRank with the LAW library’s PageRankParallelGaussSeidel , run on the transposed graph so that each node reads its in-links. The parallel version splits the nodes among threads, and each thread updates its nodes in place, reading whatever values its neighbours currently hold, including values other threads have just written. It is not the sequential Gauss–Seidel method; it mixes old and new values in an order that depends on scheduling. Because the system is diagonally dominant, such asynchronous iterations still converge, and in practice they keep most of Gauss–Seidel’s advantage while using every core. Linearity and its uses The linear form makes a linear function of the teleport vector: . Consequences: Contributions. Splitting by node splits into the PageRank each node contributes to each other node. Spam mass estimates how much of a node’s PageRank comes from a trusted core this way. Mixtures. Topic-sensitive rankings combine precomputed personalised vectors with the query’s topic weights (see Personalized PageRank ). Updates. When a few links change, the change in is the solution of the same system with a small right-hand side, so warm-starting from the old solution converges in a few sweeps. d: A node is important if important nodes link to it. PageRank makes that circular idea precise as the long-run behaviour of a random surfer who sometimes gets bored and jumps.
a: PR Google PageRank
x: PageRank scores every node of a link graph by the fraction of time a random surfer spends there. The surfer starts anywhere, follows a random out-link at each step, and every so often jumps to a random node instead. Sites that many well-visited sites link to get visited often. Larry Page and Sergey Brin introduced it in 1998 as the ranking core of the Google search engine, and it remains the reference point that every other link-based ranking is compared against. The idea Counting in-links ( Degree centrality ) treats every link as equal. PageRank adds two rules: A link from an important node counts more. Importance flows along links. A node splits its importance among its out-links. A site that links to a thousand others passes each one a thousandth of what a site linking to one passes. The definition is circular, since importance depends on importance. The The random surfer model resolves the circularity: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk , the distribution that one more step of the walk leaves unchanged. Definition Let be the number of nodes, the out-degree of , and the The damping factor , conventionally 0.85. The PageRank vector satisfies, for every node , Read it term by term. With probability the surfer teleports to a uniformly random node. With probability it follows a link: each in-neighbour sends an equal share of its own score. The last sum handles Dangling nodes : a surfer stuck on a node with no out-links teleports uniformly. The scores are positive and sum to 1. In matrix form, with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix (dangling rows replaced by the uniform row) and the all-ones vector, The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem guarantees exactly one solution, and Power iteration finds it by applying the right-hand side repeatedly. The error shrinks by a factor of about per iteration. Personalized PageRank replaces the uniform teleport with any other distribution. Worked example On the running example with , power iteration converges to a change below after 43 iterations: Node C A G B D F E PageRank 0.2977 0.2052 0.1774 0.1381 0.0653 0.0653 0.0509 In-degree 4 2 1 1 1 1 0 C wins, as in-degree predicts. The surprises are lower down: G beats B, though both have one in-link. G’s link comes from C, the top node, which splits its score two ways. B’s comes from A, which has a lower score and also splits two ways. E gets the minimum. Nothing links to E, so it receives only the teleport share plus its share of the dangling mass: . Every node with no in-links in any graph gets exactly this floor. D and F tie. Each has a single in-link from E, which splits three ways: . Try it yourself. Change α or add a link from G back to E, and watch E climb: Properties worth knowing Scores are probabilities. They sum to 1, so they shrink as the graph grows. On a graph of 120 million nodes, the average score is . Compare positions, or logarithms, not raw values (see Ranks and scores ). Adding an in-link always helps. In Boldi and Vigna’s terms PageRank satisfies score monotonicity : adding an arc raises ’s score. It fails their size axiom, though: in a graph made of one large clique and one long cycle, every node scores exactly , so PageRank cannot tell a big community from a small one (see Axioms for centrality ). Small α flattens, large α concentrates. With the running example’s range shrinks from 0.05–0.30 to 0.09–0.24. As the scores pile into the strongly connected core and convergence slows (see The damping factor ). It can be farmed. A group of sites that link to each other and to a target trap the random surfer and pump the target’s score. TrustRank , Spam mass and Harmonic centrality all respond to this weakness (see Link spam ). At web scale Each power iteration reads every arc once and updates a score vector of entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph that is 2.45 billion arcs and two vectors of 119.7 million doubles (958 MB each). Common Crawl runs the LAW library’s parallel Gauss–Seidel solver on the transposed graph, which converges in fewer passes than plain power iteration (see PageRank as a linear system ). PageRank at scale works through the memory budget, and Monte Carlo PageRank and Push algorithms approximate scores without touching the whole graph. PageRank on the real web In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph the top of the PageRank list is the infrastructure every site embeds: googleapis.com (0.0152), google.com (0.0151), facebook.com (0.0094), googletagmanager.com and instagram.com . The common ranking with Harmonic centrality diverges further down, and the divergence shows what PageRank rewards: Domain Referring domains PageRank position Harmonic position godaddy.com 1,472,755 14 135 parastorage.com 2,923,364 16 81,305 miit.gov.cn 722,788 28 981 PageRank pays most for links from sites that link to little else, because each such link carries a large share of its source’s score. godaddy.com is linked from parked pages and from sites built with its tools, and miit.gov.cn from the registration notice that Chinese sites display. Harmonic centrality ignores how a source splits its links and only asks how close the rest of the graph is. The extreme case sits further down. chaussurespuma.net has seven referring domains, yet it holds PageRank position 10,000 of 119.7 million. One of the seven is googleapis.com , the top domain, which links to only 3,686 domains. That single link passes , almost all of chaussurespuma.net ’s score of . Google Cloud Storage serves user files from storage.googleapis.com , so the link may sit on a page any customer uploaded; the domain graph credits it to googleapis.com all the same (see Page, host and domain graphs ). What it means for a domain Google’s production ranking has used many signals beyond PageRank for decades, and its link analysis runs on pages, not domains, with spam filtering and Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) applied. d: How many clicks separate two sites, and whether one can reach the other at all. Breadth-first search answers both, and geometric centralities are built on the answer.
a: Distance Shortest path Reachability Breadth-first search BFS Geodesic
x: A path from to is a sequence of arcs that starts at , follows links, and ends at . The distance is the length of the shortest such path, counted in arcs. On the web it is the minimum number of clicks a reader needs to get from one site to another. If no path exists, is unreachable from and . Distances matter because a family of rankings, the geometric centralities, score a node by how close the rest of the graph is to it: Closeness centrality , Harmonic centrality and Betweenness centrality , which counts how many shortest paths pass through a node. Distance is not symmetric In a directed graph and can differ, and one can be infinite while the other is not. In the running example, through C, but : G links nowhere and nothing links to E. Here is every distance in the running example. Row , column gives ; a dash means unreachable. from \ to A B C D E F G A 0 1 1 – – – 2 B 2 0 1 – – – 2 C 1 2 0 – – – 1 D 1 2 1 0 – – 2 E 2 3 1 1 0 1 2 F – – – – – 0 – G – – – – – – 0 Most of the table is dashes. Unreachable pairs are the norm in web graphs, not an edge case, and any measure built on distance must decide what to do with them. Closeness centrality handles them badly and Harmonic centrality handles them well, which is the main reason the second replaced the first. Reachability The set of nodes reachable from is its forward ball of infinite radius; the set of nodes that can reach is its backward ball . Reachability decomposes a graph into strongly connected components : groups in which every node reaches every other. On the web those components arrange themselves into the The bow-tie structure shape. In the running example, E reaches everything, while F and G reach only themselves. Column C is full except for F and G: every node that links anywhere eventually reaches C. Breadth-first search Breadth-first search (BFS) computes all distances from one source in time proportional to the number of arcs it touches: dist[s] = 0; queue = [s] while queue not empty: u = queue.pop_front() for v in successors(u): if dist[v] is unset: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 queue.push_back(v) BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches it has found a shortest path. Each arc is examined once, so one BFS costs . Running BFS on the transposed graph (see Adjacency matrices and lists ) gives the distances to from everywhere, which is what in-link-based centralities need. All-pairs distances are out of reach A geometric centrality needs the distances between all pairs, which naively means one BFS per node: . For Common Crawl’s domain graph, with and , that is about arc visits. At a billion visits per second it would take nearly ten years. Two ideas make geometric centralities feasible at that scale anyway: Approximate counting. You rarely need every distance, only how many nodes lie within distance for each . HyperBall estimates those counts for every node at once with HyperLogLog counters, in a few dozen passes over the graph. Common Crawl computes Harmonic centrality this way. Sampling. Run BFS from a random sample of sources and extrapolate. This is how large-scale betweenness is usually estimated (see Brandes’ algorithm ). Diameter and typical distance The diameter is the largest finite distance between any two nodes. It is a fragile statistic: one long chain of pages sets it. Network scientists prefer the distance distribution , the fraction of reachable pairs at each distance, and the effective diameter , the distance within which 90% of reachable pairs lie. Web graphs and social networks have small typical distances, the Small worlds property, and the The neighbourhood function entry shows how to measure the whole distribution at scale. On Facebook’s 2011 friendship graph, 721 million users were on average 4.74 friendships apart, a figure computed with HyperANF. Weighted distance When arcs carry lengths, BFS gives way to Dijkstra’s algorithm, which costs with a good priority queue. Link graphs rarely use weighted distances; the meaningful weights on links, such as how much importance they transfer, enter through Random walks and Markov chains instead. References Cormen, T. d: The theorem that guarantees a nonnegative matrix has a dominant eigenvector with positive entries. It is why PageRank exists, why it is unique, and why eigenvector centrality fails on graphs that are not strongly connected.
a: Perron–Frobenius Perron vector Spectral radius Irreducible matrix Primitive matrix
x: Every spectral ranking, from Eigenvector centrality to PageRank , declares the scores to be an eigenvector of some matrix built from the graph. That raises awkward questions. Does such an eigenvector exist? Is it unique? Are its entries all positive, so that they can be read as scores? Will Power iteration find it? For matrices with nonnegative entries, which all link matrices are, the theorem of Oskar Perron (1907) and Georg Frobenius (1912) answers all four. Its conditions are exactly the graph properties that teleportation was invented to supply. Positive matrices: Perron’s theorem Let be a square matrix with all entries strictly positive. Then: Its spectral radius , the largest absolute value of any eigenvalue, is itself an eigenvalue, real and positive. is a simple eigenvalue: its eigenspace is one-dimensional. There is an eigenvector for with all entries strictly positive, and up to scaling it is the only nonnegative eigenvector of . Every other eigenvalue satisfies . Point 3 gives a unique ranking. Point 4 makes power iteration converge: repeated multiplication shrinks every other eigenvector’s component relative to the dominant one. Nonnegative matrices: Frobenius’s extension Adjacency matrices are full of zeros, so Perron’s theorem does not apply directly. Frobenius extended it to nonnegative matrices with two graph-theoretic conditions: Irreducible. The matrix’s graph is strongly connected: every node reaches every other. Then points 1 to 3 still hold, with a strictly positive eigenvector. Primitive. Irreducible and aperiodic: the greatest common divisor of the graph’s cycle lengths is 1. Then point 4 holds as well, so power iteration converges from any positive start. An irreducible but periodic matrix has other eigenvalues of modulus . A graph whose only cycle is A ⇄ B has eigenvalues and ; power iteration starting from flips to and back forever. The running example The running example’s Adjacency matrices and lists matrix is reducible: D, E and F cannot be reached from the core, and F and G reach nothing. Its core {A, B, C} is irreducible, and primitive because it contains cycles of length 2 and 3. The core’s spectral radius, 1.3247, is the largest eigenvalue of the whole matrix, and its eigenvector is positive on the core and on G, which the core feeds, and zero on D, E and F. That is the Eigenvector centrality of the running example: the theorem guarantees nothing outside an irreducible piece, and on a reducible graph nonnegative eigenvectors can have zeros in exactly the places the dominant component cannot reach. How PageRank satisfies the theorem PageRank’s matrix is where is the transition matrix with dangling rows replaced by uniform rows. Every entry of is at least . is positive , so Perron’s original theorem applies without any condition on the web graph: ’s spectral radius is 1, since is row-stochastic, and 1 is a simple eigenvalue. The left eigenvector for 1, the PageRank vector, is unique and strictly positive: every page gets a nonzero score. All other eigenvalues have modulus less than 1. Haveliwala and Kamvar sharpened this to . Teleportation is the trick that turns an arbitrary, reducible, periodic web graph into a positive matrix. Without it, the theorem’s conditions fail on every real crawl, and the raw random walk’s stationary distributions are neither unique nor positive (see Random walks and Markov chains ). Bounds on the spectral radius A companion result, the Collatz–Wielandt bound, says that the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix lies between its smallest and largest row sum, and likewise for column sums. For an adjacency matrix, is at least the minimum and at most the maximum out-degree, and the same for in-degrees. Because the spectral radius of a principal submatrix never exceeds that of the whole matrix, any dense subgraph pushes up for the entire graph. This is why a single dense cluster forces Katz centrality ’s parameter to be tiny on the web, while PageRank’s matrix, with every row summing to 1, always has . Why it matters in practice Uniqueness. Two correct PageRank implementations with the same graph, , teleport vector and dangling rule must produce the same vector, up to numerical tolerance. If they disagree, one of them has a bug or a different convention. Positivity. No domain ever has PageRank zero; the floor is the teleport and dangling share (see Dangling nodes ). Convergence. The number of power-iteration passes depends on , not on the size of the graph. Failure modes elsewhere. When a spectral score has exact zeros, oscillates or depends on the starting vector, look for a violated condition: reducibility or periodicity. References Perron, O. (1907). d: PageRank with the random surfer's jumps aimed at chosen nodes instead of anywhere. It measures importance from a point of view, and underlies TrustRank, topic-sensitive search and local graph clustering.
a: PPR Topic-sensitive PageRank Random walk with restart Preference vector
x: Ordinary PageRank teleports the random surfer to a uniformly random node. Personalized PageRank (PPR) teleports it according to a chosen preference vector instead: always to one node, or to a handful of trusted sites, or to pages about one topic. The resulting scores measure importance as seen from the preferred nodes: nodes that the walk reaches often, after restarting at the preferred nodes, score high. The original PageRank paper already described this variant; it later became the basis of TrustRank , of topic-sensitive search, and of fast local algorithms for finding communities. Definition Given a probability vector over the nodes, the personalized PageRank vector satisfies with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix and the The damping factor . A walker at each step follows a random out-link with probability and jumps to a node drawn from with probability . From a dangling node it jumps according to as well (“strongly preferential”) or uniformly (“weakly preferential”). With uniform, is ordinary PageRank. When puts all its mass on a single node , the walk is a random walk with restart , and measures how close is to : it is the probability that a walk from with geometric length, mean steps, ends at . Worked example Restart every walk at E in the running example, with : Node E C A G D F B PPR from E 0.307 0.230 0.135 0.098 0.087 0.087 0.057 Ordinary PageRank 0.051 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.065 0.065 0.138 E, which has the lowest ordinary PageRank, now has the highest score, because every restart lands on it. B drops to last: it is three links away from E, the farthest node E can reach. The ranking now mixes importance with proximity to the seed. Pick a different seed in the lab to see the whole ranking shift: Linearity PPR is linear in the preference vector: if , then . (Exactly so when dangling nodes are handled the same way whatever is, for instance by letting their probability leak away; with strongly preferential jumps the mixture weights shift slightly.) Two consequences matter in practice: Topic-sensitive PageRank. Haveliwala precomputed one PPR vector for each of the 16 top-level categories of the Open Directory, each teleporting to that category’s pages. At query time he mixed the 16 vectors according to how well the query matched each topic. One query about jaguars the animal and another about Jaguar the car get different link-based rankings from the same 16 vectors. Personalization at scale. In principle, the PPR vector of every single node determines the PPR of every possible preference vector. Storing vectors of length is impossible on the web, but Jeh and Widom showed how to share most of the work through a small set of hub nodes, and Monte Carlo methods store a few walk endpoints per node instead (see Monte Carlo PageRank ). Computing it Power iteration works exactly as for PageRank, one pass over the arcs per iteration, but it computes one preference vector at a time. Local push algorithms compute an approximate PPR from a single seed while touching only the nodes near it, in time independent of the graph’s size (see Push algorithms ). Andersen, Chung and Lang used this to find communities: sort nodes by PPR score divided by degree and cut where the conductance is lowest. Monte Carlo estimation runs many random walks with restart from the seed and counts where they stop. Where it is used Spam resistance. TrustRank is PPR with the preference vector on a hand-checked set of reputable sites. Spam pages are rarely close to such seeds. Spam mass compares ordinary PageRank with this trusted version. Recommendation. “Who to follow” and “related items” features rank candidates by PPR from the user. Twitter’s original Who-to-Follow service, described by Gupta and colleagues in 2013, combined personalized PageRank with SALSA on the follow graph. Local search and clustering. PPR from one node finds the cluster around it without processing the whole graph. Link analysis for a niche. Seeding the walk with the leading sites of one industry ranks domains by their standing within that industry rather than on the web at large. Majestic’s Topical Trust Flow reports a separate link-based score for each topic category, in the same spirit (see Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) ). What it means for a domain A domain’s ordinary PageRank says how much of the web’s link attention it gets. A personalized score says how much attention it gets from the part of the web you care about. A domain with modest overall PageRank but strong PPR from authoritative sites in one field can be worth more, for that field, than a domain with high overall PageRank earned from unrelated or low-quality sources. d: Start from any distribution and apply one random-surfer step to all nodes at once, over and over. The error shrinks by a factor of about α per pass, and each pass reads every link exactly once.
a: Power method Jacobi iteration Convergence
x: Power iteration is the simplest way to compute PageRank and most other spectral rankings. Start with a guess, typically the uniform distribution. Apply the PageRank equation’s right-hand side to get a new vector. Repeat until the vector stops changing. Each pass costs one scan over all arcs. The method is old, it is slow compared with more sophisticated solvers, and it has computed more rankings than any other algorithm because it is easy to implement, parallelise and reason about. The algorithm p = [1/n] * n repeat: D = sum of p[u] over dangling nodes u q = [(1 - α + α·D) / n] * n # teleport and dangling mass for each arc u → v: q[v] += α · p[u] / outdeg[u] change = sum |q - p| p = q until change < ε The loop over arcs is the whole cost. On a graph with arcs and nodes, one pass is time with two vectors of entries in memory. The order in which arcs are visited does not change the result, which makes the pass easy to split across threads or machines. Why it converges One pass computes , where is the PageRank matrix: the row-stochastic matrix combining links, dangling jumps and teleportation. has largest eigenvalue 1 with the PageRank vector as its eigenvector (see The Perron–Frobenius theorem ). Writing the error in terms of ’s other eigenvectors, each pass multiplies the component along eigenvector by , so the error decays like , where is the second-largest eigenvalue in modulus. Haveliwala and Kamvar showed that for the PageRank matrix, so With , every 14 passes gain about one decimal digit. The bound does not depend on : a graph with 7 nodes and a graph with 120 million nodes need about the same number of passes for the same precision. Worked example On the running example, starting from the uniform vector : Pass C A G B D, F E Change 1 0.340 0.178 0.117 0.117 0.097 0.056 2 0.279 0.233 0.192 0.123 0.063 0.047 5 0.293 0.208 0.181 0.137 0.065 0.051 10 0.298 0.205 0.178 0.138 0.065 0.051 20 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 0.065 0.051 43 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 0.065 0.051 Between passes 20 and 30 the change falls by a factor of 750, about 0.52 per pass, faster than the bound of 0.85, because the two dangling nodes send every visitor back to a random node. The ranking settles long before the values do: from pass 2 on, the order C, A, G, B, D = F, E never changes. When to stop The change between passes is easy to measure, but it is not the error. For PageRank the two are related by so with the true error can be 5.7 times the observed change. Common choices: A fixed tolerance on the L1 change, often to . The L1 norm sums errors over all nodes, so a tolerance of bounds the total error but still lets a single node be off by more than 100 times the average score on a 120-million-node graph. If the order of low-ranked nodes matters, use a much smaller tolerance or check the relative change of each node. Rank stability. Stop when the top positions have not changed for several passes. Rankings converge much faster than values. A fixed number of passes. The original TrustRank paper used 20. With , 50 passes bound the L1 error by . Speeding it up Gauss–Seidel uses each updated score immediately within the same pass, typically halving the number of passes. Common Crawl uses a parallel Gauss–Seidel solver (see PageRank as a linear system ). Extrapolation. Kamvar, Haveliwala, Manning and Golub estimated and subtracted the slowest-decaying error components from a few successive iterates, cutting passes substantially on web graphs. Adaptive iteration. Most nodes converge in a few passes while a minority take many. Skipping nodes whose scores have stopped changing saves work. Block structure. Most links stay within a host. Computing local PageRank within each host first and combining the blocks gives a good starting vector (BlockRank). Local and sampling methods avoid global passes entirely when only some scores are needed (see Push algorithms and Monte Carlo PageRank ). Pull or push The loop above pushes : it reads each node’s out-links and adds to its targets. The pull form reads each node’s in-links from the transposed graph and sums contributions into one entry at a time. Pull needs the transpose but writes each entry once, so parallel threads never conflict; push needs only the forward graph but parallel writes to the same target must be synchronised. Large-scale implementations, including LAW’s, use the transposed graph and pull. PageRank at scale covers the memory and bandwidth arithmetic. Beyond PageRank The same loop computes Eigenvector centrality (without teleport, normalising each pass), Katz centrality and HITS (hubs and authorities) (alternating two products). None of them enjoys PageRank’s guarantee: their convergence rate depends on the graph’s own eigenvalue gap, which can be tiny, and periodic graphs can make the iterates oscillate forever. The teleport term is what makes PageRank’s power iteration reliably fast. References Haveliwala, T. H., & Kamvar, S. D. (2003). The second eigenvalue of the Google matrix. d: Most sites receive almost no links and a few receive millions. That heavy tail explains why link metrics live on logarithmic scales and why averages mislead.
a: Power law Heavy tail Scale-free Degree distribution Pareto distribution Zipf's law
x: A graph’s degree distribution says what fraction of nodes have each degree. In a random graph where every link lands on a uniformly chosen node, degrees cluster tightly around the average. Link graphs look nothing like that. Most nodes have tiny degrees and a few have degrees millions of times larger. When the fraction of nodes with degree falls off like a power of , the distribution is called a power law and the graph scale-free . Whether real web graphs follow a true power law is debated; that they are extremely heavy-tailed is not. Definition A degree distribution follows a power law with exponent if, for above some threshold , Equivalently, the share of nodes with degree at least , the complementary cumulative distribution (CCDF), falls like . Taking logarithms turns either into a straight line, , which is why power laws are plotted on log–log axes. The CCDF is the better plot: it needs no binning and its tail is not lost in noise. The exponent controls how extreme the tail is. For the variance diverges as the graph grows, and for even the mean does: a handful of nodes then hold a fixed fraction of all links, however many nodes there are. Domain graphs concentrate further because one domain collects the links aimed at all its pages. Fit carefully The straight line on a log–log plot is famously easy to over-read: Do not fit a line to a log–log histogram. Least squares on binned, logged counts gives biased exponents and no test of fit. Clauset, Shalizi and Newman recommend maximum likelihood instead: for discrete data, over the nodes with , plus a goodness-of-fit test against alternatives such as the lognormal. The tail is not the whole distribution. Below about 10 links the CC curve bends; 43.8% of domains have exactly one in-link and 63.8% have no recorded out-link at all, the latter mostly an artefact of what the crawler fetched. Heavy-tailed is not the same as power law. The subtitle of their paper, “a trick of the heavy tail”, is the point: many distributions look straight on log–log axes over a few decades. Where heavy tails come from The classic explanation is preferential attachment : new sites link to existing sites with probability proportional to how many links those sites already have, so the rich get richer. Barabási and Albert showed that this rule alone produces a power law with exponent 3; variants with copying or aging produce other exponents. Search engines may strengthen the effect, since sites that rank well get found, and then linked, more often. The Random graph models entry compares the main models. Scores need logarithmic scales. d: Compute personalized PageRank by pushing probability outward from the seed, one node at a time, and stopping when the leftovers are small. The work depends on the precision you want, not on the size of the graph.
a: Forward push Local push Backward push Approximate PageRank ACL algorithm Bookmark coloring
x: Power iteration touches every arc of the graph in every pass, even when you only care about the neighbourhood of one node. Push algorithms do the opposite. To compute Personalized PageRank from a seed, they keep a little probability mass at the seed and repeatedly push it outward to neighbours, settling part of it at each node they visit. When the unsettled mass left anywhere is below a threshold, they stop. The total work depends only on the threshold and the damping factor, so the algorithm answers local questions on a billion-arc graph while touching a few thousand arcs. Pavel Berkhin’s bookmark-coloring algorithm and Andersen, Chung and Lang’s local push, both from 2006, are the classic forms. Forward push Keep two vectors: an estimate , initially zero, and a residual , initially 1 at the seed and 0 elsewhere. A push at node does three things: move a share of the residual into the estimate: ; spread the remaining equally over ’s out-neighbours’ residuals (from a dangling node, send it back to the seed); set . Repeat pushes at any node whose residual is at least , in any order, until none is left. The key invariant is that the exact answer equals the estimate plus the personalized PageRank of the residual: so the error at the end is at most the total residual. Each push settles at least of mass at a cost of operations, and at most 1 unit of mass exists, so the total work is at most , independent of and . Worked example Push from E in the running example with . The first push settles 0.15 at E and gives C, D and F a residual of 0.283 each. Pushing C settles 0.043 at C and sends 0.120 to each of A and G. Pushing D settles 0.043 and sends 0.120 each to A and C. Pushing F, which is dangling, settles 0.043 and returns 0.241 to E, and so on.
