On this tiny graph the pushes revisit the same seven nodes many times; on a large graph the same budget spreads over the seed’s neighbourhood and never reaches the rest. Local clustering Andersen, Chung and Lang used push to find communities. Compute an approximate personalized PageRank from a seed, sort nodes by , and scan the prefixes of that order for the set with the lowest conductance , the ratio of arcs leaving the set to arcs inside it. They proved that this finds a cluster of near-optimal conductance around the seed in time proportional to the cluster’s size, not the graph’s. The method underlies many local community-detection tools (see Community detection ). Backward push Forward push answers “where does a walk from go?” Reversing the arcs answers “where do walks that reach come from?” Backward push starts with residual 1 at a target and pushes along in-links, estimating the contribution of every node to ’s PageRank. Andersen, Borgs, Chayes, Hopcroft, Mirrokni and Teng used it to compute the supporting set of a page: the nodes responsible for most of its PageRank. A page whose PageRank comes overwhelmingly from a small, densely interlinked supporting set is a classic Link spam signature, the same intuition Spam mass formalises with a trusted core. Bidirectional estimators Combining a backward push from the target with a few forward random walks from the source estimates a single personalized PageRank value much faster than either method alone. Lofgren, Banerjee, Goel and Seshadhri’s FAST-PPR (2014) and the later BiPPR exploit this: the backward push builds a “frontier” of nodes that are close to , and the forward walks only need to hit that frontier. Such estimators make it practical to answer “how relevant is to ?” on demand for arbitrary pairs. Global PageRank by push Pushing from a uniform residual instead of a single seed computes ordinary PageRank . Choosing the node with the largest residual at each step is the Gauss–Southwell method, which spends effort where the remaining error is largest. For global rankings it rarely beats well-tuned Gauss–Seidel sweeps over a compressed graph, because sweeps read memory sequentially while pushes jump around (see PageRank at scale ). d: Recipes for generating graphs at random, from uniform random links to preferential attachment and copying. They explain where web structure comes from, serve as null models for measurements, and provide test graphs for algorithms.
a: Erdős–Rényi model Configuration model Preferential attachment Barabási–Albert model Copying model Null model
x: A random graph model is a procedure for building a graph with some randomness: decide how many nodes there are and how links get placed, then let chance do the rest. Models serve three purposes in link analysis. They explain mechanisms, by showing which simple rule produces a given feature of real graphs. They provide null models , the baseline that says whether a measured clustering, community structure or degree correlation is surprising. And they generate test graphs of any size for checking algorithms such as PageRank or Community detection . Erdős–Rényi: every link independent Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi, and independently Edgar Gilbert, studied graphs in which each of the possible links is present independently with probability , written . The model is the reference point for everything else: Degrees are binomial, close to Poisson with mean : tightly concentrated around the average, with no hubs. A giant component appears suddenly when crosses 1, a phase transition. Above it, one component holds a constant fraction of the nodes. Distances are short, growing like . Clustering is tiny: the chance that two neighbours of a node are linked is just , which vanishes for large sparse graphs. Real link graphs have short distances like , but heavy-tailed degrees and high clustering unlike it (see Degree distributions and power laws and Clustering coefficient ). The configuration model: fix the degrees To separate the effect of degrees from everything else, the configuration model takes a given degree sequence, gives each node that many link “stubs”, and pairs stubs uniformly at random. The result is a random graph with exactly the observed degrees and otherwise no structure. It is the standard null model: Modularity compares the links inside a group with the configuration model’s expectation, . assortativity asks whether high-degree nodes link to each other more than the configuration model predicts. Molloy and Reed derived when it has a giant component: when , with the share of nodes of degree . Heavy tails make a giant component almost certain. Preferential attachment: the rich get richer Barabási and Albert proposed in 1999 that networks grow, and that new nodes link to existing nodes with probability proportional to their current degree. Grown this way, a graph develops a power-law degree distribution with exponent 3, whatever its starting point. The idea has older roots: Yule in 1925 and Simon in 1955 used the same mechanism for species and word frequencies, and Price in 1976 for citations, calling it cumulative advantage . Preferential attachment explains hubs but not much else. It produces exponent 3 only, little clustering and no community structure, and its directed variants still struggle to match the web’s in- and out-degree distributions together. Many refinements add aging, fitness or initial attractiveness to fit real data. Copying: links that imitate links Kleinberg, Kumar, Raghavan, Rajagopalan and Tomkins proposed a model specific to the web. A new page picks an existing prototype page and, for each of its links, either copies one of the prototype’s links or links to a random page. Copying produces power-law in-degrees, because a popular page is likely to be copied, and it produces many small bipartite cores: groups of pages that all link to the same set of targets, the signature of web communities and of hubs and authorities . It also matches the observation that pages near each other in name order have similar link lists, the property WebGraph compression exploits. Models of change Forest fire (Leskovec, Kleinberg and Faloutsos, 2005). A new node links to an “ambassador” and then recursively to some of its neighbours, like a fire spreading. It reproduces two observations about real graphs over time: they densify , gaining links faster than nodes, and their effective diameters shrink (see The neighbourhood function ). Kronecker graphs (Leskovec and colleagues, 2010). A small initiator matrix raised to a Kronecker power generates a self-similar graph whose degree, distance and spectral properties can be fitted to real networks. The Graph500 benchmark generates its test graphs this way. Small-world rewiring (Watts and Strogatz, 1998) explains clustering plus short paths (see Small worlds ). Why models matter for link analysis Is the structure surprising? A cluster of domains is only suspicious if it is far denser than the configuration model predicts for nodes of those degrees. Do the algorithms scale? Synthetic graphs of a billion arcs, with realistic degree distributions, test PageRank and HyperBall implementations before real data is available. What should a healthy graph look like? Deviations from a model’s smooth predictions, such as the bump of about 39,000 domains with 19,000 to 29,000 in-links in Common Crawl’s 2026 degree distribution, often mark coordinated behaviour rather than organic growth (see Degree distributions and power laws and Link spam ). d: The story behind PageRank. A surfer clicks random links, never presses Back, and now and then jumps to a random page; the share of time spent on each page is its PageRank.
a: Random surfer model Reasonable surfer Teleportation Teleport
x: Brin and Page explained PageRank with a story. Imagine a surfer who starts on a random page and keeps clicking links chosen at random, never pressing Back. Every so often the surfer gets bored and jumps to a page chosen at random from the whole web. Over a long session, some pages get visited far more often than others. A page’s PageRank is the fraction of time the surfer spends on it. The story is a random walk with one addition, the random jump or teleport , and that addition is what makes the mathematics work on the real web. The surfer’s rules At every step, the surfer on page : with probability (the The damping factor , typically 0.85), clicks one of ’s out-links, each with probability ; with probability , teleports to a page chosen uniformly from all pages; if has no out-links at all, teleports (see Dangling nodes ). The probability of being on page after the next step is then and PageRank is the distribution that this step leaves unchanged. Why the surfer needs to teleport Without teleportation the walk fails in two ways. On a page with no out-links the surfer is stuck, and on a group of pages that link only to each other it is trapped forever. In the long run, all the probability would collect in such traps: the OUT side of the The bow-tie structure , link farms that link only internally, and dead ends. Every other page, including the most popular ones, would end with PageRank zero. Teleportation repairs both failures. Every page is reachable from every other in one jump, so the chain is irreducible, and the chance of staying put through a jump makes it aperiodic. The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem then guarantees a unique, strictly positive PageRank vector. It also sets a floor: a page that nothing links to still receives from teleports, plus its share of the jumps out of dangling pages. How long the surfer stays on links The number of clicks between two teleports is geometrically distributed: the surfer clicks again with probability . With , the mean run is clicks, and a run of 20 or more clicks happens with probability . PageRank therefore mostly reflects the link structure within about half a dozen steps of each page. Links far upstream still matter, but their influence fades by a factor of per step. Simulating the surfer The story is also an algorithm. Release many surfers, let each take a random number of clicks, and count where they end. The counts estimate PageRank, accurately for popular pages after surprisingly few walks. That is Monte Carlo PageRank , and it suits distributed systems and graphs that change constantly. The lab on the PageRank page solves the equations instead, but the scores are the same. A model, not a user Real people do not browse this way. They press Back, use bookmarks and search boxes, click prominent links more than footer links, and leave. The random surfer is a modelling device that turns “important pages are linked by important pages” into a well-posed problem, not a description of traffic. Two lines of work took the user more seriously: The reasonable surfer. Google’s “reasonable surfer” patent, filed in 2004 and granted in 2010, describes weighting each link by how likely a real user is to click it, using features such as its position, font size and anchor text. A link in the main body would then pass more than one in the footer. Patents describe possibilities, not necessarily practice, but the idea is natural and widely believed to influence modern link weighting. BrowseRank. Liu and colleagues at Microsoft Research proposed in 2008 to replace the random surfer with real browsing logs, building a continuous-time Markov chain from observed page transitions and dwell times. Both keep the stationary-distribution machinery and change only the transition probabilities. What the story explains about link value The surfer model gives intuitive answers to practical questions: A link from a page with many links is worth less. The surfer on that page rarely picks yours. A link from a frequently visited page is worth more. The surfer is there more often to click it. Deep links decay. Value that has to travel through several pages loses a factor of α at each step. Pages nobody links to still exist. Teleportation gives every page a baseline, which is why PageRank never says a page is worthless, only that it sits at the floor. These are the intuitions behind most link-building advice, and the reasons a single link from a strong, focused page can outweigh hundreds from link lists (see Backlinks and referring domains ). d: A walker who follows random links visits some nodes more often than others. The long-run visit frequencies, the stationary distribution, are the mathematical core of PageRank and its relatives.
a: Random walk Markov chain Stationary distribution Transition matrix Ergodic
x: A random walk on a graph starts at some node and, at every step, moves along an out-link chosen uniformly at random. Run it for a long time and count how often it visits each node. On a well-behaved graph those frequencies settle down to a fixed distribution, the stationary distribution , which no longer depends on where the walk started. Nodes that many frequently visited nodes link to get visited often. That is the idea behind PageRank , and the theory of Markov chains says when it works. Transition matrix Write for the matrix with when links to and 0 otherwise, the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix. Row is the probability distribution of the walker’s next position when it stands on . If is a row vector giving the probability of being at each node after steps, then A stationary distribution is a probability vector that one step leaves unchanged: Each node’s stationary probability equals the probability flowing into it: . That is the PageRank equation without the teleport term. A small example Take only the core of the running example: A links to B and C, B links to C, and C links to A. The transition probabilities are and . Solving : With the probabilities summing to 1, . The walker spends 40% of its time on A, 40% on C and 20% on B. B loses because it receives only half of A’s traffic, while C receives the other half plus everything from B. When a unique answer exists Markov chain theory gives two conditions: Irreducible. Every node can reach every other, so the graph is one strongly connected component . Then exactly one stationary distribution exists, and it is positive everywhere. Aperiodic. The lengths of the graph’s cycles have greatest common divisor 1. Then converges to from any starting distribution. In a graph whose only cycles have length 2 (A ⇄ B), a walker starting on A is on A at every even step forever, and oscillates instead of settling. The core above has a cycle of length 2 (A → C → A) and one of length 3 (A → B → C → A), so it is aperiodic, and converges to . A chain that is both irreducible and aperiodic is called ergodic . The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem is the linear-algebra version of this result. Why the raw web breaks both conditions The web graph is neither irreducible nor safe to walk on: Dangling nodes. A node with no out-links has an empty row in . A walker who lands there has nowhere to go, and probability leaks out of the system. In Common Crawl’s domain graph, 63.8% of nodes are dangling (see Dangling nodes ). Traps. Groups of nodes with links in but no links out, such as the OUT part of the The bow-tie structure , absorb the walker forever. The stationary distribution of the raw walk puts all its mass in such traps and gives zero to everything else, including the core. PageRank repairs both with teleportation : with probability the walker jumps to a random node, and from a dangling node it always jumps. The repaired chain is irreducible and aperiodic by construction, so it has a unique stationary distribution, which is the PageRank vector (see The random surfer and The damping factor ). Undirected graphs are easy On an undirected graph the stationary distribution has a closed form: , proportional to degree. A random walk on an undirected graph is therefore just a slow way to compute Degree centrality . Direction is what makes random walks interesting on the web: a link from to sends traffic one way only, and the stationary distribution depends on the whole structure of who links to whom. How fast the walk forgets its start The mixing time is how many steps it takes for to get close to . It is governed by the second-largest eigenvalue modulus of the transition matrix: the distance to shrinks roughly like . For PageRank’s repaired matrix, Haveliwala and Kamvar showed that , which is why Power iteration converges in a predictable number of steps however large the graph is. Variants used in link analysis Random walk with restart. The walker teleports back to one fixed node, or a small set, instead of anywhere. Its stationary distribution is Personalized PageRank , a measure of proximity to the restart set, and the basis of TrustRank . Backward walks. Walking along in-links instead of out-links scores nodes by what they link to . That gives CheiRank and 2DRank . Alternating walks. Stepping forward along a link and then backward along another gives SALSA , a stochastic version of HITS (hubs and authorities) . Simulated walks. Instead of solving equations, run many short walks and count where they end. Monte Carlo PageRank estimates PageRank this way, accurately for the top nodes after very few walks. References Levin, D. d: Compare two rankings by how much their top lists overlap at every depth, with geometrically decreasing weight on deeper levels. Works on truncated lists and on lists that do not contain the same items.
a: RBO Top-k overlap Jaccard at k Intersection at depth
x: Many rankings are only ever seen as top lists: the first ten search results, the hundred most central domains, the top thousand by a vendor’s score. Such lists are indefinite , cut off at an arbitrary depth, and usually non-conjoint : an item in one list may not appear in the other at all. Kendall’s tau and Spearman’s rho need both rankings over the same items and cannot cope. Rank-biased overlap (RBO), introduced by William Webber, Alistair Moffat and Justin Zobel in 2010, compares two lists by their overlap at each depth, weighting shallow depths more, and gives meaningful values even when only the tops are known. Overlap at a depth Let and be the first items of two rankings. Their agreement at depth is the fraction of items they share: Comparing top- lists by alone, or by their Jaccard similarity, is common and simple, but it ignores order within the top and depends heavily on the arbitrary choice of . Definition RBO averages the agreements at all depths with geometric weights: The persistence models a reader who looks at item with probability after seeing item . Small makes RBO focus sharply on the top; close to 1 spreads attention deeper. Webber and colleagues computed that with the first ten depths carry about 86% of the total weight. RBO is 1 for identical infinite rankings and 0 for rankings that share no items at any depth. Truncated lists Real lists stop at some depth , so the sum cannot be evaluated to infinity. RBO comes with bounds: RBO_min assumes the lists share nothing beyond depth : a lower bound. RBO_res , the residual , is the most that the unseen depths could add. RBO_ext extrapolates by assuming that agreement stays at beyond depth , a point estimate inside the bounds and the value usually reported. Because the weights decay geometrically, the residual shrinks fast as grows; for and , the uncertainty is a few hundredths. Worked example: the top of the web Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, top 12 by each centrality: Position Harmonic centrality PageRank 1 googleapis.com googleapis.com 2 facebook.com google.com 3 google.com facebook.com 4 instagram.com googletagmanager.com 5 googletagmanager.com instagram.com 6 youtube.com cloudflare.com 7 gstatic.com gstatic.com 8 twitter.com wsimg.com 9 linkedin.com youtube.com 10 gmpg.org gmpg.org 11 cloudflare.com linkedin.com 12 gravatar.com cloudflareinsights.com The agreement starts at 1 (both put googleapis.com first), dips to 0.5 at depth 2, returns to 1 at depths 3 and 5, and settles near 0.75 to 0.8 from depth 10 to depth 30. Over the top 30 lists, RBO_ext is 0.81 with and 0.85 with : the two centralities largely agree on the very top of the web, and diverge more as the lists get longer, as the PageRank entry’s examples of PageRank-only domains show. Properties Order within the top matters. Swapping positions 1 and 2 lowers to 0 if neither list has the other’s first item at depth 1, and the deep terms barely notice. No common universe needed. Items that appear in only one list simply never count towards overlap, so a vendor’s top list can be compared with Common Crawl’s even if neither covers the other’s domains. Ties need a convention. RBO assumes strict orders; Webber and colleagues describe how to treat tied items as sharing their depths. Not a correlation. RBO is a similarity between 0 and 1, not a coefficient between −1 and 1, and a value of 0.8 does not mean the same thing as . When to use it Use RBO for search results, top- lists and leaderboards, especially when the lists come from different sources with different coverage: two link indexes, two crawls, or a vendor’s “top domains” against an open ranking. Use Weighted tau when both full rankings over the same items are available and ties are common; use plain overlap at a fixed only when the reader really does stop at exactly .
