d: A centrality gives each node a value; a ranking gives it a position. Positions are easy to read and easy to misread. How values are distributed, how ties are broken and how precise the values are decide what a position means.
a: Rank Position Percentile Log scale Ties Tie-breaking
x: Every centrality produces a score (a value) for each node, and sorting by score produces a rank (a position). Common Crawl’s ranks files give both for each domain: #harmonicc_pos and #harmonicc_val , #pr_pos and #pr_val . Positions are convenient: “position 10,000 of 119.7 million” sounds precise and comparable. Whether it is depends on three things the position hides: how the values are spread, how ties are broken, and how accurate the values are. Values crowd in different ways Here are Common Crawl’s 2026 domain values at the same positions for both centralities: Position Harmonic value Share of top PageRank Multiple of floor 1 28,819,640 100% 3,670,000 100 19,303,032 67% 75,800 10,000 16,972,598 59% 855 1,000,000 13,857,260 48% 8.6 10,000,000 12,448,198 43% 1.54 50,000,000 10,118,504 35% 1.014 100,000,000 7,444,818 26% 1.0000 The two columns tell opposite stories: Harmonic values are flat. Position 10,000 scores 59% of the top value and position 10 million still 43%. Millions of domains share almost the same value, so a small difference in value means a huge difference in position. wixstatic.com and parastorage.com differ by 18% in harmonic value and sit at positions 26 and 81,305. PageRank is steep at the top and flat at the bottom. The top domain has 3.7 million times the floor value, while position 50 million is within 1.4% of the floor and everything below is closer still. Below position 30 million every domain is within 8% of the floor, so the order there rests on a few weak in-links and, near the very bottom, on rounding. Neither position tells you the value without the distribution. Ties Positions must be unique; values need not be. Common Crawl’s harmonic values are single-precision floats with about seven significant digits, and only 5,940,987 distinct values occur among 119,722,885 domains. The 14,903,700 domains with value 0 are all tied. Common Crawl sorts with a stable sort on the value, so tied domains keep their vertex order, which is reversed-name order (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ): among equal scores, com.aaa… gets a better position than com.zzz… . Common tie conventions: Convention Tied nodes get Example for values 9, 7, 7, 5 Ordinal (break by id) consecutive positions 1, 2, 3, 4 Standard competition the best shared position 1, 2, 2, 4 Fractional the average position 1, 2.5, 2.5, 4 Dense consecutive distinct ranks 1, 2, 2, 3 Rank-correlation statistics differ in how they treat ties (see Kendall’s tau ), and two datasets using different conventions disagree even when their scores agree. Precision A position is only as good as the values behind it: Approximation error. Harmonic values come from HyperBall ’s probabilistic counters, with relative errors of a few percent. In a flat region, that error spans hundreds of thousands of positions. Convergence error. PageRank solvers stop at a tolerance. Values in the tail that differ in the eighth significant digit are ordered by the solver’s rounding, not by the graph (see Power iteration ). Floating-point noise. Nodes that should tie exactly, such as all nodes with no in-links under PageRank, end up with values differing in the last bits, and their positions are arbitrary. Better ways to compare Compare values, on a log scale. For PageRank, runs from 0 at the floor to about 6.6 at the top of Common Crawl’s domain graph and spreads the meaningful range evenly. Toolbar PageRank’s 0–10 scale was a bucketed log scale of this kind (see A short history of PageRank ). Use percentiles with care. “Top 1%” is meaningful for PageRank, where the top percent holds most of the mass, and much less so for harmonic centrality, where the top percent spans a narrow band of values. Treat missing as missing. Of the 1,068,241 domains in GoDaddy’s 2026-09-23 auction inventory, 89% do not appear in Common Crawl’s graph at all. They have no position, which is not the same as the worst position: they were never linked from a crawled page, or never seen. Report the distribution. Any table of positions should come with the values at a few reference positions, like the one above. Vendor scores are rescaled ranks Commercial 0–100 scores such as Domain Rating (Ahrefs) and Domain Authority (Moz) are monotone rescalings of an underlying value, described by their vendors as logarithmic. The rescaling hides the same issues: a score of 20 against 21 may be noise, while 70 against 71 may be a large difference, and the score’s meaning shifts when the vendor’s index grows or the formula changes. Compare scores from the same vendor and the same date, and prefer differences of several points to single points. References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Vigna, S. (2015). A weighted correlation index for rankings with ties. WWW 2015 , 1166–1176. Common Crawl. cc-webgraph , process_webgraph.sh (stable sort of ranks by value).

d: A practical guide for buyers. Which numbers to look at, what thresholds mean on real data, how to tell real link standing from noise, and two worked examples from the 2026-09-23 auction inventory.
a: Domain evaluation Domain appraisal Link metrics guide
x: A domain listing typically shows a dozen link numbers from several vendors. They measure related things, on different crawls, with different definitions and different blind spots. This guide puts the rest of the encyclopedia to work: what to look at first, what the numbers mean on real data, and how to tell a domain with real link standing from one whose metrics are noise. Every threshold below comes from Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph and GoDaddy’s auction inventory of 2026-09-23. Step 1: Is the domain in an open graph at all? Start with the free, reproducible source. Look the domain up in Common Crawl’s ranks file (see The Common Crawl web graph ): Absent (88.8% of the 2026-09-23 inventory): no page in three months of crawling linked to it. Whatever a vendor reports, the domain has little current link presence. Present: note its in-degree (referring domains in the graph), its harmonic position and its PageRank position. Step 2: Put the open numbers in context For domains in the graph, rough bands: Signal Weak Meaningful Strong Common Crawl referring domains 1–5 (90% of listed domains in the graph) 6–100 over 100 (676 listed domains, 0.06% of the inventory) PageRank position below 30 million (within 8% of the floor) 1–10 million (1.5 to 9 times the floor) top 1 million Harmonic position below 50 million 1–10 million top 1 million Harmonic values are flat, so positions exaggerate small differences, and PageRank is flat at the bottom, so positions there are close to arbitrary (see Ranks and scores ). A domain strong on both is well embedded; strong PageRank with weak harmonic often means one or two strong links carry it (see PageRank ). Step 3: Read the vendor scores with their caveats Subtract the floor. One vendor reports a median of 96 referring domains even for domains Common Crawl never saw linked, mostly the same few domains on every listing. Counts near that level carry no information (see Auditing vendor metrics ). Treat zero as unknown for Majestic fields delivered through the auction feed: more than half of the best-linked listed domains show zero there (see Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) ). Expect Authority Score to be flat. 87.7% of listings share the value 2 (see Authority Score (Semrush) ). Use TF/CF and DR or DA comparatively , and only from the same date and source (see Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) , Domain Rating (Ahrefs) , Domain Authority (Moz) ). Step 4: Look at who links Every number above is a summary. The list behind it decides the value: Do you recognise the referring domains? Are they related to the domain’s name or intended use? Are the links in content, or in footers, profiles and comment sections? What do the anchors say about the old site’s topic, language and history (see Anchor text )? Do the links still exist? Prefer recent crawl data over historic indexes (see Backlinks and referring domains ). Step 5: Check consistency Sources should broadly agree for a genuinely well-linked domain. When they do not, the disagreement is the finding: Pattern Likely cause Vendor counts high, Common Crawl absent or tiny spam floor, stale historic links, or links from parts of the web Common Crawl did not crawl Common Crawl strong, vendors low links from scripts, redirects or nofollow links, which Common Crawl counts and some vendors exclude High CF, very low TF many links from low-trust sources (see Link spam ) High PageRank position, low harmonic position a few strong links rather than broad reach Strong metrics, but anchors in an unrelated topic or language a repurposed or spammed domain (see Expired domains ) Two worked examples A domain with real standing. solarindustrymag.com , 19 years old, appears in Common Crawl’s graph with 619 referring domains, harmonic position 579,899 and PageRank position 262,330: in the strong band on both. Semrush lists 3,661 referring domains, led by cambridge.org , nytimes.com and theguardian.com . Majestic shows 1,309 referring domains with Trust Flow 30 above Citation Flow 22. Every source agrees, and the linking sites are recognisable and topical. The remaining questions are about history and fit, not about whether the links are real. A domain with metrics but no standing. blacknailtechs.org appears in Common Crawl’s graph with 3 referring domains, harmonic position 87,011,879 and PageRank position 85,126,572, essentially at the floor. Semrush lists 166 referring domains, but its top three are bye.fyi , shortenurls.eu and southfwb.com , domains that appear among the top referrers of a large share of all listings. Majestic shows Trust Flow 0. The vendor count is the floor; the domain’s own link standing is negligible. A third pattern is worth knowing. Another listed domain has 878 referring domains in Common Crawl and positions around 1–2 million, but Semrush counts 22,901 referring domains, 26 times as many, and Majestic shows Trust Flow 1 against Citation Flow 23. Real links exist; the vendor numbers suggest that many more come from low-trust sources. That domain needs Step 4 more than any other. What no metric tells you Link metrics cannot see Google’s discounts, manual actions or disavow files (see Link penalties and the disavow tool ), trademark conflicts, or whether the planned use fits the old links. They estimate how much of the web’s link attention reaches a name. Whether that attention is worth paying for is a judgement about the links themselves. References Common Crawl. Web Graph Release cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug. GoDaddy Auctions. Daily inventory export, 2026-09-23 ( inventory.auctions.godaddy.com ).

d: How 301s, 302s and canonical tags move link signals from one URL to another. They decide where a moved site's links end up, and they are the main mechanism by which an expired domain's links are put to new use.
a: Redirect 301 redirect 302 redirect Canonical tag rel=canonical Link equity transfer
x: Links point at URLs, and URLs change. Sites move to new domains, switch from http to https , merge pages and delete old ones. Redirects tell browsers and crawlers that a URL now lives elsewhere; canonical tags tell search engines which of several duplicate URLs is the main one. Both determine where the links pointing at the old or duplicate URLs count. For link analysis they act like special links: a redirect is effectively a page whose single out-link is the redirect target. Kinds of redirect Mechanism Meaning Typical use HTTP 301 Moved Permanently the resource has a new permanent URL site migrations, domain changes HTTP 308 Permanent Redirect as 301, but the request method must not change APIs, forms HTTP 302 Found / 307 Temporary Redirect the resource is temporarily elsewhere A/B tests, maintenance, geo-routing <meta http-equiv="refresh"> the browser loads another URL after a delay static hosting without server control JavaScript location change a script navigates away single-page apps, often unintended Permanent redirects say “update your records”: search engines should replace the old URL with the new one in their index and credit the old URL’s links to the new one. Temporary redirects say “keep the old URL”, so the old URL stays indexed. Do redirects pass link value? For years SEO lore held that a 301 passed about 85% of a page’s PageRank, by analogy with the The damping factor , and that 302s passed none. In 2016 Google’s Gary Illyes stated that 30x redirects no longer lose PageRank. Google’s documentation now treats permanent redirects as a strong signal that the target should be canonical and temporary ones as a weaker signal, without describing any loss. Whether a specific redirect passes value in practice also depends on relevance: a redirect from a page about one thing to an unrelated page may be treated like a deleted page. In a plain link graph the arithmetic is simpler. A redirecting domain is a node with one out-link. Under PageRank it passes of its score to the target each step and keeps the teleport share for itself; nothing in the formula knows it is a redirect. Redirects in Common Crawl’s graph Common Crawl’s link extractor turns HTTP redirects into links: a response with status 301, 302, 303, 307 or 308 and a Location header produces an arc from the redirecting host to the target host. A domain that redirects everything to another domain therefore appears in the domain graph with an arc to its target, and the target inherits part of its PageRank and becomes closer, in Harmonic centrality terms, to everything that reached the redirecting domain. The redirecting domain keeps its own in-links and its own position in the ranks. Canonical tags <link rel="canonical" href="…"> in a page’s head names the preferred URL among duplicates: the same product reachable through several category paths, a page with and without tracking parameters, an article syndicated to another site. Search engines treat it as a strong hint and consolidate the duplicates’ signals, including their links, on the canonical URL. Unlike a redirect, the duplicate page stays visible to users. A canonical tag pointing to an unrelated page is ignored, as is one that contradicts other signals. Chains, loops and soft 404s Chains. Each extra hop costs a crawl request and adds a chance of failure. Crawlers follow a limited number of hops; Google’s documentation says it follows up to 10. Loops. A redirect cycle makes a URL unreachable. Soft 404s. Redirecting many deleted pages to the home page, rather than to equivalent pages, is often treated as if those pages simply returned “not found”: the links to them stop counting. Redirects and expired domains The most common commercial use of redirects in domain investing is pointing an expired domain at another site to pass on its old links. The practice is legitimate when the domains are genuinely related, such as a company acquiring a competitor and merging their sites. When the old domain is unrelated and bought only for its links, search engines may discount the redirected links, and buying several such domains to redirect into one site is a recognised Link spam pattern. Google’s spam policy on expired domain abuse targets repurposing an expired domain’s reputation for unrelated, low-value content, a closely related practice. What it means for a domain Check where a domain redirects today. An expired domain that already redirects somewhere, or did until recently, shares its link profile with its target in every link index. Check what used to redirect to it. Links that arrive through redirects from other domains appear in some indexes as the domain’s own referring domains. Prefer page-to-page redirects. When moving content, redirect each old URL to its closest equivalent, not everything to the home page. References Fielding, R., Nottingham, M., & Reschke, J. (Eds.) (2022). HTTP Semantics. RFC 9110, section 15.4 (redirection status codes). Google Search Central. Redirects and Google Search. developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects. Google Search Central. How to specify a canonical URL with rel=“canonical” and other methods. developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls.

t: Reversed domain names and public suffixes
d: Why web graphs write google.com as com.google, and how the Public Suffix List decides where a registrable domain begins.
a: Reversed host names SURT Public Suffix List PSL Registrable domain eTLD+1
x: Common Crawl’s vertex files list com.google , com.facebook and uk.co.bbc , not google.com . Writing host names with their labels reversed is a small trick with large consequences: sorted alphabetically, reversed names keep every host of a domain, and every domain of a top-level domain, next to each other. Graph compression, range queries and prefix grouping all depend on that locality. The second half of the story is deciding where the domain part of a name ends, which takes a list, not a rule. Reversing labels A host name is a sequence of labels separated by dots, most specific first: blog.example.co.uk . Reversing the labels gives uk.co.example.blog , most general first, like a file path. Sorting reversed names produces a hierarchy: com.example com.example.blog com.example.shop com.examples uk.co.example uk.co.example.blog All of example.com ’s hosts form one contiguous run, and all .uk names come after all .com names. Sorting the forward names instead would scatter them: blog.example.com sorts among the b’s and shop.example.com among the s’s. The convention is old. Java package names ( org.apache.commons ) use it, and web archives sort their indexes by SURT, the Sort-friendly URI Reordering Transform , which writes http://www.example.com/a as com,example,www)/a . Common Crawl’s own URL index uses SURT keys. Why graphs care Web graph tools number nodes in sorted order. With reversed names, the numbers of related hosts sit close together: Compression. Hosts of one site link to similar targets and to each other. When related hosts get nearby numbers, successor lists repeat and the gaps between consecutive targets shrink, which is exactly what WebGraph compression exploits. Common Crawl’s vertex ids follow reversed-name order. Range queries. All domains of a top-level domain form one id range: every .de domain is a contiguous block, so “restrict to German domains” becomes a range test. Tie-breaking. Rankings with tied scores fall back on node id. Common Crawl sorts its ranks file by score with a stable sort, so ties end up in id order, which is reversed-name order (see Ranks and scores ). Public suffixes Where does the registrable domain begin? For www.example.com it is example.com , the last two labels. For www.example.co.uk it is example.co.uk , the last three, because co.uk is a suffix under which anyone can register names. No rule computes this from the name. The Public Suffix List (PSL), maintained by volunteers at Mozilla since 2007, lists such suffixes: com , co.uk , ac.jp , pvt.k12.ma.us and thousands more. The registrable domain , also called eTLD+1, is the public suffix plus one more label. The list has two sections: The ICANN section holds suffixes delegated through the domain name system: TLDs and the second-level structures registries define, such as co.uk . The private section holds suffixes that companies submit for their own platforms: github.io , blogspot.com , herokuapp.com . Browsers use these entries to stop one customer’s site from setting cookies for another’s. Whether a graph honours the private section changes its nodes. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph does not: github.io is one domain with 310,784 hosts and blogspot.com one domain with 4,113,910 hosts, though the PSL’s private section lists both as public suffixes. Each GitHub Pages site or Blogspot blog is a separate site to its owner and a separate registrable domain to a browser, but a single node in this graph. The Page, host and domain graphs entry discusses what that merging does to rankings. Names in the Common Crawl graph The 2026 domain graph spans 1,520 top-level domains and 7,482 distinct public suffixes. Its largest suffix groups: Suffix Domains .com 59,819,443 .org 6,634,711 .de 5,022,175 .net 3,751,749 .co.uk 2,691,012 Half of all domains are .com . Internationalised names appear in their ASCII-compatible xn-- form (594,228 domains), about one domain in seven contains a hyphen, and one in eight a digit. Pitfalls Matching on the last two labels is wrong for every country with second-level registries: it folds every .co.uk site into one node called co.uk . The list changes. New gTLDs and new private suffixes appear every month. A graph built with an old copy of the PSL and one built with a new copy disagree on some nodes. Hosts are not domains. A name such as www.example.com in one dataset and example.com in another are different nodes at the host level and the same node at the domain level. Normalise before joining datasets. Host counts measure DNS habits, not reach. A domain that answers for any subdomain can generate unlimited hosts, and some sites mint a subdomain per page or per user. In the 2026 graph hub.biz folds 1,222,261 hosts and adgo.kr 423,413, yet adgo.kr ranks below position 3,000,000 by harmonic centrality (see Link spam ). References Mozilla Foundation. Public Suffix List. publicsuffix.org (ICANN and private sections). Internet Archive. SURT: Sort-friendly URI Reordering Transform , as used by the Heritrix crawler and Wayback CDX indexes. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004). The WebGraph Framework I: Compression techniques. WWW 2004 , 595–602.

d: A random-walk version of HITS that alternates forward and backward steps. Its authority scores turn out to be in-degree, normalised within each group of co-cited nodes, which makes them immune to topic drift.
a: Stochastic Approach for Link-Structure Analysis
x: SALSA, the Stochastic Approach for Link-Structure Analysis , was introduced by Ronny Lempel and Shlomo Moran in 2000 as a fix for a weakness of HITS (hubs and authorities) . HITS lets a small, densely interlinked group of pages capture the dominant eigenvector and drag the results off topic. SALSA keeps the idea of hubs and authorities but replaces the eigenvectors with the stationary distributions of two random walks . The result is surprisingly simple: within each connected group of co-cited nodes, a node’s authority score is proportional to its in-degree. Definition Build a bipartite graph with a hub copy of every node that has out-links and an authority copy of every node that has in-links. Each link joins hub to authority . SALSA defines two Markov chains on this graph: The authority chain. From authority , step backward to a uniformly random in-neighbour , then forward to a uniformly random out-neighbour of . Two steps lead from one authority to another, passing through a hub that links to both. The hub chain. From hub , step forward to a random out-neighbour , then backward to a random in-neighbour of . The SALSA authority and hub scores are the stationary distributions of these chains. In matrix terms, the authority chain’s transition matrix is , where and are the Adjacency matrices and lists matrix with rows, respectively columns, normalised to sum to 1. HITS uses the unnormalised product ; the normalisation is the entire difference. The closed form Call two authorities co-cited if some hub links to both. Co-citation splits the authorities into connected components. Lempel and Moran proved that the authority chain’s stationary distribution has a closed form: for an authority in component , where is the set of all authorities. Inside a component, authority is in-degree. Between components, each component’s total share is proportional to its size. Hub scores follow the same rule with out-degrees and co-reference (two hubs linking to a common node). No eigenvector needs to be computed: one pass to count degrees and one union–find pass to find components give the exact scores. Worked example In the running example, A links to B and C, so B and C are co-cited; C links to A and G, so A and G are co-cited; D links to A and C; and E links to C, D and F. Every authority is connected to every other through these co-citations, so there is a single component holding all six nodes with in-links, and SALSA authority is simply in-degree divided by the 10 links: Node C A B D F G E SALSA authority 0.4 0.2 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.1 0 HITS authority 0.438 0.148 0.104 0.137 0.137 0.035 0 Hub scores work the same way: every node with out-links shares the target C with another, so SALSA hub is out-degree over 10, giving E 0.3, A, C and D 0.2, and B 0.1. HITS separates D and F from B and G by who links to them; SALSA does not. Why it resists topic drift HITS multiplies scores through , so a block of pages that all link to each other contributes eigenvalues around and can dominate. In SALSA the walk moves through normalised probabilities, and a dense block simply forms its own component, whose share is proportional to its size , not its density. The tightly knit community effect disappears. The price is that SALSA learns nothing from the identity of the linking hubs: within a component, a link from the best hub counts the same as a link from the worst. Axioms SALSA satisfies the density axiom and fails size and score monotonicity (see Axioms for centrality ). Monotonicity fails because a new link can merge two components and redistribute their shares: the target’s in-degree goes up, but the total in-degree it is divided by can go up more. Where it is used SALSA’s closed form makes it cheap, and its random-walk form makes it easy to restrict to a neighbourhood. Twitter’s Who-to-Follow service, as described by Gupta and colleagues in 2013, ran SALSA on a bipartite graph built around each user: a “circle of trust” from personalized PageRank on one side and the accounts they follow on the other. The authority scores ranked accounts to recommend. On the web as a whole, SALSA’s lesson is mostly conceptual. A sophisticated-looking hub-and-authority computation can reduce to in-degree within co-citation communities, which says how much of HITS’s extra information came from the dominant eigenvector’s sensitivity to dense groups. References Lempel, R., & Moran, S. (2000). The stochastic approach for link-structure analysis (SALSA) and the TKC effect. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 387–401. Lempel, R., & Moran, S. (2001). SALSA: The stochastic approach for link-structure analysis. ACM Transactions on Information Systems 19(2), 131–160. Gupta, P., Goel, A., Lin, J., Sharma, A., Wang, D., & Zadeh, R. (2013). WTF: The Who to Follow service at Twitter. WWW 2013 , 505–514.

d: Real networks combine dense local clusters with surprisingly short paths between any two nodes. That combination explains why "six degrees of separation" holds, why harmonic values crowd together and why links travel far.
a: Small-world network Six degrees of separation Watts–Strogatz model Milgram experiment
x: In 1967 the social psychologist Stanley Milgram asked people in Nebraska and Kansas to forward a letter, through acquaintances on first-name terms, to a stranger in Massachusetts. The letters that arrived took a median of about five intermediate hands. “Six degrees of separation” entered popular culture, and in 1998 Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz explained how a network can be both clustered , with most of your acquaintances knowing each other, and small , with everyone a few steps from everyone else. Web graphs share both properties, and both shape how link metrics behave. The two ingredients A network is called a small world when it has: High clustering. Neighbours of a node are often linked to each other, far more than chance predicts (see Clustering coefficient ). Short typical distances. The average shortest-path length grows only like the logarithm of the number of nodes, as in a random graph (see Paths, distance and reachability ). A regular lattice, where each node links only to its nearest neighbours, has the first property without the second: going around a ring of a million nodes takes hundreds of thousands of steps. A random graph has the second without the first. Real networks have both. The Watts–Strogatz model Watts and Strogatz started from a ring lattice in which every node links to its nearest neighbours, and rewired each link to a random node with probability . At the graph is a clustered lattice with long paths; at it is random, with short paths and no clustering. In between, a remarkable thing happens: a few percent of rewired links, acting as shortcuts across the ring, collapse the average distance almost to the random-graph value while barely touching the clustering. Short paths need only a handful of long-range links; clustering needs many local ones. Kleinberg added that short paths existing is not the same as people finding them. Milgram’s letter-holders routed with local knowledge only, which works only when long-range links follow a specific distance distribution. Navigable small worlds are a special case. Measurements Milgram’s letters. In the best-known study, 64 of 296 letters arrived, with a mean of 5.2 intermediaries. Many letters were lost, and the result has been debated, but later large-scale replications by email found similar path lengths. The web. Albert, Jeong and Barabási estimated in 1999 that two random pages were on average 19 clicks apart, growing logarithmically with the number of pages. Broder and colleagues found that, among page pairs with a directed path at all, the average distance was about 16, and about 7 when link direction was ignored. Most directed pairs had no path. Facebook. In 2011, Backstrom, Boldi, Rosa, Ugander and Vigna computed the distance distribution of the entire Facebook friendship graph with HyperANF: an average distance of 4.74 between 721 million users, so 3.74 intermediaries, not six. Domain graphs are smaller still. Folding pages into domains turns long chains of internal navigation into single nodes, and the infrastructure domains embedded on millions of sites act as universal shortcuts. Consequences for link metrics Harmonic values crowd together. If almost every domain is within a few steps of the core, then most domains’ sums of reciprocal distances fall in a narrow band. Common Crawl’s harmonic centrality at position 10 million is still 43% of the top value (see Harmonic centrality and Ranks and scores ). PageRank’s horizon covers a lot. The random surfer clicks about 5.7 links between jumps (see The random surfer ); in a small world, that reaches a large part of the graph, which is why PageRank aggregates influence from far beyond a site’s immediate neighbours. Short paths make spam harder to isolate. One link from a well-connected site to a spam domain connects the spam domain to the core in one step. Trust and distrust propagation methods ( TrustRank , Spam mass ) rely on attenuating influence per step precisely because distances are short. Effective diameter beats diameter. The longest shortest path is set by a few freak chains and says little; the distance within which 90% of reachable pairs lie is stable and meaningful (see The neighbourhood function ). Beyond Watts–Strogatz The Watts–Strogatz model produces narrow degree distributions, unlike the heavy-tailed degrees of real networks. Models with preferential attachment generate hubs, and hubs shorten paths even further: in scale-free graphs typical distances can grow like (see Random graph models ). Real link graphs owe their small-world character to both mechanisms: local clustering from topical communities, and hubs that everyone links to. References Travers, J., & Milgram, S. (1969). An experimental study of the small world problem. Sociometry 32(4), 425–443. Watts, D. J., & Strogatz, S. H. (1998). Collective dynamics of “small-world” networks. Nature 393, 440–442. Albert, R., Jeong, H., & Barabási, A.-L. (1999). Diameter of the World-Wide Web. Nature 401, 130–131. Kleinberg, J. M. (2000). Navigation in a small world. Nature 406, 845. Backstrom, L., Boldi, P., Rosa, M., Ugander, J., & Vigna, S. (2012). Four degrees of separation. WebSci 2012 , 33–42.

d: The share of a node's PageRank that does not come from known good nodes. A high-PageRank site whose rank comes mostly from outside the reputable web is a link-spam suspect.
a: Relative spam mass Absolute spam mass Mass estimation Good core
x: PageRank says how much link attention a site gets; it does not say from whom. Spam mass, introduced in 2006 by Gyöngyi, Berkhin, Garcia-Molina and Pedersen, splits a site’s PageRank into the part contributed by known good sites and the rest. A popular, legitimate site draws most of its PageRank from the reputable web. A site boosted by a link farm draws most of its PageRank from the farm. Comparing ordinary PageRank with a trust-seeded version turns that difference into a number. PageRank contributions Spam mass rests on a property of PageRank’s linear form. Write PageRank without the dangling-node correction, as the solution of a linear system: where gives each node of teleport mass and has empty rows for Dangling nodes , so mass reaching them simply leaks away. This is linear in . Split into one piece per node, with putting on alone, and splits into contributions : , where is the PageRank that node owes to random jumps landing on . Each is a Personalized PageRank vector from , scaled by . Definition Let be a good core , a set of nodes known to be reputable. The PageRank that receives from the good core is computed in one pass by teleporting only to the good core, with per good node. The absolute spam mass of is what remains, and the relative spam mass is its share: A relative mass near 0 means nearly all of ’s PageRank traces back to good nodes; near 1 means nearly none does. Worked example Take A and B as the good core in the running example, with : Node A B C G D E F Linear PageRank 0.086 0.058 0.125 0.075 0.028 0.021 0.028 From the good core 0.044 0.040 0.053 0.022 0 0 0 Relative mass 0.49 0.31 0.58 0.70 1.00 1.00 1.00 (The linear PageRank sums to 0.42, not 1, because mass that reaches the dangling nodes F and G leaks away.) D, E and F have relative mass 1: the good core cannot reach them, so all of their PageRank comes from elsewhere. C, the top node, gets 58% of its PageRank from outside the core, because D and E both feed it. That illustrates the method’s main caution: a high relative mass flags a node for review, not for condemnation. Here the “outside” nodes D and E are not spam at all; the core is simply too small. Using it to find spam The paper’s procedure: Assemble a large good core, largely automatically, from sources that rarely host spam. Compute ordinary PageRank and core-based PageRank, two power iterations over the whole graph. Consider only nodes with high PageRank, where spam does the most damage and where the estimate is reliable. Flag those whose relative mass exceeds a threshold. On a host graph from Yahoo!'s index, the share of spam among flagged hosts rose steadily with the mass threshold: the higher the relative mass, the more likely a hand-checked host was spam. Limits The core decides everything. Good sites outside the core’s reach look exactly like spam, as D and E do above. A core that under-represents a language or region flags that region wholesale. Mass needs a large PageRank to mean anything. For a low-ranked node, a few links shift the ratio a lot, so the estimate is noisy. The method targets nodes that rank high. Spammers can buy core links. A link from a good-core site carries good mass. Paid links on reputable sites, and spam links injected into comments or hacked pages of good sites, defeat the measure, as they defeat TrustRank. What it means for a domain Spam mass formalises a question every domain buyer should ask about a strong-looking metric: where does it come from? A domain with a high PageRank or a high vendor score whose referring domains are mostly obscure sites linking to each other has high relative mass, whatever the headline number says. Checking that a reasonable share of a domain’s link strength comes from sites you recognise as reputable is an informal mass estimate. The Auditing vendor metrics entry shows how much of one vendor’s referring-domain counts comes from a handful of domains that link to almost every listed auction domain. References Gyöngyi, Z., Berkhin, P., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2006). Link spam detection based on mass estimation. VLDB 2006 , 439–450. Gyöngyi, Z., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2004). Combating Web spam with TrustRank. VLDB 2004 , 576–587.

d: The ordinary correlation coefficient computed on positions instead of values. Easy to compute and explain, robust to skewed scores, and like Kendall's tau blind to whether disagreements happen at the top or in the tail.
a: Spearman correlation Spearman rank correlation ρ Rank correlation
x: Spearman’s ρ (rho), introduced by Charles Spearman in 1904, measures how well two rankings agree by computing the familiar Pearson correlation on the items’ positions rather than their values. Replacing values by positions throws away the extreme skew of link metrics, where one domain’s PageRank can be millions of times another’s, and keeps only the order. It is the rank correlation most people meet first, and the one most often reported when two SEO metrics are compared. Definition Replace each score by its position among the items, with tied items sharing the average of their positions (fractional ranking, see Ranks and scores ). Then ρ is the Pearson correlation of the two position vectors and : Without ties this simplifies to a formula in the position differences : ρ is +1 for identical rankings, −1 for reversed ones and near 0 for unrelated ones. Worked example Against PageRank on the running example: Compared with PageRank Spearman ρ Kendall τ_b Harmonic centrality 0.991 0.975 In-degree 0.915 0.866 HITS authority 0.673 0.500 Closeness 0.091 0.100 The ordering of the four comparisons is the same under both statistics, but the numbers differ. That is typical: on the same data |ρ| is usually larger than |τ| for moderate agreement, often by a factor near 1.5. Daniels’ inequality bounds the relation, , but within it the two can diverge. Always say which coefficient you report (see Kendall’s tau ). Spearman against Pearson Pearson’s correlation on raw values would be dominated by the few nodes with huge scores. On Common Crawl’s PageRank, the top domain’s value is 3.7 million times the floor; a Pearson coefficient between PageRank and anything else would mostly measure whether the two agree on a handful of giants. Spearman’s ρ gives every item equal weight, which is the right choice for skewed metrics, and taking logarithms before a Pearson correlation is a reasonable middle ground. On real data On the 119,453 domains from GoDaddy’s 2026-09-23 auction inventory that appear in Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph: Pair Spearman ρ Harmonic centrality and PageRank 0.69 Harmonic centrality and in-degree 0.69 Semrush referring domains and Common Crawl in-degree, all 119,453 0.27 Same, only the 10,045 with at least 6 referring domains in Common Crawl 0.45 The two Common Crawl centralities agree substantially but far from perfectly. The third row looks like a weak relationship between a vendor’s referring-domain count and Common Crawl’s. Most of the vendor’s counts, though, include a floor of around a hundred domains that link to almost every listed domain, which buries the real links of weakly linked domains. Among domains with real links, the fourth row, the correlation is much stronger. The Auditing vendor metrics entry unpacks this. Limits Every position counts equally. A swap at positions 1 and 2 counts the same as a swap at positions 50,000,001 and 50,000,002. Squaring position differences makes large displacements dominant, wherever they occur. For rankings where the top matters, use Weighted tau or Rank-biased overlap . Ties change the answer. Large tied blocks, such as millions of domains at the PageRank floor or with in-degree 1, all receive the same average position, which can raise or lower ρ substantially depending on how the other ranking treats them. Subsets change the answer. ρ computed over all domains, over domains in the graph, or over domains above some threshold can differ widely, as the table above shows. Report the population with the coefficient. No significance by itself. With 100,000 items, even ρ = 0.02 is statistically significant; statistical significance says nothing about whether the agreement is useful. Computing it Sorting both score vectors gives the positions in , and the correlation is one more pass, so ρ is cheaper than Kendall’s τ and trivial to compute even for 120 million items. Tie handling is the only subtlety: assign tied items the mean of the positions they occupy before correlating. References Spearman, C. (1904). The proof and measurement of association between two things. American Journal of Psychology 15(1), 72–101. Daniels, H. E. (1950). Rank correlation and population models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 12(2), 171–191. Kendall, M. G., & Gibbons, J. D. (1990). Rank Correlation Methods (5th ed.). Edward Arnold.

d: Groups of nodes that can all reach each other along links. They decide where a random surfer gets trapped and which nodes a spectral ranking can see.
a: SCC Strong components Condensation Tarjan's algorithm
x: Two nodes are strongly connected when each can reach the other by following links. Strong connection is an equivalence relation: every node is strongly connected to itself, the relation is symmetric by definition, and if and reach each other and and reach each other, so do and . It therefore splits the nodes into disjoint groups, the strongly connected components (SCCs). Inside a component, every node reaches every other; between components, traffic flows one way at most. The running example The running example (see The web graph ) has five SCCs: A B C D E F G The core A → B → C → A (with the shortcut A → C and the return C → A) is the only component with more than one node. D, E, F and G each form a component of their own. A, B and C reach each other, so they form one component. Every other node is a component by itself: D reaches the core but the core never reaches D; G is reached from the core but reaches nothing; E reaches everything and nothing reaches it; F only receives a link. The condensation Shrink each component to a single node and keep one arc between two components whenever some arc joins them. The result is the condensation , and it is always a directed acyclic graph: if two components could reach each other, they would be one component. For the running example: E → D → {A,B,C} → G E → {A,B,C} E → F The condensation shows the large-scale flow of a graph at a glance. Components with no incoming arcs are sources (E); components with no outgoing arcs are sinks (F, G and, at web scale, much larger groups). The The bow-tie structure picture of the web is the condensation viewed from its largest component. Why ranking cares Random surfers get trapped in sink components. A random walk that enters a component with no exits never leaves. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would drain into sinks; the The damping factor exists to pull it back out. Spectral rankings see only part of the graph. Eigenvector centrality gives zero to every node that the dominant component cannot reach. In the running example, D, E and F all get exactly zero, though D and E link into the core. Reachability bounds geometric centralities. A node’s Harmonic centrality counts only the nodes that can reach it. A node in a large component, or downstream of one, has far more candidates to count. Finding the components Two classic algorithms find all SCCs in linear time, : Tarjan’s algorithm (1972) runs one depth-first search. Each node records the order in which the search discovered it and the earliest-discovered node reachable from its subtree that is still on the stack (its low-link ). When a node’s low-link equals its own discovery index, the nodes above it on the stack form a complete component. Kosaraju’s algorithm runs two searches: one on the graph to record finishing order, then one on the transposed graph in reverse finishing order. Each tree of the second search is a component. Both are depth-first, and web graphs have paths millions of nodes long, so a recursive implementation overflows any call stack. Production code keeps an explicit stack. Common Crawl computes its components with the WebGraph framework’s StronglyConnectedComponents , which works directly on the compressed graph. Components in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph splits into 89,324,507 strongly connected components: Statistic Value Domains 119,722,885 Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) Domains outside the largest component 89,503,597 Domains with no out-links (each its own component) 76,352,306 One giant component holds a quarter of all domains. Everything else is shattered: the remaining 89.5 million domains form 89.3 million components, so nearly all of them are single domains. Every domain with no out-links is necessarily a singleton, which accounts for most of the count. A crawl-based graph understates the giant component. The crawler fetched only some of the 76 million domains with no recorded out-links; many of them do link back into the core in reality. Studies of page-level graphs find much larger giant components. Broder and colleagues found 28% of 203 million pages in theirs in 1999, and Meusel and colleagues found about half of 3.5 billion pages in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. Weak components Ignoring arc directions gives weakly connected components : groups linked by any chain of arcs, in either direction. The running example is one weak component. Web graphs typically have one weak component containing almost every node, plus many tiny islands. Weak components are cheap to find with union–find in nearly linear time, and they are the first thing to check when a graph looks wrong: a crawl that produced two large weak components probably mangled its URLs. References Tarjan, R. E. (1972). Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms. SIAM Journal on Computing 1(2), 146–160. Sharir, M. (1981). A strong-connectivity algorithm and its applications in data flow analysis. Computers & Mathematics with Applications 7(1), 67–72. Broder, A., et al. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320. Meusel, R., Vigna, S., Lehmberg, O., & Bizer, C. (2014). Graph structure in the web — revisited. WWW 2014 Companion , 427–432.

d: Majestic's two 0–100 scores. Citation Flow measures link volume and power; Trust Flow measures closeness in the link graph to manually reviewed trusted sites, a TrustRank-style idea. Their ratio is a popular spam heuristic.
a: TF CF Majestic Topical Trust Flow TTF TF/CF ratio
x: Majestic, a link-intelligence company running its own web crawl, publishes two headline scores for every URL and domain. Citation Flow (CF) estimates how much link power a site has, from the number and strength of the sites linking to it. Trust Flow (TF) estimates link quality : sites closely linked to a set of manually reviewed trusted seed sites score higher, and sites with questionable links score lower. The pair maps neatly onto two ideas in this encyclopedia: CF resembles PageRank and TF resembles TrustRank . Definitions Majestic’s glossary describes: Citation Flow: “a score between 0–100 which helps to measure the link equity or ‘power’ the website or link carries.” It predicts how influential a URL might be based on how many sites link to it. Trust Flow: “a score based on quality, on a scale between 0–100.” Sites closely linked to trusted seed sites can see higher scores, whereas sites that have questionable links would see lower scores. Topical Trust Flow: a set of log-scaled 0–100 scores showing a page’s relative influence within topical categories, so that a site can have high trust in, say, health and low trust in finance. Fresh and Historic Index: the Fresh index holds links seen in roughly the last 120 days; the Historic index holds links back to 2006. Scores differ between the two. Majestic does not publish formulas. The descriptions match the classic constructions: CF behaves like a link-volume score with a recursive weighting, TF like trust propagated outward from seeds with decay at each step. The TF/CF ratio Practitioners often divide TF by CF. A ratio near 1 or above suggests that a site’s links come largely from trusted parts of the web; a TF far below CF suggests many links from low-trust sources, the profile of bought or farmed links. The heuristic follows directly from the definitions: a link farm adds citation volume without adding closeness to trusted seeds, exactly as it raises in-degree and PageRank without raising TrustRank. It is a heuristic, not a law: new legitimate sites in niches far from Majestic’s seeds can also show low TF. What the auction data shows GoDaddy’s daily auction inventory includes Majestic fields (Trust Flow, Citation Flow, backlinks and referring domains) for each listed domain. On 2026-09-23, across 1,068,241 domains: Population Majestic referring domains = 0 Trust Flow = 0 All listed domains 82.7% 98.6% Not in Common Crawl’s graph (948,788) 84.1% 99.4% More than 100 referring domains in Common Crawl’s graph (676) 54.6% 66.9% Even among the best-linked domains, ones that more than 100 distinct domains link to in Common Crawl’s crawl, more than half show no Majestic referring domains at all in this feed. Where the fields are populated, they track Common Crawl’s in-degree moderately: among the 31,472 domains in Common Crawl’s graph with nonzero Citation Flow, the Spearman correlation with Common Crawl in-degree is 0.41 for Trust Flow and 0.35 for Citation Flow. These figures describe Majestic’s numbers as delivered in GoDaddy’s feed on one day. They may reflect how GoDaddy obtains or refreshes the data, for instance a particular index or update schedule, rather than gaps in Majestic’s own index; Majestic’s tools may show values where the feed shows zero. The practical point stands for anyone filtering auction lists by these columns: a zero here usually means “no data”, not “no links” (see Auditing vendor metrics ). Reading TF and CF for a domain Check both numbers and their ratio. High CF with very low TF is the classic warning sign. Look at Topical Trust Flow. A domain whose trust lies in a topic unrelated to its name or intended use probably had a different past (see Expired domains ). Distinguish Fresh from Historic. An expired domain’s Historic numbers can be far above its Fresh ones, as old links disappear. Treat zero as unknown when the data comes through a third party, and confirm in Majestic’s own tools or another index. Cross-check against Domain Rating (Ahrefs) , Domain Authority (Moz) and Common Crawl’s open centralities (see Reading a domain’s link metrics ). References Majestic. Glossary (Trust Flow, Citation Flow, Topical Trust Flow, Fresh Index, Historic Index). majestic.com/help/glossary. Gyöngyi, Z., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2004). Combating Web spam with TrustRank. VLDB 2004 , 576–587.

d: Pick a small set of sites a human has checked, and let trust flow outward from them along links, fading with each step. Spam sites, which reputable sites rarely link to, end up with little trust however many links they have.
a: Trust propagation Anti-TrustRank Seed set
x: TrustRank was proposed in 2004 by Zoltán Gyöngyi and Hector Garcia-Molina of Stanford and Jan Pedersen of Yahoo! to separate reputable sites from spam semi-automatically. Its premise is an approximate isolation of good sites: reputable sites rarely link to spam, while spam sites link freely to reputable ones (to look legitimate) and to each other. So start from a set of sites a human has checked, let trust flow along their out-links, and let it fade as it travels. A site many links away from any trusted seed, or reachable only through spam, gets almost no trust. Mathematically, TrustRank is Personalized PageRank with the jumps aimed at the seed set. Definition Let be the set of good seed sites and the uniform distribution over them. The trust vector is with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix and a decay parameter; the paper used and stopped after 20 iterations. Two forms of decay are built in: Dampening. Trust shrinks by a factor with each link it crosses, so a site links from the seeds receives at most of a seed’s trust. Splitting. A site divides its trust among its out-links, so a site that links to thousands of others passes each one very little. This is the same rule PageRank uses, and it means a page full of paid links dilutes whatever trust it has. Choosing the seeds Human review is expensive, so the seed set must be small and must reach as much of the web as possible. The authors ranked sites by inverse PageRank , PageRank computed on the graph with every link reversed, which favours sites whose out-links reach many sites quickly. They reviewed the top candidates by hand, discarded spam and unclear cases, and kept a good seed set of fewer than 200 sites from an index of about 31 million. On AltaVista’s 2003 data, ranking by trust pushed spam sites far down compared with ordinary PageRank. Inverse PageRank on the running example ranks E first (0.282): it reaches every other node in at most three steps, so it would make the best single seed. Out-link reach is also what CheiRank and 2DRank measures. Worked example Seed the running example with A alone: Node A C B G D E F TrustRank, seed {A} 0.393 0.309 0.167 0.131 0 0 0 Ordinary PageRank 0.205 0.298 0.138 0.177 0.065 0.051 0.065 D, E and F get exactly zero trust: no path leads from A to them. G, reached through C, gets about two-fifths of C’s trust. Under ordinary PageRank, D, E and F score above zero thanks to teleportation, which hands every site the same baseline whether or not anyone vouches for it. TrustRank removes that baseline: trust comes only from the seeds. Weaknesses Seed bias. Trust concentrates around the seeds. Good sites in communities the seeds do not reach, such as other languages, small countries or niche topics, get little trust and look as suspicious as spam. Larger and more diverse seed sets help; topic-specific seed sets help more. Good sites do link to spam. Comment sections, forums, user profiles and hacked pages put links to spam on reputable domains. Trust leaks through them, which is one reason Google introduced nofollow in 2005 (see Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) ). Trust is not distrust. A low TrustRank means “not vouched for”, not “spam”. New legitimate sites start with no trust at all. Anti-TrustRank Krishnan and Raj (2006) ran the idea in reverse. Start from a set of known spam sites and propagate distrust backwards along in-links: a site that links to spam is probably spam, or at least careless. The computation is TrustRank on the transposed graph with a spam seed set. Combining the two scores separates more spam than either alone. TrustRank and the SEO industry The paper left a lasting mark on how practitioners talk about links. “Trust” and “distance from trusted seeds” became common vocabulary, and commercial metrics borrowed the idea. Majestic describes its Trust Flow as a score based on how closely a site links to manually reviewed trusted seed sites ( Trust Flow and Citation Flow (Majestic) ). Ahrefs and Moz do not describe seed-based trust in their headline metrics, which rest on link quantity and the strength of the linking domains ( Domain Rating (Ahrefs) , Domain Authority (Moz) ). Whatever Google does internally is not public. The safe reading for a domain buyer: links from sites that reputable sites themselves link to are worth far more than links from sites only spam links to, and no amount of the second kind substitutes for a few of the first. Spam mass turns that intuition into a number. References Gyöngyi, Z., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2004). Combating Web spam with TrustRank. VLDB 2004 , 576–587. Krishnan, V., & Raj, R. (2006). Web spam detection with Anti-TrustRank. AIRWeb 2006 . Gyöngyi, Z., & Garcia-Molina, H. (2005). Web spam taxonomy. AIRWeb 2005 .

d: The directed graph with a node for every page, host or domain and an arc for every hyperlink between them.
a: Link graph Hyperlink graph Webgraph
x: The web graph turns the web into mathematics. Each node stands for a unit of the web: a page, a host or a whole domain. Each arc stands for a hyperlink: an arc from to says that contains a link pointing at . Once the web is a graph, questions like “which site matters most?” or “how far apart are two sites?” become questions about paths and walks that an algorithm can answer. Nodes and arcs Write the graph as , with nodes and arcs. The arcs are directed : a link from to says nothing about a link back. Most link graphs also simplify the raw data in two ways: Parallel links collapse. A page that links to the same target ten times contributes one arc, not ten. At the domain level, a million links from one domain to another still make one arc. Self-loops vanish. Links from a node to itself, such as a site’s navigation menu linking to its own home page, say nothing about how the rest of the web sees it. Common Crawl’s domain graph contains no loops at all. The out-degree counts the arcs leaving and the in-degree counts the arcs arriving at . Every arc adds one to an out-degree and one to an in-degree, so both degrees average to . The Degree entry covers them in detail. A B C D E F G The running example as a web graph. Ten arcs connect seven sites. A link from E to D does not imply one from D to E. Why direction matters The two ends of a link are not equal. A site’s owner decides what the site links to , so out-links are cheap and fully under the owner’s control. Who links to a site depends on thousands of other people. That asymmetry is the reason almost every ranking method in this encyclopedia scores a node by what points at it: PageRank , Harmonic centrality , HITS (hubs and authorities) authorities, and plain in-degree. It is also why Link spam targets in-links. A spammer cannot easily make popular sites link to them, so they manufacture sites that do. Ignoring direction throws this information away. In an undirected version of the running example, F (linked only from E) looks exactly like a site that links only to E, though the two play opposite roles. How a crawler builds the graph Nobody holds a complete copy of the web, so every web graph is a sample built by a crawler: Fetch a page and extract every href in it. Resolve relative URLs against the page’s address and normalise them (lower-case host names, drop fragments). Map each URL to a node. A page graph keeps the full URL, a host graph keeps the host name, and a domain graph keeps the registered domain. See Page, host and domain graphs . Drop duplicates and self-loops, and add the remaining arcs. The sample is lopsided. A crawler learns the out-links of the pages it fetched, but it learns about many more pages only as link targets. Those pages enter the graph with in-links and no out-links. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, 76,352,306 of the 119,722,885 domains (63.8%) have no outgoing arcs. Most of them are sites the crawl never fetched, not sites that truly link nowhere. The Dangling nodes entry explains how ranking methods cope. The size of a real web graph Common Crawl’s domain-level graph for June to August 2026 ( cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug ) gives a sense of scale: Quantity Value Domains (nodes) 119,722,885 Domain-to-domain links (arcs) 2,450,405,793 Average in-degree and out-degree 20.47 Largest in-degree 17,119,122 ( googleapis.com ) Largest out-degree 6,113,126 ( mp3fresh.net ) Domains with no out-links 76,352,306 (63.8%) Domains with no in-links 14,903,407 (12.4%) Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest strongly connected component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) The average hides enormous variation. More than half of all domains (56%) have in-degree 0 or 1, while 45 domains receive links from more than a million other domains each. The Degree distributions and power laws entry shows the full distribution. The Strongly connected components and The bow-tie structure entries explain the last two rows. Stored naively as pairs of 32-bit integers, those 2.45 billion arcs take 19.6 GB. The WebGraph compression entry shows how the WebGraph framework stores the same graph in 4.6 GB, about 15 bits per link, and still answers “who does this domain link to?” quickly. What the graph leaves out A link graph keeps only the fact that one node links to another. It drops: Where the link sits : a footer link and a link in the body of an article become identical arcs. The words of the link : see Anchor text . The link’s attributes : whether a crawler records nofollow , sponsored and ugc links depends on the pipeline. See Link attributes (nofollow, sponsored, ugc) . Time : a graph is a snapshot. Links appear and disappear, and an expired domain can keep in-links for years after its site is gone. Each omission is a design choice, and each one changes what the rankings built on the graph mean. Commercial link indexes make different choices from Common Crawl’s, which explains some of the disagreement between their metrics (see Auditing vendor metrics ). References Broder, A., Kumar, R., Maghoul, F., Raghavan, P., Rajagopalan, S., Stata, R., Tomkins, A., & Wiener, J. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320. Kleinberg, J. M., Kumar, R., Raghavan, P., Rajagopalan, S., & Tomkins, A. S. (1999). The Web as a graph: measurements, models, and methods. COCOON 1999 , LNCS 1627, 1–17. Meusel, R., Vigna, S., Lehmberg, O., & Bizer, C. (2014). Graph structure in the web — revisited. WWW 2014 Companion , 427–432.

d: How the WebGraph framework stores billions of links in a few bits each, using sorted gaps, copying from similar neighbours, runs of consecutive ids and codes tuned to power laws, while still decoding any node's links quickly.
a: BVGraph WebGraph framework Graph compression Zeta codes Reference compression
x: A web graph is mostly a list of integers: for each node, the ids of the nodes it links to. Stored plainly as 32-bit integers, Common Crawl’s 2.45 billion domain links take 9.8 GB, plus offsets. Paolo Boldi and Sebastiano Vigna’s WebGraph framework, first described in 2004, stores the same graph in 4.6 GB, about 15 bits per link, and page-level crawls in 2 to 3 bits per link, while still letting a program read any node’s successors without decompressing the rest. Common Crawl distributes its graphs in WebGraph’s BVGraph format, and the LAW tools that compute its PageRank and harmonic centrality read that format directly. The structure it exploits Boldi and Vigna built on observations by Randall and colleagues about real link lists: Locality. With nodes numbered in a sensible order, such as by reversed host name (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ), most links point to nodes with nearby ids, especially links within a site. Similarity. Nodes with nearby ids often have nearly the same successor lists: pages of one site share navigation links. Consecutivity. Successor lists often contain runs of consecutive ids, such as a page linking to all pages of a section. Skewed gaps. Differences between consecutive successors follow a heavy-tailed distribution: small gaps are very common, large gaps rare but present. The techniques Gap encoding. Each successor list is sorted. The first successor is stored relative to the node’s own id, and every later one as the gap from its predecessor. Small numbers need few bits. Reference compression. A node may name one of the previous nodes (the window ) as a reference and copy part of its list. Copy blocks, alternating runs of “copy” and “skip”, say which of the reference’s successors to keep; only the remaining extra successors are stored. A limit on reference chains ( maxrefcount ) bounds how many lists must be decoded to recover one. Intervals. Among the extra successors, runs of at least minintervallength consecutive ids are stored as a left end and a length. Residuals. Whatever is left is stored as gaps, using ζ codes . A code is designed for integers following a power law with exponent near ; Boldi and Vigna introduced the family because residual gaps on web graphs fit it better than Elias γ or δ codes. Instantaneous codes and offsets. Every number uses a prefix-free code, so lists decode bit by bit without lookahead. A separate offsets structure (Elias–Fano coded in current versions) records where each node’s bits start, which gives random access. The Common Crawl domain graph, bit by bit The .properties file that ships with cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug-domain.graph records the parameters and where the bits go: Quantity Value Nodes / arcs 119,722,885 / 2,450,405,793 Window , maximum reference chain, minimum interval 7, 3, 4 Residual code Bits per link 15.11 Arcs copied from a reference 213,946,881 (8.7%) Arcs stored in intervals 39,703,731 (1.6%) Arcs stored as residuals 2,196,755,181 (89.6%) Share of all bits spent on residuals 96.7% Average log₂ of a residual gap 11.1 The file is 4,627,056,342 bytes; the transposed graph, needed for in-links, is the same size again. Copying and intervals do little here. Nearly 90% of arcs end up as residuals, with gaps averaging around , so each costs about 15 bits. That is the price of a domain graph. Domain-level folding removes all links inside a site (see Page, host and domain graphs ), which are exactly the local, similar, consecutive links that make page graphs compress to 2 or 3 bits per link. What remains are links between unrelated domains spread across the whole id space. Fifteen bits per link is still a 2.1-fold saving over 32-bit integers. Performance Compression would be useless if decoding were slow. WebGraph decodes successors sequentially at rates of tens of millions of links per second per core, and random access to one node costs decoding at most a bounded chain of reference lists. Algorithms that scan the whole graph in id order, such as one pass of PageRank or one round of HyperBall , read the compressed file sequentially, often memory-mapped, and pay little for decompression compared with the memory bandwidth they save. A 4.6 GB graph fits in the RAM of a workstation, where 19.6 GB of raw pairs might not. Ordering matters most The single biggest factor in compression is the order of node ids. Lexicographic URL order made the original results possible. Later work found orders that cluster nodes by link structure rather than by name, and for social networks, which have no URL order at all, the choice is decisive. The Node orderings entry covers layered label propagation and its relatives, which compress many web graphs noticeably better than name order and social networks far better than any naive order. Beyond WebGraph k²-trees (Brisaboa, Ladra and Navarro) store the adjacency matrix as a quadtree of nonempty blocks, supporting both successor and predecessor queries from one structure. Log(Graph) and other recent work compress graphs for parallel processing with bit-level encodings tuned to modern hardware. CSR with 32-bit ids remains the baseline for in-memory analytics when space is available, because it decodes nothing (see Adjacency matrices and lists ). References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004). The WebGraph Framework I: Compression techniques. WWW 2004 , 595–602. Randall, K. H., Stata, R., Wiener, J. L., & Wickremesinghe, R. G. (2002). The Link Database: Fast access to graphs of the Web. For rankings, that is the wrong default: a search engine that swaps its first two results has made a more visible change than one that swaps positions 50,000,001 and 50,000,002. When to use it Use weighted τ when comparing two full rankings where the top matters most and ties are common: two centralities on the same graph, two crawls’ PageRank, or a vendor score against an open one.
